paragraphs.text: But even this was not enough. The divinity in human beings, and their humanity, must be spread outwards to all the different corners of the universe. Exceeding the margins of all horizons, they will have to rush beyond the nebulae and stars, transcending the confines of the milky ways towards the limitless boundary of the universe. On the one hand, this path is beautiful, yet on the other hand it is full of struggles – a benevolent path but certainly not strewn with flowers. This is the greater humanity (mahámánava) or Neohumanism. This is the highest fulfilment of life and living. This is to be achieved through an all-out struggle against evil forces. This complete manifestation of Parama Puruśa, this complete development of Táraka Brahma, is the Kalki bháva of Viśńu. ( 2 )
summary: But even this was not enough.
This is the greater humanity (mahámánava) or Neohumanism.
This complete manifestation of Parama Puruśa, this complete development of Táraka Brahma, is the Kalki bháva of Viśńu.

paragraphs.text: Birds and Animals, Our Neighbours [a compilation]
summary: Birds and Animals, Our Neighbours [a compilation]

footnotes.text: Each of the ten verses of this poem refers to a different one of the many Puranic, or mythological stories universally known in India. By tying them together in the appropriate order, the poet depicts in a vivid way the process of animate evolution – biological, sociological, psychic and spiritual.
Shabda Cayaniká Part 9, Discourse 60.

chapters.title: Fissiparous Creatures, Krami-Krimi, Microvita and Worms

paragraphs.text: Upon elementary analysis, living beings in the earliest stage were fissiparous by nature and split themselves from one into many. On this earth there are many such protozoa, and their bodies are constituted of one or multiple cells of the same nature; if their bodies somehow become split into two, those parts become two separate beings. If it is a unicellular creature, at the time of division the nucleus of the main cell is also split into two, and the two cells are transformed to have two separate nuclei. At the primitive stage of creation the multiplication of creatures took place in this very manner. Then came the oviparous creatures and the mammals. ( 1 )
summary: Upon elementary analysis, living beings in the earliest stage were fissiparous by nature and split themselves from one into many.
If it is a unicellular creature, at the time of division the nucleus of the main cell is also split into two, and the two cells are transformed to have two separate nuclei.
Then came the oviparous creatures and the mammals.

paragraphs.text: The words krami or krimi are derived from the root verb kram with the suffix i. Both mean the same thing. Krimi do not always remain in the same form. The form they have at the time of their birth undergoes a radical change. The changes in their form and size take place stage by stage. These stages of metamorphosis are not the same in all cases. Those which are unicellular divide their nuclei and multiply into two or more. Unicellular creatures have no sex difference, and thus there is no distinction between ovum and spermatozoa. These are creatures of primordial stage of creation in this expressed world. But all the creatures of this group are not of the same type – some are born from eggs, subsequently taking the form of larvae which undergo external metamorphosis and acquire their final forms as flying creatures. As they have an orderly growth divided into subsequent stages, they are called krimi in Sanskrit [the Sanskrit krama = “order”].
summary: The words krami or krimi are derived from the root verb kram with the suffix i.
These stages of metamorphosis are not the same in all cases.
As they have an orderly growth divided into subsequent stages, they are called krimi in Sanskrit [the Sanskrit krama = “order”].

paragraphs.text: It is worth mentioning that microvita ( 2 ) do not belong to the category of krimi. Like krimi and all other organic and psychic beings, microvita exist, multiply and die. However, unlike krimi and other organic and psychic beings, they are not directly related to carbon atoms or carbon molecules.
summary: It is worth mentioning that microvita ( 2 ) do not belong to the category of krimi.
Like krimi and all other organic and psychic beings, microvita exist, multiply and die.
However, unlike krimi and other organic and psychic beings, they are not directly related to carbon atoms or carbon molecules.

paragraphs.text: Pollution control: Krimi can only survive in certain temperatures and under specific barometric conditions. If there is an extreme temperature or air pressure variation, they will perish. But the jurisdiction of microvita is far greater than that – they are not subjected to barometric conditions. Krimi live, grow and decay within the scope of the five fundamental factors, whereas the cruder variety of microvita function within the realm of the five inferences. Due to adverse temperatures and barometric conditions, no creature can go to other planets under normal conditions. Unicellular creatures, however, have some advantages in this regard. Depending upon their shape and size, krimi can live in stones or any other solid matter, but they normally remain in water and other subtle fundamental factors. For this reason, human beings must ensure that their water and air remain pure. The purity of the soil should never be neglected. As a result of air and water pollution, the number of these varieties of krimi – particularly disease-carrying germs and bacteria – is constantly increasing and getting beyond the control of human beings. The use of pesticides and germicides may be increased, but if the noumenal cause for disease is not found, and if the degree of pollution continues to increase at the same speed as at present, a day is sure to come when the polluted earth, water and air will be the cause of the collective death of humanity.
summary: Pollution control: Krimi can only survive in certain temperatures and under specific barometric conditions.
Unicellular creatures, however, have some advantages in this regard.

The use of pesticides and germicides may be increased, but if the noumenal cause for disease is not found, and if the degree of pollution continues to increase at the same speed as at present, a day is sure to come when the polluted earth, water and air will be the cause of the collective death of humanity.

paragraphs.text: Microvita have no direct relationship to pollution; however they do have an indirect relationship. Even if the earth, air and water are not polluted, microvita will still be produced. Microvita of subtler and subtlest varieties may function within the scope of the crude mind-stuff (kámamaya kośa). Collective good thoughts can check the flow of negative microvita. For this, mental and physical development is indispensable in collective life.
summary: Microvita have no direct relationship to pollution; however they do have an indirect relationship.
Microvita of subtler and subtlest varieties may function within the scope of the crude mind-stuff (kámamaya kośa).
For this, mental and physical development is indispensable in collective life.

paragraphs.text: Intellectually and spiritually advanced people, through their thoughts, can destroy or resist the movement of enemy microvita, but if sinful people continue to create newer and newer microvita in their psychic sphere, there will always remain the possibility of creation of subtler forms of [negative] microvita. These microvita can cause immense harm in the collective sphere, not only on different planets but in the entire Cosmos. However, not all microvita are the enemies of human beings – some are inimical, some are friendly and some are neutral. Similarly, some krimi are inimical, some are friendly and some are neutral.
summary: Intellectually and spiritually advanced people, through their thoughts, can destroy or resist the movement of enemy microvita, but if sinful people continue to create newer and newer microvita in their psychic sphere, there will always remain the possibility of creation of subtler forms of [negative] microvita.
However, not all microvita are the enemies of human beings – some are inimical, some are friendly and some are neutral.
Similarly, some krimi are inimical, some are friendly and some are neutral.

paragraphs.text: I have already said that most kramis (worms and viruses) were born in water. Most viruses and bacteria are born in water and are water-borne. Worms of the stomach (in Bengali they are called krimi: both krami and krimi are etymologically correct), worms of the blood (hookworms) and guinea worms are further examples. Just as in the case of microvita, they are not all enemies of humanity – some are inimical, some are friendly, and some are indifferent. Kramis are also similar – some are inimical, some are friendly and some are indifferent.
summary: I have already said that most kramis (worms and viruses) were born in water.
Worms of the stomach (in Bengali they are called krimi: both krami and krimi are etymologically correct), worms of the blood (hookworms) and guinea worms are further examples.
Kramis are also similar – some are inimical, some are friendly and some are indifferent.

paragraphs.text: Friendly kramis and curd: The microvita that transform milk into curd [yoghurt] through the acidic coagulator are not normally inimical to humans. For about forty-eight hours, these microvita remain in positive form. But if curd remains exposed to heat for more than forty-eight hours, then the positive microvita decompose and change into negative microvita. This is why curd can be eaten for up to forty-eight hours after it has become ready for human consumption. Later, when the curd emits a rancid smell, it is unfit for human consumption because it is infested with negative microvita. As long as there are positive microvita in curd, it is more useful and nutritious than milk. In curd (whether sweetened or sour) if salt is added, the adverse effect of the dead worms is somewhat mitigated. That is why “Curd should always be consumed with salt.” ( 3 ) I have already pointed out that both the word krami and the word krimi are in use. The word krimi is more in use in Bengali. There is nothing incorrect in using this word. ( 4 )
summary: Friendly kramis and curd: The microvita that transform milk into curd [yoghurt] through the acidic coagulator are not normally inimical to humans.
As long as there are positive microvita in curd, it is more useful and nutritious than milk.
There is nothing incorrect in using this word.

paragraphs.text: Earthworm: A keṋco/kaiṋcukii/mahiilatá (earthworm) builds a house of earth and creates a shade and a cover with the help of the earth on its body. So one name of keṋco is mahiilatá [mahii means “earth”], and an earthworm is also called kuiṋja. In some parts of eastern India an earthworm is called cerá, and in some parts, joṋk. The regions where an earthworm is called joṋk, the actual joṋk, the blood-sucking joṋk (jalaoká > jalauká > jaloká [joṋk, leech]), is called bhaesá-joṋk. A cluster of earthworms is collectively described as kuiṋja.
summary: Earthworm: A keṋco/kaiṋcukii/mahiilatá (earthworm) builds a house of earth and creates a shade and a cover with the help of the earth on its body.
In some parts of eastern India an earthworm is called cerá, and in some parts, joṋk.
A cluster of earthworms is collectively described as kuiṋja.

paragraphs.text: You must have seen a centipede. This small creature born out of the earth or dwelling in the earth is called kenno in the dialect of Kolkata. In Hooghly region it is called kennui; in Burdwan, kyándái. In some parts of Midnapore I have heard it called kyáṋdrái. This centipede is also called kuiṋja. The word kuiṋja has degenerated into kenno. ( 5 )
summary: You must have seen a centipede.
In some parts of Midnapore I have heard it called kyáṋdrái.
The word kuiṋja has degenerated into kenno.

paragraphs.text: Birds and Animals, Our Neighbours [a compilation]
summary: Birds and Animals, Our Neighbours [a compilation]

footnotes.text: The foregoing paragraph is from Shabda Cayaniká Part 20, Discourse 163.

“There are entities which come within the realm of both physicality and psychic expressions which are smaller or subtler than atoms, electrons or protons, and in the psychic realm may be subtler than ectoplasm. For such objects or for such entities, I use the term “microvitum”. So far as physicality is concerned, the position of these microvita is just between ectoplasm and electron, but they are neither ectoplasm nor electron. Now, these microvita are not of the same density or the same subtlety. Some of them may come within the range of a highly developed microscope; and some of them may not come within the range of a microscope. There may be still more subtle forms of microvita which may not come directly within the scope of our perception but may come within the scope of a special type of perception. Regarding these microvita of crude order which may come within the scope of a microscope, people give them the name “virus”. But virus is a vague term. The better term will be microvitum, and not virus. Now, these microvita move throughout the entire universe, from one celestial body to another. They move unbarred, without caring for the atmospheric conditions or barometric readings. They move through sound. They may move through tactuality, through the smell, and in the case of subtler microvita, they may move through ideas. Now, what is the root cause of this universe? Which is the starting point of life or vitality? These microvita are the carriers of life in different stars, planets and satellites – not carbon atoms or carbon molecules. So the root cause of life is not the unicellular protozoa or unit protoplasmic cell, but this unit microvitum. Now, there should be extensive research work regarding this microvitum or these microvita. (Shrii Prabhat Ranjan Sarkar, “Microvitum – the Mysterious Emanation of the Cosmic Factor” in Microvitum in a Nutshell) –Trans.
Dadhi labańena saha bhakśayet. –Trans.
The foregoing two paragraphs are from Shabda Cayaniká Part 10, Discourse 66.
The foregoing seven paragraphs are from Shabda Cayaniká Part 4, Discourse 27.

paragraphs.text: In the world of living creatures, those beings which are hatched from eggs we call ańd́aj [omniparous]. This ańd́a is conceptually analogous to the brahmáńd́a [the created universe, literally “the cosmic egg”]; they are small editions of the brahmáńd́a. The Sanskrit-derived form of the word ańd́a, ańd́á ( 1 ) is prevalent throughout North India.
summary: In the world of living creatures, those beings which are hatched from eggs we call ańd́aj [omniparous].
This ańd́a is conceptually analogous to the brahmáńd́a [the created universe, literally “the cosmic egg”]; they are small editions of the brahmáńd́a.
The Sanskrit-derived form of the word ańd́a, ańd́á ( 1 ) is prevalent throughout North India.

paragraphs.text: It is not possible for creatures of the reptile class, that is, those who move by supporting themselves on their chest or ribcage, to carry a developed foetus in the womb. For this reason they carry eggs in their wombs. Although birds are technically not reptiles, when they fly they use their wings to cut through the air, thereby putting a great deal of pressure on their chest. Due to this, it is also not possible for them to carry a developed foetus in the womb, and so they also carry and lay eggs.
summary: It is not possible for creatures of the reptile class, that is, those who move by supporting themselves on their chest or ribcage, to carry a developed foetus in the womb.
Although birds are technically not reptiles, when they fly they use their wings to cut through the air, thereby putting a great deal of pressure on their chest.
Due to this, it is also not possible for them to carry a developed foetus in the womb, and so they also carry and lay eggs.

paragraphs.text: Once an egg is laid, the embryo starts developing under the impetus provided by the eggʼs contact with air, light, and heat from the environment. When the developing foetus is fully mobile, it pierces its shell and emerges into the outside world where it needs more heat than is normally present in the environment; so the mother bird or mother reptile helps the foetus develop by supplying it warmth from her own body. Of course, not all creatures hatched from eggs require this extra heat. In such cases, the mother abandons the egg once it is laid. In accordance with natureʼs law, it does not feel any instinctive affection for the egg. For those eggs which require extra heat, however, it is the law of nature that the mother feels an instinctive affection for the egg. If someone comes and takes the egg, she will often chase after them.
summary: Once an egg is laid, the embryo starts developing under the impetus provided by the eggʼs contact with air, light, and heat from the environment.
In such cases, the mother abandons the egg once it is laid.
If someone comes and takes the egg, she will often chase after them.

paragraphs.text: Because egg-producing creatures need their chest and ribs for labour, it is not possible for them to breast-feed their offspring. Thus oviparous creatures do not produce breast milk; this is natural law. Exceptions to this can be found in certain creatures from an earlier era when reptiles were making the transition to non-reptiles and becoming creatures that moved by means of their hands and feet. During that time some creatures were in an intermediate stage; for several hundred thousand years they continued to lay eggs, but at the same time they used to breast-feed their offspring in small amounts. Later, when they stopped laying eggs and started bearing their young, the amount of milk they fed their offspring increased.
summary: Because egg-producing creatures need their chest and ribs for labour, it is not possible for them to breast-feed their offspring.
Exceptions to this can be found in certain creatures from an earlier era when reptiles were making the transition to non-reptiles and becoming creatures that moved by means of their hands and feet.
Later, when they stopped laying eggs and started bearing their young, the amount of milk they fed their offspring increased.

paragraphs.text: Among the creatures we are familiar with, the cow family produces the greatest amount of milk for their offspring. They are also comparatively more intelligent than other creatures, and they show more affection for their offspring. Interestingly, they cannot run very swiftly, while the deer group, which produces very little milk and shows less affection for their offspring, can run extremely fast. The antelope family (bharal or niilgái, alpaca and black antelope) falls somewhere in between the deer and cow families in all respects, including their size, their horns, their tails, and even their excretory systems.
summary: Among the creatures we are familiar with, the cow family produces the greatest amount of milk for their offspring.
Interestingly, they cannot run very swiftly, while the deer group, which produces very little milk and shows less affection for their offspring, can run extremely fast.

The antelope family (bharal or niilgái, alpaca and black antelope) falls somewhere in between the deer and cow families in all respects, including their size, their horns, their tails, and even their excretory systems.

paragraphs.text: Bear in mind that while the word niilgái is similar to gái [cow], it is not a member of the cow family, nor is it a member of the deer family. It belongs to the antelope family. We often make the mistake of thinking that certain animals are either in the cow family or in the deer family, when actually they are part of the antelope family. We can use the word go-hariń [cow-deer] for the antelope family.
summary: Bear in mind that while the word niilgái is similar to gái [cow], it is not a member of the cow family, nor is it a member of the deer family.
We often make the mistake of thinking that certain animals are either in the cow family or in the deer family, when actually they are part of the antelope family.
We can use the word go-hariń [cow-deer] for the antelope family.

paragraphs.text: That rare member of the cat family known as the duckbill (platypus), which is found in Southeast Asia and certain parts of Australia, is a nearly extinct, prehistoric creature. Although this fast-disappearing creature lays eggs, it also breastfeeds its offspring. Because it uses its chest area more for locomotion and other activities in comparison with other milk-producing creatures, it continues to lay eggs. But in comparison with reptiles and birds, it uses its chest less, and so it can still breastfeed its children. Proper efforts should be made to save the duckbill (platypus) from extinction.
summary: That rare member of the cat family known as the duckbill (platypus), which is found in Southeast Asia and certain parts of Australia, is a nearly extinct, prehistoric creature.
Because it uses its chest area more for locomotion and other activities in comparison with other milk-producing creatures, it continues to lay eggs.
Proper efforts should be made to save the duckbill (platypus) from extinction.

paragraphs.text: Among the aquatic creatures, fish are oviparous; the reason being that the way fish move through water is somewhat similar to the way reptiles slither along the ground or the way birds move through the air. Thus in the broader sense, they can also be considered reptiles. They also use their chest and ribs a great deal and so are unable to carry developed offspring ( 2 ) in their womb or breastfeed their young. Thus, according to the law of nature they produce eggs.
summary: Among the aquatic creatures, fish are oviparous; the reason being that the way fish move through water is somewhat similar to the way reptiles slither along the ground or the way birds move through the air.
They also use their chest and ribs a great deal and so are unable to carry developed offspring ( 2 ) in their womb or breastfeed their young.
Thus, according to the law of nature they produce eggs.

paragraphs.text: There are other aquatic creatures, such as whales, seals and walruses, which use their chests and ribs less in their movements than fish do. Most probably the whale was also once a land animal like the dolphin. Later, under the pressure of circumstances, they took to the water. Like the hilsa and the shark, they are not ancient aquatic creatures. Although they live in water, they are not a fish species. To call a whale a fish is a gross error. Therefore, such creatures bear their young, breastfeed their offspring and, according to natural law, have more affection for their progeny.
summary: There are other aquatic creatures, such as whales, seals and walruses, which use their chests and ribs less in their movements than fish do.
Like the hilsa and the shark, they are not ancient aquatic creatures.
Therefore, such creatures bear their young, breastfeed their offspring and, according to natural law, have more affection for their progeny.

paragraphs.text: In other words, we see that those egg-producing creatures which do not incubate their eggs also show no affection towards them. Those that incubate their eggs show comparatively more affection, and those creatures that bear their young as well as breastfeed them will in certain cases not even stop at sacrificing their lives for their offspring.
summary: In other words, we see that those egg-producing creatures which do not incubate their eggs also show no affection towards them.

Those that incubate their eggs show comparatively more affection, and those creatures that bear their young as well as breastfeed them will in certain cases not even stop at sacrificing their lives for their offspring.

paragraphs.text: The crocodile is a land reptile – an ancient species from the Cretaceous Age. Generally speaking, all members of this family are terrestrial by nature, and all are egg-producing. The crocodile, fish-eating crocodile (mecho-kumiir), iguana (gosáp; in Sanskrit, godhá or godhiká; in indigenous Bengali, goháŕgil, goh, gosáp), girgit́i [a type of lizard], t́ikt́iki [a small house lizard], takśaka [a venomous snake] (the word guisáp is used in East Bengal), áiṋjuni [also a type of lizard] – all these egg-producing creatures have a similar nature; they differ only in their level of cruelty. The man-eating crocodile is extremely ferocious. The rest of these creatures are also ferocious with the exception to some extent of the iguana, which, despite being a meat-eater, has a somewhat timid nature. When they see people, they will flee if they have some place to run. The Indian iguana is predominantly of two types: the black iguana and the golden iguana, both of which share this timid nature.
summary: The crocodile is a land reptile – an ancient species from the Cretaceous Age.
The man-eating crocodile is extremely ferocious.
The Indian iguana is predominantly of two types: the black iguana and the golden iguana, both of which share this timid nature.

paragraphs.text: While it is true that the otter (in Sanskrit, udbiŕála) goes into the water to catch fish, it is a land animal like the crocodile. Otters live near ponds or other water reservoirs, and they are milk-producing, not egg-producing. The Bengali otter is somewhat smaller than the South American otter, but it is more active and highly intelligent. Because it is a milk-producing creature and not egg-producing, according to the law of nature, it is relatively keen-witted.
summary: While it is true that the otter (in Sanskrit, udbiŕála) goes into the water to catch fish, it is a land animal like the crocodile.
The Bengali otter is somewhat smaller than the South American otter, but it is more active and highly intelligent.
Because it is a milk-producing creature and not egg-producing, according to the law of nature, it is relatively keen-witted.

paragraphs.text: Normally we observe that the young of any species are not fully developed at the time of birth. Whether human, dog or cat, all are born in a helpless state, unable to hear or see. This helpless state is even more pronounced in egg-producing creatures. When tadpoles are hatched, they cannot move properly. They need a tail in order to adjust with their environment. After adapting to their environment, the tail falls off. From this we can deduce that the ancestors of the frog had tails. ( 3 )
summary: Normally we observe that the young of any species are not fully developed at the time of birth.
When tadpoles are hatched, they cannot move properly.
From this we can deduce that the ancestors of the frog had tails.

paragraphs.text: However undeveloped milk-producing animals may be, egg-producing animals are even more so; by comparison they also show significantly less affection as well as other sentiments. Many do not even recognize their own children; those who do not hatch their eggs feel little or no affection and tend to be much more malicious by nature. Crocodiles become extremely vicious at a very young age.
summary: However undeveloped milk-producing animals may be, egg-producing animals are even more so; by comparison they also show significantly less affection as well as other sentiments.
Many do not even recognize their own children; those who do not hatch their eggs feel little or no affection and tend to be much more malicious by nature.
Crocodiles become extremely vicious at a very young age.

paragraphs.text: Another characteristic of the egg-producing animals is that some of them, such as the shark and hilsa fish, are completely carnivorous, while you will not find a single, completely carnivorous, milk-producing animal. Tigers may not eat uncooked rice but they will eat cooked rice or bread; they may not eat raw vegetables but they will eat them if they are cooked, while the shark, hilsa fish, vulture and certain hawks and owls (especially the white lakśmii owl) are extremely carnivorous.
summary: Another characteristic of the egg-producing animals is that some of them, such as the shark and hilsa fish, are completely carnivorous, while you will not find a single, completely carnivorous, milk-producing animal.

Tigers may not eat uncooked rice but they will eat cooked rice or bread; they may not eat raw vegetables but they will eat them if they are cooked, while the shark, hilsa fish, vulture and certain hawks and owls (especially the white lakśmii owl) are extremely carnivorous.

paragraphs.text: Another characteristic of the carnivorous, egg-producing animals is that their bodies have a high fat content and give off a strong odour. Those who are familiar with the hilsa fish know how strong a fish smell it has. The reason for this is that the hilsa prefers rotten meat to fresh meat. The shark is the same way. It also has a very strong fish-smell. People who eat shark often remark that it is similar to hilsa. It also has a high fat content. In fact, shark oil is used as a medicine (bear in mind that the shark is a fish, not a crustacean like crab or shrimp). The vultureʼs nature is quite similar. It prefers decomposed flesh to fresh meat.
summary: Another characteristic of the carnivorous, egg-producing animals is that their bodies have a high fat content and give off a strong odour.
People who eat shark often remark that it is similar to hilsa.
It prefers decomposed flesh to fresh meat.

paragraphs.text: It is worth mentioning again that such egg-producing creatures do not, for all intents and purposes, feel affection. Many do not even recognize their own children, and some of them eat their own eggs.
summary: It is worth mentioning again that such egg-producing creatures do not, for all intents and purposes, feel affection.
Many do not even recognize their own children, and some of them eat their own eggs.

paragraphs.text: Before the foetus is created, milk-producing animals produce an ovum in the motherʼs womb. Rather than producing an egg, however, a foetus develops. In the world of egg-producing creatures, especially birds, there are exceptions to this. Some of them can produce unfertilized eggs. Particularly some varieties of ducks lay unfertilized eggs frequently. With such eggs there is no possibility of offspring, even if they are incubated. Commonly such eggs take longer to spoil. Many people, who have a weakness for eggs but do not want to harm a living embryo, are partial to taking unfertilized eggs; they contend that this way they are not killing a foetus. They should keep in mind that while it is true that they are not killing a foetus, they are still at fault for taking non-vegetarian food, because these unfertilized eggs still contain the defects of non-vegetarian food.
summary: Before the foetus is created, milk-producing animals produce an ovum in the motherʼs womb.
Particularly some varieties of ducks lay unfertilized eggs frequently.

They should keep in mind that while it is true that they are not killing a foetus, they are still at fault for taking non-vegetarian food, because these unfertilized eggs still contain the defects of non-vegetarian food.

paragraphs.text: Snakes lay a great many eggs at one time, but because they eat their own eggs, very few of them have an opportunity to hatch. The result of this is that there is a check or a limit to the number of snakes – this is arranged by nature.
summary: Snakes lay a great many eggs at one time, but because they eat their own eggs, very few of them have an opportunity to hatch.
The result of this is that there is a check or a limit to the number of snakes – this is arranged by nature.

paragraphs.text: Among fish, those whose offspring remain helpless at the time of birth show an instinctive affection for their young and keep them nearby, often sheltering them in some part of their body.
summary: Among fish, those whose offspring remain helpless at the time of birth show an instinctive affection for their young and keep them nearby, often sheltering them in some part of their body.

paragraphs.text: It is quite normal for snake mothers to eat their own eggs. It is not a full meal for them, perhaps, but rather more like a light snack! ( 4 )
summary: It is quite normal for snake mothers to eat their own eggs.
It is not a full meal for them, perhaps, but rather more like a light snack!

paragraphs.text: Birds and Animals, Our Neighbours [a compilation]
summary: Birds and Animals, Our Neighbours [a compilation]

footnotes.text: Áńd́a .> áńd́á; d́imba > d́imba > d́im. The one exception among the North Indian languages is Gorkhalii in which d́im [egg] is called phul [flower]. In spoken Bengali, that which takes shelter in the motherʼs womb in creatures who are not produced from eggs, is also called phul. When the child is born, the flower blossoms.
Śhávaka [offspring] + lá + u =shávakal; shávakal > sháoyál > cháoál > cháliá > chele [boy]. The word chele is not a native Bengali word at all; it is a Sanskrit derivative.
Vi – auṋga = vyáuṋg [frog], the one whose limbs are loose. In Sanskrit its synonyms are bhek, maṋd́uka, dardur.
Shabda Cayaniká Part 1, Discourse 1.

paragraphs.text: Fish – different varieties: The colour of the rohi fish is reddish. Like the iilish [hilsa], it is not all silver-plated. Iil means “to go down into the water”. Of those which go down into the water, the hilsa is the most important. Hence this name. Due to its reddish hue it (the rohi) is called lohit or rohit (rohit > rohia > rohi > ruhi > rehu > rui). In North India the form rehu is popularly used. Again, the young offspring of the rohi are called rohitaka > rohiaa > reoyá. The smaller categories of rohi are called reoyá in Urdu, but those with larger bodies are known as rehu in Urdu.
summary: Fish – different varieties: The colour of the rohi fish is reddish.
Due to its reddish hue it (the rohi) is called lohit or rohit (rohit > rohia > rohi > ruhi > rehu > rui).
The smaller categories of rohi are called reoyá in Urdu, but those with larger bodies are known as rehu in Urdu.

paragraphs.text: Like many other words, the names of fish are determined by their qualities and descriptions. The taste of the catechu fish (khayrá) is somewhat alkaline. Hence its Sanskrit name is khadirá. Khadir means khayer, that is, catechu (khadirá > khairá > khayrá). The Sanskrit name of puṋt́i [channa fish, a small fresh-water fish] is saphari. In the past, women who became physically weak or feeble and who used to eat non-vegetarian food were served a soup of puṋt́i fish for their nourishment. Paośt́ik > paot́t́hia > pot́i > puṋt́i. A little girl in the rural areas is even today affectionately called puṋt́i or put́uráńii. ( 1 ) The shol [shoal fish] is called shol in Sanskrit also. The word is derived from sholaka. It might be big in shape and appearance but it is not that heavy; it floats like sholá [sponge wood]. That is why it is called sholaka or shol. Paśt́á > pat́ht́á > pát́há that is the reason why the flesh of the fish, which tastes very much like goat meat [pát́há] and is inedible for most people, is called pát́hin in Sanskrit. If that fish is eaten in excessive amounts, it may cause palpitation of the heart. That is why it has another name – bakśári > bahári > boyári > boyáli > boyál. The Sanskrit nomenclature of boyál [large flounder] is bakśári or pát́hin.
summary: Like many other words, the names of fish are determined by their qualities and descriptions.
( 1 ) The shol [shoal fish] is called shol in Sanskrit also.
The Sanskrit nomenclature of boyál [large flounder] is bakśári or pát́hin.

paragraphs.text: A fish which has a circular or round skin is called goláraka [in Sanskrit], in Hindustani goral or goralá [prawn or shrimp]. This word is not in use in Bengali. That fish is actually like an insect of the water, it leaps up in the water almost as if it is frolicking. Due to its habit of childlike frolicking, it is called ciḿŕi [a word related to frolicking] fish. Ciḿŕi is a Bengali word. In Sanskrit another name of the goláraka is icchá matsya. If you cannot catch any fish, you might come across ciḿŕi fish near pools and drains. That is why it is called icchá matsya [wishing-fish] or icá fish. In western Ráŕh and in certain parts of East Bengal, ciḿŕi fish are called icá fish. In western Ráŕh there are quite a few villages called Icágaŕh, Icádihi, etc. ( 2 )
summary: A fish which has a circular or round skin is called goláraka [in Sanskrit], in Hindustani goral or goralá [prawn or shrimp].
In Sanskrit another name of the goláraka is icchá matsya.
In western Ráŕh there are quite a few villages called Icágaŕh, Icádihi, etc.

paragraphs.text: Poisonous effects of fish-eating: Rotten meat, faeces, rotten insects of different varieties, floating mucus and various kinds of infected substances in the water are the favourite food items of fish. In the drains and outlets of a city where polluted water collects, not only worms with tails but also fish, especially t́yáḿrá [small scaleless fish], kai [anabas], phyáṋsá and nyát́á, come to flourish. The ponds where people wash themselves or clean themselves of excreta are all crowded with lobsters, t́yáḿrá and kai fish. Hence they are well nourished in appearance. It is said that creamy lobster curry, kai fish curry, and the hot gravy of phyáṋsá and tyáḿrá are very tasty! The fish has a natural affinity for rotten and polluted substances. Amongst fish, garáiṋ [dwarf fish] and phyáṋsá are adept at consuming and absorbing polluted substances. If any poison is absorbed by the fish a short while after consuming those substances, then no impact of that poison is felt by human beings when they eat that fish, although it does have an adverse effect on their mind.
summary: Poisonous effects of fish-eating: Rotten meat, faeces, rotten insects of different varieties, floating mucus and various kinds of infected substances in the water are the favourite food items of fish.
It is said that creamy lobster curry, kai fish curry, and the hot gravy of phyáṋsá and tyáḿrá are very tasty!

If any poison is absorbed by the fish a short while after consuming those substances, then no impact of that poison is felt by human beings when they eat that fish, although it does have an adverse effect on their mind.

paragraphs.text: According to the sage Manu, one who eats fish eats everything, because fish consume everything. Whether the qualities of all this polluted matter are present or not in the fish eaters, the negative effects will nevertheless be present. Fish quarrel excessively amongst themselves, and swallow one another; they are extremely envious of one another and are often tyrannical. Hence in ancient days people believed that amongst fish eaters these evil traits were infectious. So the kingdom of fish was called “Mátsyanyáya”. It meant a disorderly or chaotic condition. When we see that the big and the powerful are swallowing the weak, when in social life or political life such a situation arises, we say that in socio-political life there is Mátsyanyáya.
summary: According to the sage Manu, one who eats fish eats everything, because fish consume everything.
Hence in ancient days people believed that amongst fish eaters these evil traits were infectious.
When we see that the big and the powerful are swallowing the weak, when in social life or political life such a situation arises, we say that in socio-political life there is Mátsyanyáya.

paragraphs.text: Even if, in the case of a fish that has consumed poisonous or polluted matter and is caught shortly after it has eaten that substance [before the poison is absorbed], people tear open its stomach (containing such things as bones of a corpse, rotten flesh and excreta) and remove the poisonous material, still the effect of the poison remains. The impact of the poisonous substance is greater in the case of the phyáṋsá fish than in the case of the nyát́á [Chana punetatus] fish. You must have seen in the newspaper a news item saying, “After eating the phyánsá fish five people suffered a premature death.”
summary: Even if, in the case of a fish that has consumed poisonous or polluted matter and is caught shortly after it has eaten that substance [before the poison is absorbed], people tear open its stomach (containing such things as bones of a corpse, rotten flesh and excreta) and remove the poisonous material, still the effect of the poison remains.
The impact of the poisonous substance is greater in the case of the phyáṋsá fish than in the case of the nyát́á [Chana punetatus] fish.
You must have seen in the newspaper a news item saying, “After eating the phyánsá fish five people suffered a premature death.

paragraphs.text: From the word garaghni has come the word garáiṋ. In some parts of Ráŕh and elsewhere in Bengal, the nyát́á fish is called the garáiṋ fish. But in and around Kolkata, this fish is called the nyát́á or lyát́á fish. ( 3 )
summary: From the word garaghni has come the word garáiṋ.
In some parts of Ráŕh and elsewhere in Bengal, the nyát́á fish is called the garáiṋ fish.
But in and around Kolkata, this fish is called the nyát́á or lyát́á fish.

paragraphs.text: Hilsa fish: In Indian English, that which is called hilsa [an Indian herring] is known in Bengali as iilish or iilse. This fish lives in saline water. It lives in shallow water near the mouth of the Gauṋgá and Brahmaputra Rivers. ( 4 ) It is primarily carnivorous in nature and particularly likes rotten flesh. The scales of the hilsa fish emit a foul smell. Due to its rich oil content, the hilsa fish is very tasty. Although it is a fish belonging to saline water, its eggs become spoiled therein. Hence during the rainy season, when the rainwater flows to the mouth of the river, the hilsa fish moves upstream. Immediately after laying its eggs in fresh water, it travels back downstream and returns to the sea. Hence large hilsa can be found during the middle of the rainy season along the upstream flow, and at the end of the rainy season along the ebb tide.
summary: Hilsa fish: In Indian English, that which is called hilsa [an Indian herring] is known in Bengali as iilish or iilse.
Due to its rich oil content, the hilsa fish is very tasty.
Hence large hilsa can be found during the middle of the rainy season along the upstream flow, and at the end of the rainy season along the ebb tide.

paragraphs.text: When moving upstream, the female hilsa are full of eggs, and when they return they are no longer carrying their eggs. When they run upstream for sweet water, it becomes extremely essential for them to obtain this water from any source. When the rain drizzles, in expectation of sweet water the hilsa move a little closer to the water surface and get caught in the fishermanʼs net. That is why such a rain is called iilsheguṋŕi.
summary: When moving upstream, the female hilsa are full of eggs, and when they return they are no longer carrying their eggs.
When the rain drizzles, in expectation of sweet water the hilsa move a little closer to the water surface and get caught in the fishermanʼs net.
That is why such a rain is called iilsheguṋŕi.

paragraphs.text: Just a little while ago, it was said that rotten meat is very dear to the hilsa fish. So while slicing up the hilsa fish, certain foul-smelling, polluted substances, which are injurious to health, may emerge from its stomach. Since it is too oily and emits excessive smell from its scales, it is not good for the [human] stomach at the peak of the rainy season. People are frequently stricken with cholera due to taking too much hilsa fish or taking rotten hilsa fish.
summary: Just a little while ago, it was said that rotten meat is very dear to the hilsa fish.
Since it is too oily and emits excessive smell from its scales, it is not good for the [human] stomach at the peak of the rainy season.
People are frequently stricken with cholera due to taking too much hilsa fish or taking rotten hilsa fish.

paragraphs.text: Eggs are released by the hilsa fish in a natural process. While drifting downstream in the sweet river water, the eggs are released and then split up in the waves, and the baby hilsa float towards the sea. At this time, because they are very small in appearance, few of them get caught in the fishermanʼs net. However, those who take longer and return only in the autumn become bigger in size and they often get caught in the fishermanʼs net. We call them khoká iilish [baby hilsa] in the language of Kolkata. Sometimes the eggs and young hilsa are caught in their net, along with the eggs and smaller fish of other species. They are then released into ponds along with other fish species. During floods also some hilsa, losing their way, enter the ponds. The hilsa inhabiting the ponds, due to the absence of saline water and the absence of rotten flesh as food, are much less oily and tasty. These types of fish are sold at high prices, with their true background concealed, along with the real hilsa. Those hilsa grown in ponds are called viilish by villagers of certain regions.
summary: Eggs are released by the hilsa fish in a natural process.
Sometimes the eggs and young hilsa are caught in their net, along with the eggs and smaller fish of other species.
Those hilsa grown in ponds are called viilish by villagers of certain regions.

paragraphs.text: Since river water is used so extensively for irrigation, in most parts of the world the rivers are drying up, causing the seawater to enter the river at its mouth and forming an estuary. The water close to the mouths of most rivers is becoming highly saline. Apart from rivers drying up, dams and barrages have been built on rivers in different parts of the world. As a result, those fish species that require sweet water for laying their eggs are no longer able to swim upstream. Being unable to lay their eggs in the sweet water of the river, they drift downstream towards the sea and lay their eggs, and those eggs are spoiled by the saline water. For this very reason, the number of hilsa fish is dangerously declining. As a result, in a short period of time, just like the blue whales, the hilsa also will soon be on the verge of extinction.
summary: Since river water is used so extensively for irrigation, in most parts of the world the rivers are drying up, causing the seawater to enter the river at its mouth and forming an estuary.
As a result, those fish species that require sweet water for laying their eggs are no longer able to swim upstream.
As a result, in a short period of time, just like the blue whales, the hilsa also will soon be on the verge of extinction.

paragraphs.text: Mango fish: The tapse [mango] fish, like the hilsa, is a marine fish which thrives at the mouth of rivers. During winter they move upstream. Even until the other day, a little ways upstream in the Rupnarayan River, close to Kolaghat, plenty of mango fish were available. But they are no longer found there, for the reasons mentioned above. Since the river is drying up, the salinity of the water has increased. For similar reasons, mango fish are no longer available in the Damodar River. How could they be available? They are presently battling against extinction. They will probably cease to exist after some time. Because this mango fish has something resembling an [asceticʼs] beard on the upper part of its body, it is called tapasvii – tapasvii > tapsiá > tapse. ( 5 )
summary: Mango fish: The tapse [mango] fish, like the hilsa, is a marine fish which thrives at the mouth of rivers.
For similar reasons, mango fish are no longer available in the Damodar River.
Because this mango fish has something resembling an [asceticʼs] beard on the upper part of its body, it is called tapasvii – tapasvii > tapsiá > tapse.

paragraphs.text: Channa fish (puṋt́i): Puṋt́i is a pure Bengali word meaning a small thing. Although the puṋt́i [channa] fish looks somewhat like the rohi fish, it is a smaller fish. It lays eggs even in the fields of áman paddy [pre-winter paddy]. The people of Ráŕh generally catch puṋt́i fish in large numbers from the paddy fields with their small nets. There are eleven types of puṋt́i in Bengal. Of course, nine types of these puṋt́i have almost disappeared. Only about two types still remain: 1) the small puṋt́i, or bitter-tasting puṋt́i, and 2) the big puṋt́i or saral puṋt́i (in the language of Kolkata it is called saral puṋt́i, in rural areas some people call it sar puṋt́i).
summary: Channa fish (puṋt́i): Puṋt́i is a pure Bengali word meaning a small thing.
The people of Ráŕh generally catch puṋt́i fish in large numbers from the paddy fields with their small nets.

paragraphs.text: Flat fish (bhet́ki): In English the flat fish is called bhet́ki. In Bengali the word bhet́ki is very prevalent. In certain rural areas it is also called korál fish. This queer-looking, oily and tasty fish is also a fish of saline water. They also live in the sea, close to the mouth of a river. Where the water near the mouth of the river is saline, bhet́ki is available. Even in the sweet water of the river Padma, for a limited distance the bhet́ki moves upstream. Like the hilsa, this fish is very fond of rotten flesh. And just like the hilsa fish, it also has odorous scales.
summary: Flat fish (bhet́ki): In English the flat fish is called bhet́ki.
They also live in the sea, close to the mouth of a river.
And just like the hilsa fish, it also has odorous scales.

paragraphs.text: Catechu fish (khayrá): Khadira means khayer [catechu]. Khadira > khair > khayer. Khayer is a plant that belongs to the Acacia genus. Báblá also belongs to this genus of plants. Acacia babul and Acacia catechu look almost identical from a distance. Collecting the juicy wood of this tree and boiling it in a cauldron, the sap, while still hot, is poured out in the form of a thick paste. While the paste is still soft, it is cut into squares or other shapes. The khayer products at Janakpur on the Indo-Nepal border are considered to be qualitatively of the best variety. Because khayer is produced from the sap of the khayer tree, it is called katthá in Hindi.
summary: Catechu fish (khayrá): Khadira means khayer [catechu].
Acacia babul and Acacia catechu look almost identical from a distance.
Because khayer is produced from the sap of the khayer tree, it is called katthá in Hindi.

paragraphs.text: The fish which has a taste somewhat like the tasteless catechu is called khadirá in Sanskrit. Khadirá > khairá > khayrá. The khayrá closely resembles the hilsa. The large-sized khayrá could be mistaken for baby hilsa. Khayrá is a small fish; it can lay its eggs to hatch even in bogs. ( 6 )
summary: The fish which has a taste somewhat like the tasteless catechu is called khadirá in Sanskrit.
The khayrá closely resembles the hilsa.
Khayrá is a small fish; it can lay its eggs to hatch even in bogs.

paragraphs.text: Crustacea (ciḿŕi): Many people wrongly describe the ciḿŕi as a fish. There is no relation between ciḿŕi and fish. Ciḿŕi is like an insect of the water. It thrives and multiplies in putrid water. In some parts of Ráŕh and in other regions of Bengal, it is called icá fish. Some villages are also known as Icádih, Icágaŕ, etc. In English ciḿŕi is not called fish, it is called “lobster”; so why should it be described as a fish when it is in fact not a fish? Those who are permitted to take fish, such as Gaoŕiiya Vaeśńavas [Vaishnavites of Bengal], eat it as fish. I say once again, ciḿŕi is not a fish; it is a kind of insect from putrid water. There are ciḿŕi of different types, belonging to both sweet and saline water. Ciḿŕi of reddish hue are found in the estuaries and rivers adjacent to the sea. These shrimp are hard to digest and cause ailments to those who partake of them. Amongst the sweet water ciḿŕi available in Kolkata are lobster, bágdá ciḿŕi [another big-size ciḿŕi], kuco ciḿŕi, mocá ciḿŕi, kádá ciḿŕi, etc. [all smaller and still smaller varieties]. Although people of Kolkata do not eat them, in some parts of Bengal people also eat dried shrimp (shut́ki ciḿŕi). Like the salted hilsa, these dried shrimps are foul-smelling and rather bad for digestion. As some flying insects look like prawns, they are called ucciḿŕe (ur [flying] + ciḿŕe = ucciḿŕe). ( 7 )
summary: Crustacea (ciḿŕi): Many people wrongly describe the ciḿŕi as a fish.
I say once again, ciḿŕi is not a fish; it is a kind of insect from putrid water.
As some flying insects look like prawns, they are called ucciḿŕe (ur [flying] + ciḿŕe = ucciḿŕe).

paragraphs.text: Turtle (Kúrma): From the verbal root kúr + suffix man, we get the word kúrma, meaning different types of water turtle, such as ket́ho, bárkol, etc. Amongst carnivorous creatures, the water turtle has the greatest longevity.
summary: Turtle (Kúrma): From the verbal root kúr + suffix man, we get the word kúrma, meaning different types of water turtle, such as ket́ho, bárkol, etc.
Amongst carnivorous creatures, the water turtle has the greatest longevity.

paragraphs.text: The word kúrma normally refers to turtles that live on land. People of ancient times believed that amongst the graminivorous creatures, the land turtle was the longest-lived and that it lived for nearly five hundred years. Amongst all creatures, probably human beings are the most cruel. Despite the fact that most of the water turtle is very hard to digest, out of greed for its meat, human beings continue to kill them so as to eat their flesh. The meat of the land turtle is even more indigestible. Yet after catching them, people recklessly kill them, and in addition eat their eggs. In this manner, human beings have almost obliterated the turtle. People in nearly all parts of the world are equally guilty of this crime. In ancient Bengali literature there is reference to curry prepared with leafy vegetables and turtle eggs.
summary: The word kúrma normally refers to turtles that live on land.
The meat of the land turtle is even more indigestible.
In ancient Bengali literature there is reference to curry prepared with leafy vegetables and turtle eggs.

paragraphs.text: There is another popular name for turtle, dulik. Although the term has been applied to all species of turtle, it is specifically used to describe the land turtle.
summary: There is another popular name for turtle, dulik.

paragraphs.text: Kamat́a also means “[water] turtle.” There are generally two types of turtles, the land-dwelling turtle or tortoise, and the water-dwelling turtle. The tortoise has great longevity. They live on grass and leaves. The [water] turtle is also long lived. In the opinion of some, the tortoise lives up to nearly five hundred years in age, while the turtle can survive for up to three hundred years.
summary: Kamat́a also means “[water] turtle.
They live on grass and leaves.
In the opinion of some, the tortoise lives up to nearly five hundred years in age, while the turtle can survive for up to three hundred years.

paragraphs.text: The water turtle is highly carnivorous. However, the water turtle also comes onto land in order to lay its eggs. It removes some sand or soft earth and lays its eggs in that depression. Afterwards it covers up the eggs and returns to the water. With the help of the internal heat of the sand or earth, the young break their shell and emerge. The moment the young ones are born, they run straight for the water. Normally most of the young turtles are eaten by birds or other carnivorous creatures before they can make it from land to the water. While the tortoise also lays its eggs underneath the sand or earth, it remains nearby, so fewer of its children die. The water turtle lays a great quantity of eggs, while in comparison the tortoise lays far fewer. People eat both kinds of turtle eggs. A perusal of old Bengali literature shows that the Bengalees of that time used to eat turtle eggs with bitter greens [a bitter vegetable green]. Not all water turtles are edible.
summary: The water turtle is highly carnivorous.
Normally most of the young turtles are eaten by birds or other carnivorous creatures before they can make it from land to the water.
Not all water turtles are edible.

paragraphs.text: According to differences in size and nature, turtles are known by different names in Bengali, such as kacchap, ket́ho (“hard as wood”), káut́há, bárkol, and so on. All kinds of turtles are called kamat́a in Sanskrit and refined Bengali.
summary: According to differences in size and nature, turtles are known by different names in Bengali, such as kacchap, ket́ho (“hard as wood”), káut́há, bárkol, and so on.
All kinds of turtles are called kamat́a in Sanskrit and refined Bengali.

paragraphs.text: Shark: The shark is called kámat́a in Sanskrit and refined Bengali. Those sharks that are large in size and live in the ocean are normally called háuṋgar in Bengali, and those sharks that live in coastal rivers, backwaters or estuaries, are called kámat́a in spoken Bengali. They are somewhat smaller in size than the háuṋgar. At one time there were a great number of kámat́as in the rivers of Midnapore, 24 Paraganas and Khulna Districts. Taking bath in those rivers was dangerous during that period. The oil of these kámat́a sharks has medicinal qualities. As the cod fish began disappearing, shark oil began to be used as a substitute for cod liver oil, and from that time began the annihilation of the kámat́a species. Nowadays the number of kámat́as has greatly diminished. ( 9 )
summary: Shark: The shark is called kámat́a in Sanskrit and refined Bengali.
Taking bath in those rivers was dangerous during that period.
Nowadays the number of kámat́as has greatly diminished.
