summary: Birds and Animals, Our Neighbours [a compilation]

footnotes.text: The foregoing six paragraphs are from Shabda Cayaniká Part 26, Discourse 229.
The foregoing two paragraphs are from Shabda Cayaniká Part 7, Discourse 49.

paragraphs.text: Garud́a bird, Eagle and Condor: The word khecara stands for large-sized birds such as vultures, eagles, condors and the garud́a bird of Bihar, which circle a spot for some time, similar to airplanes. The garud́a bird is normally seen during the autumn in the fields of autumn crops in North Bihar. They come from cold countries on the other side of the Himalayas. When the seeds are sown in the fields, they come and dig them out and eat them. The common people call them garud́a birds. They drive them away by scaring them, but they do not kill them. They do not even eat them. Garud́a birds are not large in number. Sometimes only one will arrive in a village during a particular year, and may be none in another year. From a distance it can be mistaken for a human being. In height it looks like an ordinary person. Once I saw such a bird in a field of black grams on the northern bank of the Buŕigańd́ak River in the Khagariya District of North Bihar. On another occasion I saw such a bird in wintertime in a field of lentils near Rátábáŕi in the Karimganja district of Assam. The word khecara will also apply to these birds. ( 1 )
summary: Garud́a bird, Eagle and Condor: The word khecara stands for large-sized birds such as vultures, eagles, condors and the garud́a bird of Bihar, which circle a spot for some time, similar to airplanes.
Garud́a birds are not large in number.
The word khecara will also apply to these birds.

paragraphs.text: The derivative meaning of the word garud́a is, that which drenches from beginning to end. The Puranic name of the bird Garud́a of which you have heard – why is it so named? Has it from its very birth been drenching the heaven, earth and the netherworld? Yes, according to theologians, it has continued to drench all these spheres with devotional feelings. The Puranic legend concerning Garud́a says that the wife of sage Káshyapa laid several eggs. In due time, when the eggs burst, innumerable infant snakes crawled out. Having so many offspring, his wife, Kadru, was very delighted. With a great sense of glory and pride, she looked at her co-wife, Vinata. Vinata had given birth to only two eggs. The two eggs took a long time to burst. Seeing the great fortune of her co-wife Kadru and her own misfortune, she lost her mental balance. She forcibly burst open one of her eggs. A crimson-coloured male figure emerged. That newly born man told Vinata, “You have forcibly burst the egg in an untimely manner. Hence it will not be possible for me to remain on this earth. I am leaving. I will be the charioteer of the sunʼs seven-coloured, horse-driven chariot.”
summary: The derivative meaning of the word garud́a is, that which drenches from beginning to end.
Vinata had given birth to only two eggs.
I will be the charioteer of the sunʼs seven-coloured, horse-driven chariot.

paragraphs.text: Thus the light that appears in the sky on the threshold of the sunrise, is known as Aruńa, the first child of Vinata. The first streak of light of the risen sun at bráhmamuhúrta ( 2 ) [daybreak] is also called aruńa, and hence, the first rays of the sun seen at bráhmamuhúrta are also called aruńa. In English this colour is called crimson. The morning suffused with this sunlight is called the crimson dawn. To distinguish the variety of red colours, some people describe the colour of the morning sky as crimson red. No, the phrase “crimson red” is not correct; it should be “crimson colour”. Yes, it is truly a unique variety of the colour red.
summary: Thus the light that appears in the sky on the threshold of the sunrise, is known as Aruńa, the first child of Vinata.
The morning suffused with this sunlight is called the crimson dawn.
Yes, it is truly a unique variety of the colour red.

paragraphs.text: Vinata became alert. The second egg was not forcibly broken open. She waited for the time when it would spontaneously burst open. Out of the second egg came a large bird. And the large bird came to be known as Garud́a.
summary: The second egg was not forcibly broken open.
Out of the second egg came a large bird.
And the large bird came to be known as Garud́a.

paragraphs.text: The word garud́a means “one whose job is to drench others”. According to the Puranic legend, after coming out of the eggshell, Garud́a told his mother Vinata that his firm resolve was to preach the glory of the Lord. Since by remaining at home on earth it would not be possible for him to fulfil his vow, he would have to move out into the vast expanse of the cosmos. As the mount of Lord Náráyańa, he would go around the world and throughout the universe preaching the glory of the Lord. He would drench the minds of all creatures of the world with tender feelings of devotion. So it was proper to name such a being as Garud́a, whose job was to drench all beings with devotional feelings from birth until death. This entire Puranic story was allegorical. Garud́a represents the devotee of the Lord, and Náráyańa the Supreme Lord. The mind of the devotee is the váhana [mount or vehicle] of the Lord. Devotees want to attain supreme fulfilment by drenching the mind of universal humanity with devotional feelings. Here the word váhana is not used in the literal sense of a physical vehicle. It is in the metaphorical sense of the carrier of the Lordʼs glory. In that sense, the name Garud́a is justified.
summary: The word garud́a means “one whose job is to drench others”.
This entire Puranic story was allegorical.
In that sense, the name Garud́a is justified.

paragraphs.text: From all available accounts, the garud́a bird appears to be a large bird like the eagle. The nest of the eagle and the condor is called eyrie [also spelled eyry, ayrie, aerie and aery]. Some people describe the condor as the largest of the eagle subfamily. The eagle of the prehistoric era, which was known as kyádárá or kyádárine, is now extinct from the earth. The Sanskrit name of the kyádárá or kyádárine was the bátávi bird. A smaller version of this bird is found in limited number near the North Pole. The comparatively smaller version of the bátávi bird is called garud́a in Sanskrit. Probably to establish a link with the Puranic bird, the name garud́a was given.
summary: From all available accounts, the garud́a bird appears to be a large bird like the eagle.
The Sanskrit name of the kyádárá or kyádárine was the bátávi bird.
Probably to establish a link with the Puranic bird, the name garud́a was given.

paragraphs.text: You might be aware that in India today we do not have eagles as permanent residents. Occasionally during winter a few eagles appear from the northern sky seeking temporary refuge, and with the end of the cold season they depart for distant lands, their original homelands, although those places may be unknown to us.
summary: You might be aware that in India today we do not have eagles as permanent residents.

Occasionally during winter a few eagles appear from the northern sky seeking temporary refuge, and with the end of the cold season they depart for distant lands, their original homelands, although those places may be unknown to us.

paragraphs.text: Amongst the birds of the eagle family, the largest are the condor, which is found in the region adjacent to the Southern Alps. The vibration created by the beating of their wings makes the nearby area quake. They can see objects from afar while sitting on the mountain. You must have come across the expression “condor eye” or “condor vision”. Condors are a dwindling species of bird. Eagles are of various sizes. They are larger in size than the ganders and flamingos of India. Monkey-eating eagles are quite large in size and have terrific strength. They can swoop down on a monkey and lift it up. If the monkey is too large and cannot be lifted, then, with the thrusts of its wings and claws, and tearing it apart with its beak, the eagle forces it into submission and often eats [the monkey] while it is still alive. Eagles are mostly dark grey or grey in colour. A limited number of eagles are golden in colour. Once upon a time in Great Britain golden eagles abounded. These medium-sized birds were a source of great pride for Britain. During the reign of King Henry VIII, the people of France and Italy used to come to Britain to see the golden eagles. However, that standard of glory is no more. Nearly a hundred years ago, the last surviving golden eagle was shot dead by a cruel hunterʼs bullet. With that event, the era of the golden eagle came to an end.
summary: Amongst the birds of the eagle family, the largest are the condor, which is found in the region adjacent to the Southern Alps.

If the monkey is too large and cannot be lifted, then, with the thrusts of its wings and claws, and tearing it apart with its beak, the eagle forces it into submission and often eats [the monkey] while it is still alive.
With that event, the era of the golden eagle came to an end.

paragraphs.text: Today the Bengali or Sanskrit name of the eagle is sitashakunta. If you like, you can use this name. In India vultures always maintain their unique custom that they will never eat any animal alive. As long as it sees that the tail of the dying cow is moving and stirring, the vulture will not fly down from the tree and put its beak on the animal. Only after making sure that the cow is dead will it begin feasting on its flesh. Eagles and other birds belonging to this family are not guided by such psychology. They attack even living birds and animals. However, they maintain nobility in distinguishing between edible and non-edible prey, which the Indian vultures do not maintain. Almost all dead animals are food for the vultures but are not for the eagles.
summary: Today the Bengali or Sanskrit name of the eagle is sitashakunta.
Only after making sure that the cow is dead will it begin feasting on its flesh.
Almost all dead animals are food for the vultures but are not for the eagles.

paragraphs.text: One favourite haunt of the eagles is the Alps, the spine of Europe. They do not build their nests in trees for two reasons: first, in order to build a nest for such a large bird, one needs a very large tree. You know the vultures do not build their nests in small, ordinary trees; they build them in banyan or pákuŕ trees [Ficus benjamina]. It is difficult to find proper trees in which eagle nests can be built. Although eagles of smaller size build their nests in trees, larger-sized eagles dig holes in caves or crevices in the upper part of the Alps and build their nests by removing larger pieces of rock. They have no other means to build their nests.
summary: One favourite haunt of the eagles is the Alps, the spine of Europe.
It is difficult to find proper trees in which eagle nests can be built.
They have no other means to build their nests.

paragraphs.text: Some years back, near a place in Baiguiyo in the Philippines, a monkey-eating eagle was found. Of the pure eagle family, this was probably the largest bird. It is said that this monkey-eating eagle can kill an entire monkey. Eagles are known to fly over a long distance.
summary: Some years back, near a place in Baiguiyo in the Philippines, a monkey-eating eagle was found.
It is said that this monkey-eating eagle can kill an entire monkey.
Eagles are known to fly over a long distance.

paragraphs.text: Adjutant Stork (Hárgile): It is a semi-Indian bird, which resides in India and also migrates to other regions. It is mostly seen during winter in the Sundarbans. Of course, they are also found in other seasons. They might not fly at great altitude; nevertheless they fly at a considerable height. ( 3 )
summary: Adjutant Stork (Hárgile): It is a semi-Indian bird, which resides in India and also migrates to other regions.
Of course, they are also found in other seasons.
They might not fly at great altitude; nevertheless they fly at a considerable height.

paragraphs.text: Vulture (Shakunta): Vultures are found in almost all parts of the world. Of course, they are of varied species. Each species flies at a considerable height in the sky. They feel discomfort while flying at a lower height, since they have to flap their wings too often to break the air. Vultures build their own nests on the upper part of the banyan, pákuŕ or similar trees. They live amongst the higher branches for two reasons: first, because they have less discomfort in flying to and from the nest; second, from such a height they can easily command a good view of animal corpses lying in different places. As they fly high in the sky, they have greater speed and acceleration, and they take short time to find corpses in different parts of a field.
summary: Vulture (Shakunta): Vultures are found in almost all parts of the world.
They feel discomfort while flying at a lower height, since they have to flap their wings too often to break the air.
As they fly high in the sky, they have greater speed and acceleration, and they take short time to find corpses in different parts of a field.

paragraphs.text: There are several species of vultures in the world. Vulture indica is part of the vulture species. Their throats appear to be different from that of other birds. Even though they are akin to eagles, there is no resemblance between their necks and the necks of other birds. In Sanskrit gridhra (feminine, gridhińii), shakuni (feminine, shakunii), shakunta (feminine, shakuntii) are different names for the same bird. In ancient times three varieties of this bird were found in India – krśńa shakuni, svet shakuni and the raktakańt́ha shakuni [the red-throated vulture]. Krśńa shakunis [black vultures] refer to those that we see even today. Svet shakunis [white vultures] are rarely found; raktakant́ha shakunis are even rarer. There is ample scope for further research on this subject – as to why the white species and red-throated species are on the verge of extinction. No people of any community ever eat vultures. Yet why is their number dwindling so rapidly?
summary: There are several species of vultures in the world.
In ancient times three varieties of this bird were found in India – krśńa shakuni, svet shakuni and the raktakańt́ha shakuni [the red-throated vulture].
Yet why is their number dwindling so rapidly?

paragraphs.text: The food for vultures is animal corpses. To represent the paradox, in Bengali it is said, “To whatever height a vulture might rise, its attention is always on carrion.” ( 4 )
summary: The food for vultures is animal corpses.
To represent the paradox, in Bengali it is said, “To whatever height a vulture might rise, its attention is always on carrion.

paragraphs.text: Whether it be tropical or cold countries, some species of vultures are sure to be found. Vultures of tropical countries are mostly of the Indian variety. They build their nests on the upper part of tall trees, primarily of banyan trees. While other birds build their nests with bits of dry grass and straw, vultures never do so. Their nests are somewhat open; however, for the protection of the eggs, straw is added. They lay their eggs in sparse quantity. The eggs are a light blue colour, quite large in size. The mother vulture cannot properly hatch her eggs. Instead, they break open with the heat of the sunlight. When vultures go to a distant dung-heap, during their absence salamanders come and eat up the eggs. Some say that due to eating too many of these eggs, the salamanders or iguanas often die. The body of the vulture bristles with different kinds of worms. These worms are found even in their nests.
summary: Whether it be tropical or cold countries, some species of vultures are sure to be found.
The eggs are a light blue colour, quite large in size.
These worms are found even in their nests.

paragraphs.text: Among birds, vultures are very sharp-sighted. Their beaks are extremely hard and can even pierce stones. The strength of their beaks is very close to that of a bird called banrui. They eat the flesh of animals by slicing them neatly with their beaks. Even when eating rotten flesh, they do not get food poisoning. Vultures are natureʼs self-created scavengers. In Bengali it is said, “On land the vulture, in water, the shark”. In Sanskrit the verb shak means “do”. The sentence “He can do it” is sah shaknoti in Sanskrit. With the suffix ktin we obtain the word shakti. In translating the word “battery” we have the verb shak, and adding lyut́ to it, we have the word shakan. With the verb shak and with the suffix uń we derive the word shaktu, meaning fried gram-powder, which gives strength when eaten. Shaktu > shattu > shátu > chátu. From the verb shak we derive the name of the bird shakunta. ( 5 )
summary: Among birds, vultures are very sharp-sighted.
In Sanskrit the verb shak means “do”.
From the verb shak we derive the name of the bird shakunta.

paragraphs.text: We have said that although the shakun (vulture) is carnivorous, it does not eat the flesh of living animals. When an animal lies in the dung-heap, so long there is any life in it, the vulture never comes to eat its flesh. In this regard, the vulture is superior to human beings. Humans kill living animals to eat their flesh, while the vulture never eats the flesh of living animals. It only eats the flesh of dead animals, which are its natural food. Human beings think that vultures are cruel creatures; they think that tigers are monsters and are very cruel. Yet even the tigress – the legendary she-monster – has endless affection for her baby:
summary: We have said that although the shakun (vulture) is carnivorous, it does not eat the flesh of living animals.
Humans kill living animals to eat their flesh, while the vulture never eats the flesh of living animals.
Human beings think that vultures are cruel creatures; they think that tigers are monsters and are very cruel.

paragraphs.text: [The tigress is always tempted to drink blood, Yet for her own babies she has boundless affection. Putaná as milkmaid murders the children of others, Yet never failed in her duty to nurse her own babe. The tigress, the she-monster, so cruel in this world, Yet they are hundred times better than ourselves.]
summary: [The tigress is always tempted to drink blood, Yet for her own babies she has boundless affection.
Putaná as milkmaid murders the children of others, Yet never failed in her duty to nurse her own babe.
The tigress, the she-monster, so cruel in this world, Yet they are hundred times better than ourselves.

paragraphs.text: Even the vulture has tremendous affection for its own child. This bird appears cruel but is highly devoted in her maternal love, and is said to have carefully nurtured and nourished the deserted daughter of a celestial nymph until the sage Kanva took her to his hermitage. Since the bird shakunta nurtured the baby, the sage Kanva named the baby girl shakuntalá or “the girl nurtured by shakunta”. Yes, all these terms are for the Indian vulture or Vulture indica. In the country of utmost cold, covered with snow on top of the Alps, some vultures also live. The best vultures species in the world live on top of the Alps.
summary: Even the vulture has tremendous affection for its own child.
Yes, all these terms are for the Indian vulture or Vulture indica.
The best vultures species in the world live on top of the Alps.

paragraphs.text: [As told earlier] eagles, like vultures, cannot build compact nests with bits of dry grass and straw. On the Alpine mountains they gather pieces of stone and press them together to build something similar to a house in which they have their nest. Yes, the eagle is part of the larger family of vultures. Yet some eagles species are much larger in size than the species of Indian vultures or Vulture Indica. Monkey-eating eagles or sheep-snatching eagles are much larger in size than Indian vultures. Eagles of the Pacific Ocean region swoop down upon monkeys, lift them up and eat them. Alpine eagles swoop down upon the lambs of their choice in a herd of sheep and lift them up. They even swoop down and carry away big sheep. The condor species of Alpine eagle residing in the Alps are the largest among flying birds. Individually some of them look like large men. They fly at a terrific speed. They also cannot build their nests; they live in eyrie. Yet whether it is the eagle, condor or Indian vulture, each has a very hard beak. The vulture, of course, is looked upon as an ominous bird. The god Saturn whom people want to keep away from out of fear and to worship outside their house, touching their hands to their heads, taking prasád [sacred offerings] of the god but never carrying them home ( 6 ) – according to some Puranas, the vulture is the mount of that god Saturn. ( 7 )
summary: [As told earlier] eagles, like vultures, cannot build compact nests with bits of dry grass and straw.
They even swoop down and carry away big sheep.

The god Saturn whom people want to keep away from out of fear and to worship outside their house, touching their hands to their heads, taking prasád [sacred offerings] of the god but never carrying them home ( 6 ) – according to some Puranas, the vulture is the mount of that god Saturn.

paragraphs.text: Kite: River-gull, seagull and white-breasted kite: Kites (cil) are everywhere in the world except in predominantly cold countries. Indian kites are usually subdivided into three different species: the ordinary or black kites (krśńa cil), white kites, and river gulls or seagulls. Gradually kites are diminishing in number. Seagulls (gáuṋg cil) build their nests in big trees adjoining ocean beaches. Even their number is decreasing. White kites (shauṋkha cil) are barely visible. In our childhood we used to see two to four white kites every day. We used to see the nilkant́ha or blue-throated bird, phiuṋe [fork-tailed bird], and doel [magpie robin of Bengal] (it is a small bird, yet extremely carnivorous; not as cruel as hawks, and having a pleasant voice). Yet in later times, for mysterious reasons the blue-throated bird, fork-tailed bird and magpie robin of Bengal were all lost to an unknown world. I surmise that since the air of the adjoining city became polluted, and due to the absence of ozone in the air, they are disappearing rapidly. I hardly come across white kites, that is, shauṋkha cils; yet in the art of swooping down to earth from on high to carry away their prey, they surpass the black kites and seagulls. In the Jhumur songs of Ráŕh it is mentioned:
summary: Kite: River-gull, seagull and white-breasted kite: Kites (cil) are everywhere in the world except in predominantly cold countries.
White kites (shauṋkha cil) are barely visible.
I hardly come across white kites, that is, shauṋkha cils; yet in the art of swooping down to earth from on high to carry away their prey, they surpass the black kites and seagulls.

paragraphs.text: Black kites are becoming extinct due to shortage of food. Seagulls are decreasing in number due to water pollution. Water pollution is prevalent all over the world. Due to polluted water from mills and factories, the water of rivers and oceans has become polluted, causing fish to die in endless numbers. Since fish and frogs are dying in such large numbers, for this very reason seagulls are nearly extinct. Hence water pollution is responsible for the extinction of seagulls.
summary: Black kites are becoming extinct due to shortage of food.
Due to polluted water from mills and factories, the water of rivers and oceans has become polluted, causing fish to die in endless numbers.
Hence water pollution is responsible for the extinction of seagulls.

paragraphs.text: Similarly, due to the polluted water that flows into the Mediterranean from European countries, its water has been rendered poisonous, and its marine life is about to become extinct. The flying fish and flying frog have disappeared behind the black curtain of history. That is why the seagulls of the Mediterranean coastal areas are becoming extinct. During my stay in Spain in Valencia, I used to sit on a hillock near the Mediterranean coast. Yet I never came across a single seagull. I enquired of the local people and gathered that since the fish are becoming scarce, the seagulls are also becoming extinct.
summary: Similarly, due to the polluted water that flows into the Mediterranean from European countries, its water has been rendered poisonous, and its marine life is about to become extinct.
During my stay in Spain in Valencia, I used to sit on a hillock near the Mediterranean coast.
I enquired of the local people and gathered that since the fish are becoming scarce, the seagulls are also becoming extinct.

paragraphs.text: In Bengal, especially East Bengal, which was earlier famous for its ample supply of fish, the fish have now become scarce and costly. The shrimp, mango fish, hilsa, and flat fish (bhet́ki) are not only scarce, even the semi-marine fish that live in sweet as well as saline water are also rapidly decreasing in number. By eating them, the seagulls manage to survive. Thus they are also advancing towards extinction. Human beings do not eat white kites. Then why are they becoming extinct? This should be investigated. ( 8 )
summary: In Bengal, especially East Bengal, which was earlier famous for its ample supply of fish, the fish have now become scarce and costly.
Thus they are also advancing towards extinction.
This should be investigated.

paragraphs.text: Crane: In the whole world there were about twenty six different species of cranes (sárasa). Of these, seven species reside in India. By the word kośacaiṋcu we mean the seven types of cranes, and not other species. Today the crane is looked upon as an ancient bird of India. It is surmised that in the remote past this bird came to India from central eastern Asia, from the outer Mongolian region. Compared to the inclement climate of outer Mongolia, they preferred to remain in the more congenial environment of India. Indian cranes today are wholly Indian, and even with the changes of season they never stir outside India and migrate to other regions as do the shyámá bird [a song bird of the thrush family], blue-throated bird and cátaka [rainy season bird]. Although the crane is a completely carnivorous bird, it is not lacking in tenderness. Yet people never try to domesticate them as pets. Probably in a domesticated environment, they might not be able to adjust and would die prematurely. Once in India there were plenty of brown-coloured cranes. Nowadays, one does not see enough of these birds. Just like white kites, they are either on the way to extinction or are wholly extinct. ( 9 )
summary: Crane: In the whole world there were about twenty six different species of cranes (sárasa).

Indian cranes today are wholly Indian, and even with the changes of season they never stir outside India and migrate to other regions as do the shyámá bird [a song bird of the thrush family], blue-throated bird and cátaka [rainy season bird].
Just like white kites, they are either on the way to extinction or are wholly extinct.

paragraphs.text: The second meaning of karat́a is “crane”. This long-billed crane is found in nearly every place in the world, regardless of whether it is predominantly cold or hot. The only places it avoids are those where the water freezes, because then there is a shortage of food. If it sees the probability of water freezing in a particular place, it abandons that spot just prior [to its freezing]. It does so with the help of its rather advanced deductive powers. Thus, if in any particular location it is seen that the cranes are leaving, it can be deduced that very cold weather is coming in the near future, just as it can be known that the rainy season is imminent when the cátaka [swallows] are seen flying westwards at the end of the hot season.
summary: The second meaning of karat́a is “crane”.
If it sees the probability of water freezing in a particular place, it abandons that spot just prior [to its freezing].

Thus, if in any particular location it is seen that the cranes are leaving, it can be deduced that very cold weather is coming in the near future, just as it can be known that the rainy season is imminent when the cátaka [swallows] are seen flying westwards at the end of the hot season.

paragraphs.text: The rainy season begins a day or two after the rain clouds reach the Bengal coastal region from the Bay of Bengal. The cátaka bird is native to Africa. In the spring it crosses over the Arabian Sea and the southern peninsula and enters Bengal. It remains in Bengal during the summer. Once the monsoon starts, it heads westward, crosses back over the Arabian Sea and returns to its homeland – Africa.
summary: The rainy season begins a day or two after the rain clouds reach the Bengal coastal region from the Bay of Bengal.
In the spring it crosses over the Arabian Sea and the southern peninsula and enters Bengal.
Once the monsoon starts, it heads westward, crosses back over the Arabian Sea and returns to its homeland – Africa.

paragraphs.text: As with the crane, this deductive power is highly developed in the egret. Some people call it intuition. Be that as it may, the crane is native to this country. ( 10 )
summary: As with the crane, this deductive power is highly developed in the egret.
Some people call it intuition.
Be that as it may, the crane is native to this country.

paragraphs.text: In ancient times in the central part of Bengal, in the deserted part of the River Mathabhanga, a huge watershed was created. It was a reservoir full of fish. Many mango trees surrounded the reservoir. A flock of cranes used to sit in these trees and spend their days eating fish in the watershed. Due to the overcrowding of these cranes, the place came to be known as Bagula – in spoken Bengali, Boglá. Another place in Báuṋgálisthán was Boguŕá – in spoken language, Bogŕá. In English it was called “Bogŕe”, in Bengali it was spelled Baguŕá. The place in Nadia district I am speaking of is Bagula; even now the elderly people call it Boglá. It is no longer a village; today it is a small town.
summary: In ancient times in the central part of Bengal, in the deserted part of the River Mathabhanga, a huge watershed was created.
Due to the overcrowding of these cranes, the place came to be known as Bagula – in spoken Bengali, Boglá.
It is no longer a village; today it is a small town.

paragraphs.text: Be that as it may, you are well acquainted with the crane. The crane will sit silently, its beak lowered for hours at a time, beside any body of water. It appears as if absorbed in some sort of meditation. Actually, it is not. In reality it is silently sitting there, fixing its gaze on the fish. Lest the fish become alert at the sound of its wings, it continues to maintain that silence. If any person makes a false show of their piousness, or when one in reality is planning something otherwise, we call them vakadhármika [like a crane falsely appearing to be pious]. If any of you are “falsely pious like a crane”, show your true face and let the people know who you are.
summary: Be that as it may, you are well acquainted with the crane.
In reality it is silently sitting there, fixing its gaze on the fish.
If any of you are “falsely pious like a crane”, show your true face and let the people know who you are.

paragraphs.text: The indigenous crane is usually of a pearly white colour. Of course, on the other side of the Himalayas in Tibet, outer Mongolia and Siberia, there are cranes of butter oil colour and of a pale yellow colour. Compared to the Indian cranes, they are slightly smaller in appearance. Each has a small crest on its head. These cranes are very fond of sport. While gathering food, they devote their time for the necessary period, sitting beside the water, lying in wait for unsuspecting fish. Thereafter they become wholly engaged in playing with other cranes. But the use of the word “falsely pious” with reference to these kinds of cranes would not be appropriate. To lay their eggs they come down to the plains in the waterlogged areas of India surrounded by forests, and they settle down there temporarily. At the end of winter, with their little ones in tow – the babies have by this time learned to fly – they cross over to their original home beyond the Himalayas. ( 11 )
summary: The indigenous crane is usually of a pearly white colour.
While gathering food, they devote their time for the necessary period, sitting beside the water, lying in wait for unsuspecting fish.
At the end of winter, with their little ones in tow – the babies have by this time learned to fly – they cross over to their original home beyond the Himalayas.

paragraphs.text: Swan: Most birds belonging to the swan genus are not permanent residents of India. The rájahaḿsa or Indian swans, although they belong to the swan genus, have hardly any ability to fly. The swans we see during the winter are residents of cold countries. To escape from the cold weather and to lay eggs, they come to the comparatively warmer climates of countries like India. These birds come during winter to the Sundarbans of Bengal, to the Kaziranga forest areas of Assam, the wetlands between the Barak and Surma Rivers of Cachar [Assam], Chalanbil of North Bengal, Hizali Bill of Ráŕh, ma-an of Bettiah, (in Bihar the wetland or bill is called ma – a – n), to the ma – an of Lakhandei River near Muzaffarpur, Unnao district of Uttar Pradesh, Bharatpur area of Rajasthan and the region close to the small Rhann of Kucch. They fly at a great height so that hunters cannot kill them easily. ( 12 )
summary: Swan: Most birds belonging to the swan genus are not permanent residents of India.
To escape from the cold weather and to lay eggs, they come to the comparatively warmer climates of countries like India.
They fly at a great height so that hunters cannot kill them easily.

paragraphs.text: Flamingo: The meaning of karaka is a certain type of bird from cold countries that normally comes to India from the end of the month of Karttik [late autumn] to the end of the month of Mágh [winter] and makes temporary nests in areas near different reservoirs and ponds. These guest birds usually make their nests in the tall trees near reservoirs and ponds. They are the old inhabitants of northeast China, Siberia, Russia and Tibet, but due to the oppressive cold in those lands during wintertime it becomes impossible for them to sustain themselves. It is extremely cold, and moreover there is a scarcity of food. Thus they come to India and other hot countries during the winter and remain there for a few months. During this time they lay their eggs, and after their young are somewhat grown they teach them how to fly and how to gather food. Then, when the hot winds begin to blow, they return to their homeland. They return to the exact place they came from, and every year they again return to the same place. By attaching a marker to their legs or through other means, their incredibly- developed intuition and ability to recognize places has been verified. Great crowds of [these flamingos] gather during winter in the Kolkata Zoo, Sandeshkhali of 24 Paraganas, and Bharatpurʼs bird sanctuary. At one time, great numbers of them used to come to Dimdiha village in Purulia District [in Anandanagar]. Since they came here to lay their eggs [d́im], the name of that place became D́imdihá. They can be seen in the marshlands of Bengal during wintertime. Karaka refers to the birds of this flamingo family. ( 13 )
summary: Flamingo: The meaning of karaka is a certain type of bird from cold countries that normally comes to India from the end of the month of Karttik [late autumn] to the end of the month of Mágh [winter] and makes temporary nests in areas near different reservoirs and ponds.
They return to the exact place they came from, and every year they again return to the same place.
Karaka refers to the birds of this flamingo family.

paragraphs.text: Diver bird (pánkaoŕi): Karkat́a is a bird of the kot́ik (kaoŕi) family. When we mention the kot́ika bird family, what is generally seen in Bengal, is the páńkaoŕi [the diver bird, similar to a cormorant]. At one time the diver bird was found in good number in large reservoirs, ponds and marshlands of Bengal. This tri-habitat bird (aquatic, terrestrial and aerial) is similar in nature to the swan or goose. Its body is a blackish colour. Like other non-Indian birds, they are seen in good number in Bengal during the winter season, but also remain there at other times. The author saw flocks of diver birds in Murshidabad Districtʼs Hizalbil during the winter of 1942. One hears that there are not so many pánkaoŕis nowadays. They have been and are still being slaughtered by human beings.
summary: Diver bird (pánkaoŕi): Karkat́a is a bird of the kot́ik (kaoŕi) family.
Its body is a blackish colour.
They have been and are still being slaughtered by human beings.

paragraphs.text: According to the Puranas, just as the mount of the goddess Gauṋgá is the makara [a mythological aquatic creature like the crocodile], similarly Yamunaʼs mount is the pánikot́ika, or pánkaoŕi. According to some of the Puranas, the mount of the god of machines, Vishvakarmá, is also the pánkaoŕi. However there is a difference of opinion about this. ( 14 )
summary: According to the Puranas, just as the mount of the goddess Gauṋgá is the makara [a mythological aquatic creature like the crocodile], similarly Yamunaʼs mount is the pánikot́ika, or pánkaoŕi.
According to some of the Puranas, the mount of the god of machines, Vishvakarmá, is also the pánkaoŕi.
However there is a difference of opinion about this.

paragraphs.text: Migratory bird of the rainy season (cátaka, phiuṋe): Kokila is a word which stands for the Banzalitis (Bánglá or Bánjálá, Latin adjective, Banzalitis) group of phiuṋe birds [fork-tailed birds]. However, in Sanskrit the Banjalities group of birds are not merely called kokila, rather they are called Bauṋga kokila. The original habitat of the phiuṋe or fork-tailed bird is Bengal. Of course, today they are found in all parts of India except the hottest and coldest regions. Usually they do not go outside India even for a change of weather. If at all they migrate, it will be only a brief journey.
summary: Migratory bird of the rainy season (cátaka, phiuṋe): Kokila is a word which stands for the Banzalitis (Bánglá or Bánjálá, Latin adjective, Banzalitis) group of phiuṋe birds [fork-tailed birds].
Of course, today they are found in all parts of India except the hottest and coldest regions.
If at all they migrate, it will be only a brief journey.

paragraphs.text: Birds that arrive in India during winter are not looked upon as Indian birds. We consider them as birds that have arrived to lay eggs. After laying their eggs, they again return to their homeland. There are one or two exceptions, however. The swallow (cátaka), for instance, is an exception. It is a bird of African origin. Normally at the end of winter it crosses the Arabian sea to India and stays for the spring and summer seasons. As the monsoon air arrives from the Bay of Bengal, the cátaka [swallow], with its natural intuition, understands and before the rainy season starts and the monsoon air blows, it begins its journey back home. With the return of the swallow, the ornithologists understand that in a week or maximum ten days time, the rainy season will begin. The phiuṋe are found to cross over the northern part of the Bay of Bengal; they do not like to go often to the southern part. So in the Andamans, the phiuṋe of Indian species are scarcely found. The phiuṋe of Indonesian variety are found in the Nicobar islands. Phiuṋe are not ferocious like doels. ( 15 )
summary: Birds that arrive in India during winter are not looked upon as Indian birds.
Normally at the end of winter it crosses the Arabian sea to India and stays for the spring and summer seasons.
Phiuṋe are not ferocious like doels.

paragraphs.text: Parrot, Cockatoo: You surely must be aware of the fact that talking birds are by common consensus divided into two groups: one group is called shuk, and the other group is known as sárii or sáriká. These two groups of birds are talking birds. The beaks of the birds, called shuk, are thick at the source and thin or pointed at the end; they are curved. The beaks of shuks are generally red in colour. Of course, there are some birds of the shuk group whose beaks are not exactly red in colour. Our family birds like t́iyá [parrot], ban-tiyá [wild parrot], candaná [a kind of parrot having red streaks around its throat] and kákátuá (cockatoo) all belong to the shuk group. They appear to be green, yellowish-green or white in outward appearance. Owls do not come out in the day time. Yet, they are similar in appearance to the shuk birds. Owls, however, are not talking birds. Shuks are called sugá in Urdu. The exquisitely red beak of the shuk became sweet indeed in the poetʼs imagination. When looking at the lush red colour of palásh [Butea monosperma] blossoms in the spring, a question arose in the poetʼs mind as to whether it was really a flower or the red beak of the shuk bird. Speaking in Sanskrit, the poet asked, “Was it shuk?” “Kiḿ Shuka?” So from Sanskrit the flower came to be known as kiḿshuka.
summary: Parrot, Cockatoo: You surely must be aware of the fact that talking birds are by common consensus divided into two groups: one group is called shuk, and the other group is known as sárii or sáriká.
Owls do not come out in the day time.
” So from Sanskrit the flower came to be known as kiḿshuka.

paragraphs.text: Among these talking birds, the parrot, the wild parrot and candaná belong to eastern India, and in particular are the local birds of Bengal. The cockatoo is a bird that comes from outside India.
summary: Among these talking birds, the parrot, the wild parrot and candaná belong to eastern India, and in particular are the local birds of Bengal.
The cockatoo is a bird that comes from outside India.

paragraphs.text: The beak of birds belonging to the sárii group is straight and pointed. Our indigenous myna ( 1 ) were the primary species among the birds of the sárii category. Its original habitat was eastern India, especially Ráŕh and Orissa. Millions [of these birds] thrived in the forests of Midnapur, Bhanjabhum, Bankura and Birbhum. The parrot, the wild parrot, the wild myna or pied myna belong to the shuk category of birds. Of course they cannot talk like the mynas. Mynas also have a well developed vocabulary. They articulate many words among themselves.
summary: The beak of birds belonging to the sárii group is straight and pointed.
The parrot, the wild parrot, the wild myna or pied myna belong to the shuk category of birds.
They articulate many words among themselves.

paragraphs.text: The quarrelling among the shálikhs [small, yellow beak birds of the house-myna species] is indeed worth watching. In South Bengal, in the wetlands surrounded by small patches of marshland, there once lived many shálikhs [sárii group] in a big banyan tree, due to which the village came to be known as Shálikhá. It is now an important part of Howrah town. Some people erroneously call this area Salkia. This mistake should be corrected.
summary: The quarrelling among the shálikhs [small, yellow beak birds of the house-myna species] is indeed worth watching.
It is now an important part of Howrah town.
This mistake should be corrected.

paragraphs.text: Our familiar birds – the bábui (weaver-bird, báyá ciŕiá in Urdu), t́unt́uni (tailor bird in English, in Urdu julhá-ciŕiyá), bulbuli (in English nightingale, in Urdu bulbul) – they all belong to the sárii group. Those of you who are familiar with Vaeśńava literature must have heard or read the narrative of Shuk-Sárii called Krśńakathá related to Rádhá and Krśńa. Among the talking birds of Bengal, the candaná belonging to the shuk group and the myna belonging to the sárii group are more gifted than other birds. During the last fifty years, thousands of birds have been exported abroad from Tripura, Midnapur and Bhanjabhum. India is becoming devoid of myna birds. I am drawing the attention of everyone to this development. Candaná are normally very limited in number. Their numbers are continuing to diminish. Perhaps they are also being secretly exported abroad.
summary: Our familiar birds – the bábui (weaver-bird, báyá ciŕiá in Urdu), t́unt́uni (tailor bird in English, in Urdu julhá-ciŕiyá), bulbuli (in English nightingale, in Urdu bulbul) – they all belong to the sárii group.
India is becoming devoid of myna birds.
Perhaps they are also being secretly exported abroad.

paragraphs.text: There was a time when most people belonging to the middle class along with wealthy families used to keep birds as pets in their houses. They normally kept myna or candaná as pets. These two kinds of birds are very calm and quiet. Cockatoos are also talented talking birds. However, they are comparatively larger in size. Their attitude is quite aggressive. That is why they are kept chained to a stand. During the Moghul period even the parrots and candaná were kept chained to a stand. Today they are simply kept in cages. The number of birds is rapidly diminishing. Due to a dearth of money, householders are giving up many of their luxurious habits. Like the dodo birds, these other birds are also awaiting their final days. ( 2 )
summary: There was a time when most people belonging to the middle class along with wealthy families used to keep birds as pets in their houses.
That is why they are kept chained to a stand.
Like the dodo birds, these other birds are also awaiting their final days.

paragraphs.text: Myna, Magpie Robin: Mynas are talking birds. An entity which speaks its own language and also utters the words of others, that is, speaks various words, is known as harabolá [capable of mimicking various voices]. The word har [various] comes from the Persian language. In between the house myna and myna there is a bird species that the villagers of Burdwan district call guye myná or guye nyákŕá [wild myna]. These can also be trained to talk. Normally people do not keep wild mynas as pets, but they do keep other mynas. In Sanskrit mynas are called sáriká. Among the more familiar birds of Ráŕh are mynas, red-throated parrots and cockatoos.
summary: Myna, Magpie Robin: Mynas are talking birds.
These can also be trained to talk.
Among the more familiar birds of Ráŕh are mynas, red-throated parrots and cockatoos.

paragraphs.text: Among the birds belonging to the parrot order, there are cockatoos of different colours – light-green, yellowish, with specks in the throat – candanás of normal appearance and green, hefty parrots, wild parrots and the green-coloured magpie robin (doyel) of Bengal, which are commonly seen in northern Bengal and rarely seen in southern Bengal. Of this group, candanás prefer to stay away from human localities; cockatoos prefer to stay in a humid environment at a distance from such localities. Wild parrots remain in the forest and fly over human localities. They rarely rest at any particular spot. Magpie robins live close to settled habitats, always moving in search of insects. They are very cruel and ferocious in nature.
summary: Among the birds belonging to the parrot order, there are cockatoos of different colours – light-green, yellowish, with specks in the throat – candanás of normal appearance and green, hefty parrots, wild parrots and the green-coloured magpie robin (doyel) of Bengal, which are commonly seen in northern Bengal and rarely seen in southern Bengal.
They rarely rest at any particular spot.
They are very cruel and ferocious in nature.

paragraphs.text: Amongst all these, candanás and cockatoos are talking birds. Magpie robins are not talking birds, but their notes are very sweet. Parrots and wild parrots do not have sweet notes, but are very impressive in appearance. In Sanskrit the parrot is called shuk, and their beaks are scarlet-red in colour like ripe telakucás [vegetables like the wax gourd but without stripes]. There is a couplet [a riddle] about the pineapple which says, “From the forest emerges the parrot, with a golden crown on its head.” ( 3 )
summary: Amongst all these, candanás and cockatoos are talking birds.
Parrots and wild parrots do not have sweet notes, but are very impressive in appearance.
There is a couplet [a riddle] about the pineapple which says, “From the forest emerges the parrot, with a golden crown on its head.

paragraphs.text: Pigeon: By kapota we mean pigeon. From the word kapota comes the word kabutar, and from the word párávat is derived the word páyrá. Kapotaraka > kaotara > kautar > kabutara. By adding the suffix kan to kapota we form the word kapotaka. The word kapota refers to any aircraft, but the word kapotaka means pigeon and nothing else. The etymological meaning of grha kapota is any domesticated pigeon. In common usage it refers to house pigeon or golá páyrá. In ancient times, the people of Ráŕh had boundless affection for birds and animals. To prevent people from flaying the skin of dead animals, they even used to dig pits near the path by their home to bury the corpses of dead animals [cows and other animals] so that no one could come to flay their skin secretly or carry away their flesh by digging them out. To prevent hawks and greedy persons from killing the pigeons, local people, while constructing their mud homes, used to insert clay pitchers at a slant in the wall. Pigeons could use the pitchersʼ opening as an entrance to reach their nests inside. I do not know if this is done nowadays, but they used to do it earlier. Since pigeons lived in homes, they were called grha kapota [domesticated pigeons] or golá páyrá. They were so called because they used to live on the paddy corns of the corn bin in houses. ( 1 )
summary: Pigeon: By kapota we mean pigeon.
In ancient times, the people of Ráŕh had boundless affection for birds and animals.
They were so called because they used to live on the paddy corns of the corn bin in houses.

paragraphs.text: Ka means “water”, pota means “ship”. That which does a shipʼs work at the time of crossing a large reservoir, lake or sea is kapota. That is its etymological meaning. The colloquial meaning of the word kapota is ghugu [“dove”] and páyrá [“pigeon”]. In olden days, when roads were not well-developed, people used to send messages to distant lands with the help of trained pigeons or doves. Generally a letter was attached to one of the birdʼs limbs. Once those trained doves or pigeons arrived at their destination, they would then carry back a reply. This system of mail delivery with the help of these birds was prevalent for many years on the battlefield. Pigeon post was even used in some places in India during British rule. From this word kapota or kapotaraka we obtain the word kabutara (in Mymensingh Bengali, kaetara). However, for “pigeon” the word páyrá is better than the word kabutara, because páyrá has come from the Sanskrit word párávata. Párávata refers only to “pigeon” and not to “dove”, but kapota means both “pigeon” and “dove”. The feminine form of kapota is kapotii; another meaning of kapotii is “a small, ocean-going vessel”.
summary: Ka means “water”, pota means “ship”.
Once those trained doves or pigeons arrived at their destination, they would then carry back a reply.
The feminine form of kapota is kapotii; another meaning of kapotii is “a small, ocean-going vessel”.

paragraphs.text: The original home of our well-known domesticated pigeon (golá páyrá) is Bengal, but the non-domesticated pigeon (lakká páyrá) came from elsewhere. The dodo bird, which disappeared from the earth approximately one hundred years ago due to the malevolence of human beings, evolved from this domesticated pigeon.
summary: The original home of our well-known domesticated pigeon (golá páyrá) is Bengal, but the non-domesticated pigeon (lakká páyrá) came from elsewhere.
The dodo bird, which disappeared from the earth approximately one hundred years ago due to the malevolence of human beings, evolved from this domesticated pigeon.

paragraphs.text: People scatter kernels of grain in front of pigeons, or on their usual path, for them to eat. This scattering is called “pigeon feeding.” At the end of autumn, when the paddy fields are somewhat muddy, seeds are scattered in those paddy fields where it is not possible to sow seeds for the winter season, or where, due to lack of water, those seeds will not sprout in the dead of winter even if sown. These sprout and grow into plants in the spaces between the paddy. When the paddy is harvested, the tops of these plants are also cut. As a result, more branches grow, and at the end of the cold season they yield a generous amount of flowers and pods. This type of seed-scattered crop is called the “pyra crop” [pigeon-harvest]. Small lentils, gram or blackish-coloured small gram [also called t́hikre cholá], pea [blackish-coloured, small pea, also called t́hikre mat́ar], rapeseed, khesári or teoŕá (triput́ii or triput́iká – Lathirus sativas) – these crops are generally produced as part of the pyra crop. In most parts of Bihar, the pyra cropping is called páyruyá. On land where there is no system of irrigation, or where the soil becomes hard or cracked at the end of winter, the produce from the pyra cropping is of great benefit to the farmers. Moreover, this pyra crop increases the soilʼs fertility and productivity. As for the surplus, the stalks, pod husks and chaff make excellent bird food and cattle fodder. If mustard is planted, it yields oil cake which can be used as both fertilizer and bird food.
summary: People scatter kernels of grain in front of pigeons, or on their usual path, for them to eat.
This type of seed-scattered crop is called the “pyra crop” [pigeon-harvest].
If mustard is planted, it yields oil cake which can be used as both fertilizer and bird food.

paragraphs.text: Although it is slightly off the topic, it is worth mentioning that, as far as possible, it is better not to feed pigeons by scattering wheat grains, because in many peopleʼs opinion, pigeons may contract dysentery if they eat too much wheat grain [gam]. Godhúma > gohúma > gaham > gam. The word gaham is prevalent in western Ráŕh and Orissa. That river water which is transparent like the eyes of a pigeon is called kapotákśa in masculine gender and kapotákśii in feminine gender. Michael Madhusudhan Datta was born in Sagardáṋri village, which is situated on the bank of the Kapotákśii River in Jessore District. ( 2 )

The word gaham is prevalent in western Ráŕh and Orissa.

paragraphs.text: Peacock: The peacock (mayúr) is a special bird of India. Its original habitat is Southeast Asia. The male peacock can spread its tail and dance; the female peacock has no tail and never dances. It is also ugly to look at. It generally prefers a dry climate, and cannot lay eggs in a humid environment. There may be peacocks in damp forest areas, but for laying eggs they move away to distant drier climates. In Bengal, rather in eastern India, there are few peacocks in the forest areas due to excessive rain. In the Bankura and Purulia districts of western Ráŕh, some peacocks are found in the forests because of the dry climate. Due to the dry climate in western India, especially in Rajasthan and Gujarat, peacocks abound.
summary: Peacock: The peacock (mayúr) is a special bird of India.
It generally prefers a dry climate, and cannot lay eggs in a humid environment.
Due to the dry climate in western India, especially in Rajasthan and Gujarat, peacocks abound.

paragraphs.text: There are generally three different types of peacocks: (1) Our very familiar, colourful peacocks, (2) yellowish peacocks, and (3) white peacocks from Burma and Thailand (Shyámdesh). White peacocks can somehow tolerate a humid environment. Another name for peacock is shikhii. The call of the peacock is known as keká. Hence the word keká means peacock. In ancient times the peacock was a favorite food item for human beings. Emperor Ashoka did not entirely forbid the butchering of peacocks in his kitchen, even after his transformation into Dharmáshoka [non-violent or Buddhist Ashoka].
summary: There are generally three different types of peacocks: (1) Our very familiar, colourful peacocks, (2) yellowish peacocks, and (3) white peacocks from Burma and Thailand (Shyámdesh).
The call of the peacock is known as keká.
Emperor Ashoka did not entirely forbid the butchering of peacocks in his kitchen, even after his transformation into Dharmáshoka [non-violent or Buddhist Ashoka].

paragraphs.text: Mayúr is originally a Sanskrit word; the feminine of mayúr is mayúrii. The Hindi translation of the word is mor; its feminine form is morni. The meat of the female peacock tastes bitter. That is why normally people never kill female peacocks. Today the peacock has been given recognition as the national bird of India. ( 3 )
summary: Mayúr is originally a Sanskrit word; the feminine of mayúr is mayúrii.

paragraphs.text: Crow: The verbal root kae means “to give a dreadful shout” or “to give an ear-splitting cry”. By adding the suffix kan to the verbal root kae, we obtain the word káka, whose etymological meaning is “one who shouts in an ugly manner”. Bhola Mayra [a literary character] has said – “If the cawing of crows and the beating of drums cease, it is good.”

By adding the suffix kan to the verbal root kae, we obtain the word káka, whose etymological meaning is “one who shouts in an ugly manner”.

paragraphs.text: There are many colloquial meanings of the word káka, the ordinary crow that we commonly see. According to biologists, the crow is not a very old bird. This half-carnivorous bird (it has an equal fondness for both vegetarian and non-vegetarian food) is renowned for its intelligence. In Bihar it is said, manukhme (one writes it as mánuś but pronounces it manukh) naová, ciṋŕai me kaová. [“Among humans the barber, and among birds the crow.”] That is, among human beings, the most intelligent are the barbers; among birds it is the crow. Their solidarity is also praiseworthy.
summary: There are many colloquial meanings of the word káka, the ordinary crow that we commonly see.
In Bihar it is said, manukhme (one writes it as mánuś but pronounces it manukh) naová, ciṋŕai me kaová.
Their solidarity is also praiseworthy.

paragraphs.text: The solidarity of crows is indeed laudable. If someone kills a single crow, then within a short period of time a great number of crows will gather there and try to collectively harass the killer. When crows gather somewhere in a group, that assembly of crows is also called káka, but the word for this assembly of crows is feminine plural, that is, kákáh (like the plural form of latá). ( 4 )

If someone kills a single crow, then within a short period of time a great number of crows will gather there and try to collectively harass the killer.
When crows gather somewhere in a group, that assembly of crows is also called káka, but the word for this assembly of crows is feminine plural, that is, kákáh (like the plural form of latá).

paragraphs.text: Perhaps you know that crows are generally of three types – (1) general crow, (2) jackdaw (raven), and (3) white crow.
summary: Perhaps you know that crows are generally of three types – (1) general crow, (2) jackdaw (raven), and (3) white crow.

paragraphs.text: You might have seen general crows very often in the streets and on the rooftop and courtyard of your house. Jackdaws are fewer in number, somewhat larger in size and black in colour. Their voice is extremely harsh… something like ka, ka, ka (kka). Their beaks are a little longer and harder than those of general crows. The colour of white crows is not exactly white; rather, it is grey. In ancient times, white crows used to be called báyasa. Nowadays báyasa means any type of crow. In northern India crows are called kaová, and jackdaws are called kág. In Auṋgiká language, jackdaws are called dṋáŕkaová. In the language of Ráŕh, Bengal, they are called ko or koy.
summary: You might have seen general crows very often in the streets and on the rooftop and courtyard of your house.
In ancient times, white crows used to be called báyasa.
In the language of Ráŕh, Bengal, they are called ko or koy.

paragraphs.text: Crows make many hard food items edible by pecking. They can very easily pierce the meat of any animal into pieces and eat it. Hence all species of crows are called khat́akhádaka. Crows have absolutely no prejudice against any type of food. Hence they will even eat something that is unfit for consumption (in Sanskrit, called kákánna).
summary: Crows make many hard food items edible by pecking.
Hence all species of crows are called khat́akhádaka.
Hence they will even eat something that is unfit for consumption (in Sanskrit, called kákánna).

paragraphs.text: The second meaning of khat́akhádaka is byághra (vi – a – ghra + a = byághra) or tiger. That is, an animal whose sense of smell is very strong. If a tiger gets a promising scent, it easily locates the prey and pounces on it. Just as a crow is termed a khat́akhádaka due to the strength of its beak, so also a tiger is called a khat́akhádaka by virtue of its strong claws and teeth. Another characteristic of the tiger is that, simply by supposition, it makes a calculated leap so as to fall exactly on its prey.
summary: The second meaning of khat́akhádaka is byághra (vi – a – ghra + a = byághra) or tiger.
If a tiger gets a promising scent, it easily locates the prey and pounces on it.
Another characteristic of the tiger is that, simply by supposition, it makes a calculated leap so as to fall exactly on its prey.

paragraphs.text: Another meaning of the word khat́akhádaka is sheyál or jackal (synonymous words are shrgál, shibá, jambuka). Jackals will eat the rotten meat that even vultures are averse to eating. Hence jackals are also famous as khat́akhádaka.
summary: Another meaning of the word khat́akhádaka is sheyál or jackal (synonymous words are shrgál, shibá, jambuka).
Jackals will eat the rotten meat that even vultures are averse to eating.
Hence jackals are also famous as khat́akhádaka.

paragraphs.text: Even in the case of human beings, you will come across some who are khat́akhádaka. Just go to a fish market at the peak of the rainy season and you will see many gentlemen buying rotten hilsas. Are these human beings in any way superior to jackals? Hence for this kind of person, you can certainly use the word khat́akhádaka. You will sometimes find certain ladies cutting freshwater barbel and catfish in a very cruel manner…, breaking the claws of a Chilka lake lobster, stabbing young anabas and twisting and wringing them ruthlessly. They are, of course, ladies, but they are certainly khat́akhádaka. ( 5 )
summary: Even in the case of human beings, you will come across some who are khat́akhádaka.
Hence for this kind of person, you can certainly use the word khat́akhádaka.
They are, of course, ladies, but they are certainly khat́akhádaka.

paragraphs.text: Owl and Crow: Kákári: Káka + ari = kákári. Kákasya arih ityarthe kákárih (śaśt́ii tatpuruśa samása ( 6 ). Ari means “enemy”. Thus the etymological meaning of kákári is “owl”. Owls (pecá or pecaka) cannot see during the day. If a crow spies an owl during the day it will peck at it. Fearful of crows, the owl hides itself in the dark crevices of trees during the day. Crows cannot see at night, so if an owl sees a crow at night it attacks it. But since crows have more strength in their beaks than owls they save themselves somehow. Thus, it is seen that it is the crowʼs young that are generally killed by owls. If an owl is not overly hungry it will not eat crow-meat. Since the crowʼs meat is bad-tasting, no bird will eat it apart from the vulture. It is said that the crow eats any kind of meat, but it also will not eat crow-meat. ( 7 )
summary: Owl and Crow: Kákári: Káka + ari = kákári.
Crows cannot see at night, so if an owl sees a crow at night it attacks it.
It is said that the crow eats any kind of meat, but it also will not eat crow-meat.

paragraphs.text: The story goes that the cuckoo is unable to give warmth to its eggs. So in the absence of the crow, it goes to the crowʼs nest and lays its eggs there. The crow mistakenly treats the cuckooʼs eggs as its own, provides them warmth and takes care of them. When the young appear, breaking through their shells and beginning to cry, the sound of the cuckoo is noticed. When the crow realizes that it has mistakenly taken care of young babies not its own, it drives them out of the nest. That is why the crow which tends the children of others is called paravrta and the cuckoo is also called paravrta because it has been looked after by others. In this context it should be remembered that the sweet cooing of the cuckoo is done by the male bird in the spring season, not by the the female cuckoo (kokilá). In one Hindi poem it is said: koeli nahi bolti hái. [The female cuckoo does not sing.] In reality, during the rainy season it is the dardoor [male frog] that calls and not the darduri or dáduri, although in one song it is said, dáke dáduri [the female frog sings].

The female frog looks on calmly; it is the male frog that swells its wind pipe and cries loudly.

paragraphs.text: Sparrow: The meaning of the word grhacát́aka is sparrow or caŕuii bird. Cát́aka > cad́a-a > cad́ái > caŕái; cát́akii >cad́a-i > cad́ui > caŕui. In Bengali both the words cat́ái and caŕui are in use. In western Ráŕh, most people in rural areas call the bird cat́ui. The word cat́ui comes from the word cat́aka. In the Magahii language of Bihar it is called garbaiyá. In Maithili also it is called garbaiyá or sometime phuddi. In Bhojpuri it is called phurguddi. The sparrow is divided into two groups: those that build nests in the cornices of wealthy houses called grhacát́aka or sparrows. Sparrows cannot build their nests carefully and neatly with straw and dry grass as pigeons do.

paragraphs.text: In the world of birds, the largest ones – the eagles and the condors – also cannot build their nests. Although belonging to the eagle group but comparatively smaller in appearance, Indian vultures somehow build their resting places on the thicker branches of large trees. Smaller birds like weaver birds build strong nests. They usually build their nests on palm trees or on the higher branches of tall trees. Tailor birds also build strong nests by stitching up the leaves of trees with their beaks. Both pigeons and sparrows, since they are incapable of building their nests [in trees], have their resting places in the crevices of rocks or hills. Titir or partridge birds also do the same, although they somehow manage to build lower quality homes for themselves in the cornices of wealthy houses.

paragraphs.text: The wild sparrows that do not stay in houses live instead in small trees close to paddy fields. The primary activity of these birds is to pick up and eat whatever remnants of crops remain in the fields after harvesting. In Bengal there are very few swallow species. In the winter, they arrive in limited numbers from western countries after the paddy is harvested. They live close to the paddy fields in small trees. They stay for a fortnight or more and then return to the west.

paragraphs.text: Ducks and Chickens: Ke + ru + ac = Keraba. The word ke means “in water”. The verb ru means to make noise in joy. So the word koeraba means the bird that makes noise when submerged in water. Keraba means “ducks” (pátiháṋs). When they come across water, they run and utter joyful sounds like ‘quack, quack’. In this connection, we should remember that although the Bengali word háṋs has come from the Sanskrit word haḿsa, in Sanskrit the word haḿsa does not refer to any particular species of duck; it refers only to the swan (rájhaḿsa). For swan there is another word in Sanskrit, marál, which is now known to belong to the flamingo group. For different species of ducks (háṋs) familiar to us, the Sanskrit name is keraba; for the swan, marál or Haḿsa. In Sanskrit the use of the word rájhaḿsa is very limited; rather, it is hardly used. For duck, the word keraba is used, and for another variety of duck, that is, for the Chinese duck (ciiná patiháṋs), the Sanskrit word is krśńa-keraba or piuṋgal keraba. For sand-coloured duck (báli háṋs), the name used is baláká [a small goose capable of flying high].
summary: Ducks and Chickens: Ke + ru + ac = Keraba.

In this connection, we should remember that although the Bengali word háṋs has come from the Sanskrit word haḿsa, in Sanskrit the word haḿsa does not refer to any particular species of duck; it refers only to the swan (rájhaḿsa).
For sand-coloured duck (báli háṋs), the name used is baláká [a small goose capable of flying high].

paragraphs.text: Although the technical title for Chinese duck is ciiná pátiháṋs, the phrase is self-contradictory. The word páti refers to anything indigenous. So how can anything indigenous to India be Chinese? This is very much like the word ‘lemon-indica’ or ‘lemon banjalitis,’ which in Bengal is called páti nebu. This slightly elongated lemon with sweet-smelling skin that we call kágjii nebu has come from overseas. Some kágjii Muslims of the Hoogly district of West Bengal were engaged in the business of producing a thick, ancient variety of paper called kágaz. After their traditional occupations were ruined, they went to South America and brought the elongated lemon back with them to India. Since it was a group of kágjii Muslims that brought these lemons to India, they have come to be known as kágjii nebu.
summary: Although the technical title for Chinese duck is ciiná pátiháṋs, the phrase is self-contradictory.
This slightly elongated lemon with sweet-smelling skin that we call kágjii nebu has come from overseas.
Since it was a group of kágjii Muslims that brought these lemons to India, they have come to be known as kágjii nebu.

paragraphs.text: Towards the end of the Moghul period, a particular kind of duck brought from China has come to be known as ciiná háṋs. They lay more eggs than the indigenous ducks. There is very little expenditure in keeping indigenous ducks. All that is required is some food for the ducklings and a room to keep them safe from snakes, mongooses and jackals. This takes very little expense. The maintenance of the Chinese duck is quite similar, although not identical. Chinese ducks are quite prone to disease – at the slightest infection they die in droves. The jackals, of course, make an inroad on the duck population, but only when they get opportunity and time. However, they do pay more attention to the Chinese ducks. Hence to maintain Chinese ducks, the owner has to be additionally concerned about their safety. For these reasons, despite their yielding a greater quantity of eggs, the domestication of Chinese ducks never became popular. In contrast, the people of Bengal have been keeping indigenous ducks for at least three thousand years.
summary: Towards the end of the Moghul period, a particular kind of duck brought from China has come to be known as ciiná háṋs.
Chinese ducks are quite prone to disease – at the slightest infection they die in droves.
In contrast, the people of Bengal have been keeping indigenous ducks for at least three thousand years.

paragraphs.text: Unlike maintaining hens, there is very little risk in keeping indigenous ducks. Since they do not eat up any vegetation, there is no danger of getting involved in quarrels with the neighbours. They do not enter the houses and make them dirty, since they are drawn only to the water.
summary: Unlike maintaining hens, there is very little risk in keeping indigenous ducks.
Since they do not eat up any vegetation, there is no danger of getting involved in quarrels with the neighbours.
They do not enter the houses and make them dirty, since they are drawn only to the water.

paragraphs.text: The Ráŕh region of Bengal is a land of sticky [clay] soil. Hence the ponds of that area have greater capacity to retain water, and there are greater numbers of these ponds. Due to the easy availability of these ponds, keeping ducks has been a very popular practice in present day Ráŕh, what to speak of ancient Ráŕh.
summary: The Ráŕh region of Bengal is a land of sticky [clay] soil.
Hence the ponds of that area have greater capacity to retain water, and there are greater numbers of these ponds.
Due to the easy availability of these ponds, keeping ducks has been a very popular practice in present day Ráŕh, what to speak of ancient Ráŕh.

paragraphs.text: The presence of ducks, unlike that of hens, has never been detrimental to the health of householders. For this reason people have always built a room for ducks near the doorstep. In the morning the doors are thrown open, and the ducks immediately run to the ponds. The resident then retrieves the eggs from their room. We experienced this regularly in our childhood days.
summary: The presence of ducks, unlike that of hens, has never been detrimental to the health of householders.
In the morning the doors are thrown open, and the ducks immediately run to the ponds.
We experienced this regularly in our childhood days.

paragraphs.text: In ancient Bengal, although there were plenty of wild hens, cocks and waterfowl, people rarely kept hens (murgii) at home, chiefly because the hens made the houses and courtyards dirty, ate up the neighboursʼ plants and trees, and ate repulsive offal before the very eyes of their owners. Of course, the people of Bengal also hunted wild cocks and hens in those days. Wild cocks can fly; even the domesticated fowl can fly to an extent, but certain ducks are unable to fly. So it is quite convenient for people to keep ducks. For the indigenous ducks it is also convenient because otherwise their lives would have been endangered.
summary: In ancient Bengal, although there were plenty of wild hens, cocks and waterfowl, people rarely kept hens (murgii) at home, chiefly because the hens made the houses and courtyards dirty, ate up the neighboursʼ plants and trees, and ate repulsive offal before the very eyes of their owners.
Wild cocks can fly; even the domesticated fowl can fly to an extent, but certain ducks are unable to fly.
For the indigenous ducks it is also convenient because otherwise their lives would have been endangered.

paragraphs.text: Most birds belonging to the class of flamingos or geese can fly well – they can fly ceaselessly for several hundred miles. Despite also belonging to that class, the common duck cannot fly. Hence by maintaining geese, only the geese themselves are benefited. People are hardly benefited because goose eggs are very hot and are hence unpopular. They also lay fewer eggs.
summary: Most birds belonging to the class of flamingos or geese can fly well – they can fly ceaselessly for several hundred miles.
Hence by maintaining geese, only the geese themselves are benefited.
They also lay fewer eggs.

paragraphs.text: Wild cocks are primarily birds that fly in the sky, while ducks are birds that live in water or at times are amphibious – they live in water as well as on land. Both geese and ducks eat water insects and moss and keep the ponds clean. From that point of view, geese and ducks have an important role to play in the rural ecology.
summary: Wild cocks are primarily birds that fly in the sky, while ducks are birds that live in water or at times are amphibious – they live in water as well as on land.
Both geese and ducks eat water insects and moss and keep the ponds clean.
From that point of view, geese and ducks have an important role to play in the rural ecology.

paragraphs.text: Those who keep geese, ducks and Chinese ducks must ensure that there are no big holes or ditches around the ponds in which jackals might live. I do not want jackals to be destroyed as a species. Let them live near the river beds or in the forests; but if they reside on the banks of ponds, the lives of ducks are endangered. People who keep ducks in their home should always have some lime and turmeric paste handy. When the jackals attack the ducks and leave them behind after a chase, the application of lime and turmeric paste helps the wounded ducks to survive. ( 1 )
summary: Those who keep geese, ducks and Chinese ducks must ensure that there are no big holes or ditches around the ponds in which jackals might live.
Let them live near the river beds or in the forests; but if they reside on the banks of ponds, the lives of ducks are endangered.
When the jackals attack the ducks and leave them behind after a chase, the application of lime and turmeric paste helps the wounded ducks to survive.

paragraphs.text: The word koke stands for ducklings. You all know that most birds peck at crumbs of food or grains. So, most of them belong to the group called koke. This word properly applies to ducks and especially to ducklings. They eat more food than required and hence, many ducklings die of stomach ailments.
summary: The word koke stands for ducklings.
So, most of them belong to the group called koke.
They eat more food than required and hence, many ducklings die of stomach ailments.

paragraphs.text: This also applies to hens, especially their little ones. Due to excessive eating, and indiscriminate intake of food that is unfit for consumption, they often have epidemics of stomach ailments. In a short time, due to such epidemics, villages can loose their entire hen population.
summary: This also applies to hens, especially their little ones.
Due to excessive eating, and indiscriminate intake of food that is unfit for consumption, they often have epidemics of stomach ailments.
In a short time, due to such epidemics, villages can loose their entire hen population.

paragraphs.text: Those who keep hens or ducks must pay strict attention to this habit of overeating by the chicks and ducklings. Sometimes, thousands of them are involved. They must see to it that the little ones do not eat any kind of food indiscriminately. The chicks and ducklings should be given tender leaves and only little snails to eat; big snails must not be given to them as food. They must not be given grains of paddy; only when they are slightly grown up can they be given paddy grains. Wheat grains should not be given to hens or ducks of any age. Ducks, hens and pigeons can suffer from diarrhea due to eating wheat grains. ( 2 )
summary: Those who keep hens or ducks must pay strict attention to this habit of overeating by the chicks and ducklings.
The chicks and ducklings should be given tender leaves and only little snails to eat; big snails must not be given to them as food.
Ducks, hens and pigeons can suffer from diarrhea due to eating wheat grains.
