paragraphs.text: Evolution of the ape family – tailless apes:
summary: Evolution of the ape family – tailless apes:

paragraphs.text: You all know that animals are chiefly of two types, graminivorous (feeding on grasses and cereals) and carnivorous. Graminivorous animals usually have hooves and are without paws, while carnivorous animals have paws for feet. Graminivorous animals have sparkling white teeth which are carefully arranged. Carnivorous animals have uneven teeth, slightly yellowish, or reddish yellow in colour. They have canine teeth on both sides of the mouth for tearing flesh.
summary: You all know that animals are chiefly of two types, graminivorous (feeding on grasses and cereals) and carnivorous.
Graminivorous animals have sparkling white teeth which are carefully arranged.
They have canine teeth on both sides of the mouth for tearing flesh.

paragraphs.text: Among graminivorous animals, particularly those creatures belonging to the zebu species (or bison genus) had an ability to store food in their appendix. This developed during ancient times, when they lived in a volatile situation, unsure of obtaining food at all times. Apes, humans and goats all developed this capacity. Cows and buffaloes also did, and they still do today. As life becomes more and more secure, the necessity for this appendix also diminishes. This has happened to humans, apes and certain other animals. During leisure time, by regurgitating food from the appendix, these animals make it fit for digestion with the help of saliva. In English this is called rumination or chewing the cud; in Bengali it is called románthan or jábar kát́á. Carnivorous animals do not have this capacity, because the meat they have eaten quickly decomposes and develops a foul odour. It cannot be used for rumination or for chewing the cud.
summary: Among graminivorous animals, particularly those creatures belonging to the zebu species (or bison genus) had an ability to store food in their appendix.
This has happened to humans, apes and certain other animals.
It cannot be used for rumination or for chewing the cud.

paragraphs.text: In ancient times, those land-dwelling, graminivorous animals without horns or claws for self-preservation began to climb trees in search of safe refuge. For those animals, just as the necessity for using hooves came to an end, they now felt the need for using their forelimbs to catch hold of tree branches. They used their hind legs partly for clutching and partly for running. They used their forelimbs for clutching branches of trees as well as for other tasks. In ancient times, the forelimbs were earlier called kara, and later hasta. Australopithecines, creatures of the ape family, and human beings are all equipped with kara. In fact, they have four limbs; but human beings are not quadrupeds because their forelimbs are used for clutching objects.
summary: In ancient times, those land-dwelling, graminivorous animals without horns or claws for self-preservation began to climb trees in search of safe refuge.
They used their forelimbs for clutching branches of trees as well as for other tasks.
In fact, they have four limbs; but human beings are not quadrupeds because their forelimbs are used for clutching objects.

paragraphs.text: In order to climb trees and to leap up, the creatures of the ape family required a tail. However, for the more intelligent [members] of this family who no longer needed to leap as much, the importance of the lymphatic gland diminished and their tails dropped off. This superfamily of creatures – the apes – gradually split into two family lines. Both families had well-arranged teeth and no canine teeth. Both had an intestinal appendix, but one family had a tail and the other was tailless. Those with tails, belonging to the ape family, are called monkeys – in Bengali bánar or bádar, and the females bánarii or bádarii, in Urdu bandar, and the females bandariá. The tailless monkeys had greater intellectual development than those with tails. They also evolved into two different classes: one ordinary and the other more developed. Of the ordinary tailless apes there were again three distinct genuses; 1) gorillas, 2) orang-utans (in Malay language it means “men of the trees”) and 3) chimpanzees. Today the developed, tailless apes are known as humans. The word “man” stands for “mentally developed ape”.
summary: In order to climb trees and to leap up, the creatures of the ape family required a tail.
Those with tails, belonging to the ape family, are called monkeys – in Bengali bánar or bádar, and the females bánarii or bádarii, in Urdu bandar, and the females bandariá.
The word “man” stands for “mentally developed ape”.

paragraphs.text: This is how we differentiate the types of graminivorous animals. The human being is naturally a vegetarian creature without a developed intestinal appendix. So regular intake of meat might cause the ailment of appendicitis in humans – this does occur often. Regular intake of meat for humans is an unnatural habit which does not provide any benefit. ( 1 )
summary: This is how we differentiate the types of graminivorous animals.
So regular intake of meat might cause the ailment of appendicitis in humans – this does occur often.
Regular intake of meat for humans is an unnatural habit which does not provide any benefit.

paragraphs.text: The ape family: Ku+d́ikhin = kikhi. The verbal root ku is used in many senses. One meaning is grinning and grimacing. So the etymological meaning of the word kikhi is “one who grimaces”. One speciality about the suffixes d́ikhin and kvan is that the last phoneme of the verbal root can alternately be i. For example, if you add the suffix kvan/kvas to the verbal root kan, the resulting word will of course be kańva, but it can also be kińva. Similarly, if you add the suffix d́ikhin, it can be both kukhi and kikhi. But the kukhi form is not prevalent. In common usage, the word kikhi means monkey. On the slightest occasion, either due to fear or excitement, a monkey grimaces with clenched fists. So it is called kikhi. This habit of the monkey is prehistoric. Although the ancestors of human beings and monkeys are the same, they were separated at least one million years ago. So a human being also, when frightened or excited, clenches the fist and grimaces. A small child keeps its fist clenched most of the time, and the habit of grimacing also remains predominant in childhood. ( 2 )
summary: The ape family: Ku+d́ikhin = kikhi.
But the kukhi form is not prevalent.
A small child keeps its fist clenched most of the time, and the habit of grimacing also remains predominant in childhood.

paragraphs.text: Monkey leader – importance of singular leadership:
summary: Monkey leader – importance of singular leadership:

paragraphs.text: You know that some animals live in herds or groups and others live by themselves. The sheep, the lion and the elephant live collectively, but the goat, the tiger and the cat live separately, on their own. Yes, the creatures of the ape group also live collectively. All creatures with herd instinct have a leader. They do not have any form of milita netrtva [collective leadership] amongst themselves. This is because collective leadership ultimately creates fissures in the saḿgha [an association or organisation or society], and this goes against the very nature of existence. The human being is also a creature that leads a collective life. However much one might use vocal pyrotechnics or speak eloquently against hero-worship, in their heart of hearts humans have always longed for strong and firm leadership. They are collective-minded creatures; if one finds an ideal leader, one comes and offers all oneʼs love and devotion to them on the one hand, and on the other hand does not hesitate to face death willingly, at their command. This is the inner characteristic of human thinking which keeps oneʼs mind and heart always fulfilled. Even those who oppose hero-worship only do it verbally but not from the core of their heart.
summary: You know that some animals live in herds or groups and others live by themselves.
This is because collective leadership ultimately creates fissures in the saḿgha [an association or organisation or society], and this goes against the very nature of existence.
Even those who oppose hero-worship only do it verbally but not from the core of their heart.

paragraphs.text: In any case, these apes are a group of creatures associated with humans. Like humans, they have herd instinct and unlimited love and devotion for their leader. When the leader becomes old, he or she hands over the leadership to a younger monkey and retires. Whether they are red-faced, dark-faced or small-sized monkeys or baboons, they will have a leader. Since very ancient times, the word gabaya was used to describe a monkey leader. In spoken Bengali, we call this gabaya, viir hanumán. ( 3 )
summary: In any case, these apes are a group of creatures associated with humans.
Whether they are red-faced, dark-faced or small-sized monkeys or baboons, they will have a leader.
In spoken Bengali, we call this gabaya, viir hanumán.

paragraphs.text: The word kusháku, if it is used in the masculine gender, or if we spell it by using the Sanskrit spirant (visarga), then its meaning becomes “the powerful monkey” – such as viir hanumán. There are several hundred species of monkeys. They are diverse in appearance and nature. Some are calm and quiet, gentle and disciplined, and others are very brave like kushákuh. Some have a brown face and colour, others are black, and still others are red in colour. Among the red-faced monkeys, those that are smaller in appearance are called ulluk in Sanskrit. They are very intelligent. According to their degree of advancement on the evolutionary path, monkeys vary in their vocabularies. Some have only two to four hundred words in their language, and others have six to seven hundred words that they use. There is very little difference between the vocabulary size of extremely underdeveloped humans and of highly-developed monkeys. This means that if there is some addition to the vocabulary of developed monkeys, it would come close to the language of underdeveloped humans. Judging by their language, the developed monkeys with tails are more advanced than the tailless monkeys (gorillas, chimpanzees and orangutangs). Overall, of course, orangutangs have more advanced intelligence.
summary: The word kusháku, if it is used in the masculine gender, or if we spell it by using the Sanskrit spirant (visarga), then its meaning becomes “the powerful monkey” – such as viir hanumán.
They are very intelligent.
Overall, of course, orangutangs have more advanced intelligence.

paragraphs.text: In physical strength none can compare with the gorillas. Among these apes, those with tails, which are more powerful – those dark-faced monkeys – are called hanumán in spoken Bengali, and in northern India languor. They have great physical strength. Male apes are called viir hanuman in colloquial language. These viir hanumáns belong to the kusháku genus. ( 4 )
summary: In physical strength none can compare with the gorillas.
They have great physical strength.
These viir hanumáns belong to the kusháku genus.

paragraphs.text: Leaf-hoppers (Shyámápoká): The Sanskrit word for shyamápoká is kot́ika. At the end of the rainy season, with the advent of autumn, these small insects are born in the millions and swarm across the sky and the land. Although they are very small in size, these creatures of the grasshopper suborder are very harmful for the crops. In Sanskrit they have another name, shalavá, meaning “enemy of the crops”. During early autumn they eat up the heads of the paddy crops in the fields, and in the late autumn they eat up the flowers of paddy. In ancient times, farmers found no way to save the crops from these insects. Though their onslaught continues throughout the day, they become more active when night falls, because they become irritated by sunlight.
summary: Leaf-hoppers (Shyámápoká): The Sanskrit word for shyamápoká is kot́ika.
In Sanskrit they have another name, shalavá, meaning “enemy of the crops”.
Though their onslaught continues throughout the day, they become more active when night falls, because they become irritated by sunlight.

paragraphs.text: In ancient times, farmers used to burn certain objects near the field to create fumes so as to drive them away and thereby save the crops from such an invasion. This proved barely effective. Although the fumes killed some and drove others away, they were not completely exterminated. The smoke did not harm the crops; rather it benefited them, since farmers used to fumigate the crops before flowering and not afterwards. Creating fumes amongst the barren pineapple plants causes them to bear fruit. In some countries of the world, pineapple plants are fumigated with the help of a trellis. This results very shortly in the appearance of golden pineapples.
summary: In ancient times, farmers used to burn certain objects near the field to create fumes so as to drive them away and thereby save the crops from such an invasion.
The smoke did not harm the crops; rather it benefited them, since farmers used to fumigate the crops before flowering and not afterwards.
This results very shortly in the appearance of golden pineapples.

paragraphs.text: Let us come back to the main subject. Failing to evolve any effective means to save the crops from the green leaf-hopper insects, farmers all over the world took the decision that they would arrange flames of light simultaneously during Kárttikii Amávasyá [the new moon night in the seventh month of the Bengali calendar]. The invasion of these flies would be at its worst during that time, and millions would meet their death by jumping into the flames. This configuration of lights is the prime reason behind the emergence of the festival of lights (diipávalii); other reasons for this festival came much later. The poet Candiidas has said:

paragraphs.text: In Bengali the name of this fly is shyamá or shyamápoká. The word shyamá has several meanings. Of these, the most widely accepted is “green”. You must be aware of the fact that the prince Sahasraváhu of post-Buddhist Ráŕh, conquered a large part of Southeast Asia and established a colony there. At that time, the capital of Ráŕh was Siḿhapur (Singur – earlier in Burdawn district, now in Hoogly district). To replicate this city, he created his capital [in Southeast Asia] called Siḿhapur (or Singapur) as a city. Prince Sahasraváhu, charmed by the greenery of the entire region (Thailand), called it Shyámdesh. Even today, along with the name Thailand, its other name of Shyámdesh is also prevalent.
summary: In Bengali the name of this fly is shyamá or shyamápoká.
At that time, the capital of Ráŕh was Siḿhapur (Singur – earlier in Burdawn district, now in Hoogly district).
Even today, along with the name Thailand, its other name of Shyámdesh is also prevalent.

paragraphs.text: In any case, this insect is green in colour, due to which its name shyamá has been appropriately given. This has no connection with the goddess Shyámádevii [goddess Kali] or with Shyamápújá. Due to its green colour, these insects become lost in the greenery and create a natural camouflage of colour or natural camouflage. Although it does not have the ability of changing colour (varńa corá), it does become lost in the greenery. So it becomes very difficult to determine whether the paddy field has been invaded by these insects. In Sanskrit, of course, shyámá has other reflective connotations.
summary: In any case, this insect is green in colour, due to which its name shyamá has been appropriately given.
Although it does not have the ability of changing colour (varńa corá), it does become lost in the greenery.
In Sanskrit, of course, shyámá has other reflective connotations.

paragraphs.text: The lifespan of these insects is normally about a fortnight. Yet, after investigation it has been noted that unless there is any serious damage to their bodies or life, they can live up to two months. During the late autumn, however, due to the excessive mists, they die out. They usually lay their eggs on the upper part of grass blades. The eggs remain there for about a year. Many animals grazing in the fields eat up these eggs along with the blades of grass. Sometimes the scorching rays of the sun dry up the grass and kill the eggs. During the floods, these eggs, still attached to the blades of grass, float towards the sea. Of course, the eggs are numerous; in fact, there are millions and millions of eggs. So many of them may die [along the way], but not all. With the sprinkling of rain these eggs come to life again. At the end of the rainy season, the baby shyámápoká come out of their eggs and move about independently. They do more harm than good to humans. Yet they are food for many small-sized birds and other creatures. In that sense, they help to a great extent in maintaining the ecological balance in the world.
summary: The lifespan of these insects is normally about a fortnight.
During the floods, these eggs, still attached to the blades of grass, float towards the sea.
In that sense, they help to a great extent in maintaining the ecological balance in the world.

paragraphs.text: Nurjahan, the empress of India, was a poetess. She had a sensitive, scrutinizing mind with which she looked at all the beautiful things in life. She declared that no roses should be offered at her grave, because it would cause pain to the bulbul birds [a bird of the Pycnonotus genus] residing in the rose garden from where the roses would be plucked. She also said that no lamps should be lit there because in the flames, countless green flies would be burnt to death. She would not be able to endure it.
summary: Nurjahan, the empress of India, was a poetess.

She declared that no roses should be offered at her grave, because it would cause pain to the bulbul birds [a bird of the Pycnonotus genus] residing in the rose garden from where the roses would be plucked.

paragraphs.text: Locust (pauṋgapál): The meaning of the word kot́ika is shalabhá (locust), in Bengali pauṋgapál, in northern India t́id́d́i, and in Bhojpuri t́iiṋŕii.
summary: Locust (pauṋgapál): The meaning of the word kot́ika is shalabhá (locust), in Bengali pauṋgapál, in northern India t́id́d́i, and in Bhojpuri t́iiṋŕii.

paragraphs.text: Pauṋgapál (locust) is a peculiar kind of insect. Generally it appears only in desert areas on occasion, when sultry weather abounds. You know, the heat of the desert is usually dry. Surely you must be aware of the fact that the heat of Jodhpur is much more intense than that of Kolkata. Yet the Kolkata climate, because of greater humidity, causes people to sweat profusely. Due to this perspiration, excessive salt exudes from the body and this weakens the power of activity. More than Kolkata, in East and North Bengal this sultriness is even more intense. So according to the theory of East and Wet ( 2 ) [humidity factor], the people of East and North Bengal are less industrious than those of Ráŕh. Again, the people of Assam suffer more from humid climate than those of East and North Bengal. That is why the people of Assam are far less industrious. Although the heat of Jodhpur is more intense than that of Kolkata, there is hardly any humidity. That is why there is less sweating and therefore less fatigue. While staying in Rajasthan, I personally experienced this. In any case, even in this desert region, if there is one percent increase in humidity, the locusts increase by the millions. In fact, locust eggs lie in a dormant state for several years in the desert, and once it becomes humid they bloom into life. This happens not only in Rajasthan, in Thar (Sindh), in the northern desert regions of Gujarat, but also in Persia (Iran), Baluchistan, Sahara and Gobi. Even in the deserts of South America such phenomena occur to some extent.
summary: Pauṋgapál (locust) is a peculiar kind of insect.
Again, the people of Assam suffer more from humid climate than those of East and North Bengal.
Even in the deserts of South America such phenomena occur to some extent.

paragraphs.text: Though locusts are very close to grasshoppers as a suborder of insects, there is hardly any similarity in their nature or habits. The habitat of grasshoppers, especially their birthplace, is the extensive sandy beds of large rivers. They cannot, however, live far from a humid environment. They live in verdant fields and eat green leaves. Thus as a natural camouflage, their colour is deep green. Similarly, locusts are insects that feed on leaves of grass. However, because they are born in deserts, their colour is different. Bengal is far away from deserts, and so there are scarcely any locust attacks in Bengal. In assessing their nature and habits, the primary difference between grasshoppers and locusts is that grasshoppers do not live in groups, while locusts always do so. When they fly together in the millions, their dark shadow overcasts the sky. Whatever region they fly over finds its vegetation destroyed. These shalabhá or locusts are food for human beings in certain regions of the earth.
summary: Though locusts are very close to grasshoppers as a suborder of insects, there is hardly any similarity in their nature or habits.
However, because they are born in deserts, their colour is different.
These shalabhá or locusts are food for human beings in certain regions of the earth.

paragraphs.text: Yogiráj [king of yogis] Matsyendranath was a prince of the erstwhile East Bengal. Moynamati was the capital of Shriibhúmi (British Tripura – now Coomilla district of present Bangladesh). Since the pre-Buddhist era, this Moynamati was famous for handwoven yarns, especially for colourful shirts. This prince was the inventor of the yogic postures Matsyendrásan [twist posture], and Shalabhásan [locust posture]. In Shalabhásana, people look like locusts, and hence the name.
summary: Yogiráj [king of yogis] Matsyendranath was a prince of the erstwhile East Bengal.
Since the pre-Buddhist era, this Moynamati was famous for handwoven yarns, especially for colourful shirts.
In Shalabhásana, people look like locusts, and hence the name.

paragraphs.text: Moynamati was the mother of Yogiráj Matsyendranath. She not only raised her son, but also ruled this kingdom in Bengal as regent until her son came of age. She is still remembered with deep love and respect. ( 3 )
summary: Moynamati was the mother of Yogiráj Matsyendranath.
She not only raised her son, but also ruled this kingdom in Bengal as regent until her son came of age.
She is still remembered with deep love and respect.

paragraphs.text: Grasshopper (gauṋgáphaŕiḿ): Grasshoppers are quite large in size. There are certain similarities in the appearance of these creatures and of locusts; of course, there are more dissimilarities between them. The Sanskrit word for locust is shalabhá, which can be spelt with s or sh or śa.
summary: Grasshopper (gauṋgáphaŕiḿ): Grasshoppers are quite large in size.
There are certain similarities in the appearance of these creatures and of locusts; of course, there are more dissimilarities between them.
The Sanskrit word for locust is shalabhá, which can be spelt with s or sh or śa.

paragraphs.text: As told earlier the birthplace of locusts is the desert. There are some wet and humid places in the desert. It must be understood that the water table in those areas is comparatively high. Sometimes an oasis is close by (even if an oasis is not near, it can be created by the artesian effect). Locusts lay their legs under the leaves of thorny plants or under a layer of sand. The eggs do not hatch regularly. In certain years, due to severe dust storms or from enhanced humidity in the atmosphere, the eggs burst forth in millions and give birth to young ones, which grow very rapidly. They then move out in search of green corn fields. Locusts born in the desert of Rajasthan usually fly away towards the fields of Eastern India, and to the north in Punjab and Haryana. Only a few fly southwards. Some people eat these locusts.
summary: As told earlier the birthplace of locusts is the desert.
The eggs do not hatch regularly.
Some people eat these locusts.

paragraphs.text: The case of grasshoppers is somewhat different. Large plants grow on the sandy beds of the Ganges or large rivers. Grasshoppers lay their eggs under the leaves of these plants. If excessively humid air blows there, the eggs thrive and give birth to nymphs. Usually they move within a five mile radius of the banks of large rivers (the Ganges and other rivers). In other words, they love to move in those places near the humid atmosphere of the river. Sometimes they can even be found close to small rivers. They do not move to the hills or far away from the riverbeds. Almost every year their eggs hatch and give birth to babies.
summary: The case of grasshoppers is somewhat different.
Usually they move within a five mile radius of the banks of large rivers (the Ganges and other rivers).
Almost every year their eggs hatch and give birth to babies.

paragraphs.text: The number of grasshoppers increases during any year in which there is greater rainfall or more humidity. They are fond of eating green leaves. As a natural camouflage, their body is green like the leaves. Thus when they are sitting on greenery or on leaves, it is difficult to discover these grasshoppers. The opportunity exists for all grasshoppers in natural surroundings to become lost in the midst of the green leaves. Locusts are creatures of the desert, and hence their colour matches that of the desert. Once in our childhood, millions of locusts flew over Bihar and northern Bengal towards China. I remember that for a few minutes darkness descended everywhere. The blue sky was overcast with locusts.
summary: The number of grasshoppers increases during any year in which there is greater rainfall or more humidity.
The opportunity exists for all grasshoppers in natural surroundings to become lost in the midst of the green leaves.
The blue sky was overcast with locusts.

paragraphs.text: Locusts live in groups, but grasshoppers normally live singly. Sometimes it is found that grasshoppers are longer in appearance than locusts. Physically however, locusts are sturdier than grasshoppers. They can eat more than grasshoppers. God gives with one hand and takes with another. In the ancient science of agriculture, some of the enemies of crop cultivation mentioned are excessive rainfall, drought, political revolution, crop diseases and locusts; but the droppings of locusts are very good fertilizers.
summary: Locusts live in groups, but grasshoppers normally live singly.
They can eat more than grasshoppers.

In the ancient science of agriculture, some of the enemies of crop cultivation mentioned are excessive rainfall, drought, political revolution, crop diseases and locusts; but the droppings of locusts are very good fertilizers.

paragraphs.text: The postures of grasshoppers sitting and flying are somewhat like that of horses that stop suddenly while running or when they begin to run. That is why in Bihar, especially in Magadha, the grasshopper is called Rámjiike ghoŕá [Lord Ramʼs horse]. ( 4 )
summary: The postures of grasshoppers sitting and flying are somewhat like that of horses that stop suddenly while running or when they begin to run.
That is why in Bihar, especially in Magadha, the grasshopper is called Rámjiike ghoŕá [Lord Ramʼs horse].

paragraphs.text: Cricket (ucciḿŕe): The meaning of kośaja is “any creature born of eggs” – specifically lizards, and more specifically, ucciḿŕe or ghurńiipoká or crickets. Ucciḿŕe is an insect of the locust or shalabhá family. Of course, for shalabhá, the right environment is the desert. Their eggs give rise to nymphs in the desert after just a few days of wet or cloudy weather. It is not the same with grasshoppers (pauṋgapál). They grow in each and every country. Of course, wet and soft soil is the proper breeding ground for grasshoppers. The rainy season is their favourite season. Another point of difference between shalabhá and grasshoppers is that the former are fond of green leaves and trees. Hence although born in the desert, they then migrate to green fields and vegetation. Grasshoppers normally do not do so. They remain in whichever country they are born. They are also very fond of the green leaves of trees, but are not averse to other kinds of food.
summary: Cricket (ucciḿŕe): The meaning of kośaja is “any creature born of eggs” – specifically lizards, and more specifically, ucciḿŕe or ghurńiipoká or crickets.
Of course, wet and soft soil is the proper breeding ground for grasshoppers.
They are also very fond of the green leaves of trees, but are not averse to other kinds of food.

paragraphs.text: Grasshoppers do not try to bite humans; in contrast, people in certain countries catch them in countless swarms by throwing nets, store them in baskets and then eat them. Crickets also do not normally bite people, and they are not eaten by people in any country. However, people in certain countries do eat locusts and other insects of the grasshopper suborder. According to some people, St. John [the Baptist] lived on grasshoppers dipped in honey during his simple, unassuming life. I do not know how far this is true, but one should not be surprised, since in ancient times humans did eat insects, particularly when they did not yet know the art of cultivation or did not know how to use fire. In the Vedas it is mentioned:

chapters.title: Bees, Wasps and Hornets, and White Ants

paragraphs.text: Bee: The word náyaka means “one who leads”. Kośanáyaka means “one who carries weapons” or “the carrier of weapons or treasures who does it for the sake of preservation”. So, one of the literal meanings of kośanáyaka is the Apis indica type of bee. In India there are three types of bees (maomáchi): rock bee, bush bee and Apis indica. Rock bee is a large bee species that produces honey in large quantities. They have large honeycombs, normally on banyan trees or other large trees. Sometimes the honeycombs are so large that they break apart, and the honey oozes out and drips onto the ground. The honey produced by the rock bees is somewhat pungent. It is known as ugraviirja [inducing vitality]. When human vitality is reduced, when the coldness of death descends upon oneʼs exhausted body, many a time this type of honey called ugraviirja comes to instil new life and energy.
summary: Bee: The word náyaka means “one who leads”.
They have large honeycombs, normally on banyan trees or other large trees.
When human vitality is reduced, when the coldness of death descends upon oneʼs exhausted body, many a time this type of honey called ugraviirja comes to instil new life and energy.

paragraphs.text: In a human body that has reduced vitality, so long as there is no blood-consuming disease, ten drops of this particular honey, if consumed in the morning along with the leaves of krśńa-tulasii [black basil] on an empty stomach, will yield excellent results. However if a person has blood dysentery or any ulcer in the body, then one must not take it. The honey must be sucked [or licked], not swallowed. That is why in Indian ayurvedic science it is called avaleha.
summary: In a human body that has reduced vitality, so long as there is no blood-consuming disease, ten drops of this particular honey, if consumed in the morning along with the leaves of krśńa-tulasii [black basil] on an empty stomach, will yield excellent results.
The honey must be sucked [or licked], not swallowed.
That is why in Indian ayurvedic science it is called avaleha.

paragraphs.text: Bush bees are small-sized bees. They are ancient inhabitants of India. Instead of building honeycombs on trees, they prefer to build them on the walls of mud houses. In the villages of Ráŕh Bengal, when ants make their home in mud houses built with clayish soil, if the bush bees find an opportunity to occupy them, they build their choicest and most beautiful honeycombs there. We obtain minimum honey from such individual honeycombs; but the honey is well-refined and pleasant in taste and scent. On the other hand, it is lower in vitality than any other honey. Good quality neem honey (obtained from the neem flower) is produced by these bees. It is surmised that they are the original bees of Ráŕh Bengal. They do not sting readily. Even when they sting, there is hardly that unbearable pain which is caused by the sting of rock bees.
summary: Bush bees are small-sized bees.
On the other hand, it is lower in vitality than any other honey.
Even when they sting, there is hardly that unbearable pain which is caused by the sting of rock bees.

paragraphs.text: Apis indica are the original bees of India. They are medium in size and live in medium-sized trees. Some trees produce floral nectar in plenty, and these bees build their honeycombs there or in neighbouring areas. If there is no fear of enemies, they build their honeycombs on the lower branches of trees. They are found all over Bengal; but they are mostly seen in large numbers in southern Bengal; especially in southern Ráŕh. They can fly for a long distance. Their stings cause severe pain. They prepare good honey from mustard flowers. At one time physicians preferred honey produced by these bees in the preparation of ayurvedic medicines. The very name Apis indica denotes their identity as the original bees of India. In Ráŕh they normally build their honeycombs in areas adjacent to rivers or at the confluence of rivers, mostly on trees of medium height. In the Sundarbans at the end of winter, they are the first to come forward to begin building their honeycombs. The wax of these honeycombs is quite pliable and soft. There was a time when it was sold at a very high price. Another good name of these Apis indica bees is kośanáyaka. ( 1 )
summary: Apis indica are the original bees of India.
They prepare good honey from mustard flowers.
Another good name of these Apis indica bees is kośanáyaka.

paragraphs.text: Wasp and hornet (boltá and bhiimrul): The hornet is such a creature that wherever it goes it builds a honeycomb nearby, so it is very much prone to building shelters. That is why one meaning of the word grhakárii is “hornet”. The difference between the wasp and the hornet is that the former is lean, thin and yellowish in colour, while the latter is stout and sturdy and has a reddish band near the waist. The sting of the hornet is more painful than that of the wasp. As far as I understand, the word bhiimrul has come from bhiim (severe) and hul (sting). Instead of hul, the villagers of Ráŕh pronounce it as rul. In Sanskrit, boltá is called baŕat́á, in Hindi baŕre; the Sanskrit word for bhiimrul is grhakárii, in Hindi, birńii. ( 2 )
summary: Wasp and hornet (boltá and bhiimrul): The hornet is such a creature that wherever it goes it builds a honeycomb nearby, so it is very much prone to building shelters.
The sting of the hornet is more painful than that of the wasp.
In Sanskrit, boltá is called baŕat́á, in Hindi baŕre; the Sanskrit word for bhiimrul is grhakárii, in Hindi, birńii.

paragraphs.text: White ant: Ui [white ant] is a native Bengali word. In North India, diimak is used; on the Bengal and North India border, diiyaṋk or diiyáṋ is used; in English ui means “white-ant”, and in Sanskrit valmiikakiit́a or pluśińa is used. In many parts of Bengal, a is used in place of ra, and ra is used in place of a. For this reason ui are called rui nearly everywhere in southern Bengal. The mushroom that grows on anthills is called rui-chátu [ant-mushroom]. This tiny creature belonging to the ant group increases its numbers at an extremely fast rate. They cannot see anything in the sunlight. Their sense of touch also diminishes when exposed to sunlight. Thus they build little tunnels out of the earth to protect themselves from sunlight and use them to move around in because their sense of touch and other senses come to life in the darkness of these tunnels. Under certain conditions, the different branches and sub-branches of these tunnels that they construct right and left become visible as a mound or hillock. In spoken Bengali we call this ui-dhibi, in English “anthill”, in Sanskrit valmiika. An anthill was built around the entire body of a sage who remained motionless for many days during the practice of his austerities. At the time that he sat for meditation, he was known by the name of Ratnákara. The people gave him the name Válmiiki because at the time that he finished his penance and rose from his seat, his body was encased in an anthill.
summary: White ant: Ui [white ant] is a native Bengali word.
Their sense of touch also diminishes when exposed to sunlight.
The people gave him the name Válmiiki because at the time that he finished his penance and rose from his seat, his body was encased in an anthill.

paragraphs.text: People in many countries of the world eat ants – even civilized people in some places. They say that ants are tasty and have a sweet and sour flavour.
summary: People in many countries of the world eat ants – even civilized people in some places.
They say that ants are tasty and have a sweet and sour flavour.

paragraphs.text: In Sanskrit the word pluśińa was more widely used than the word valmiikakiit́a. Sama pluśińa sama mashakena sama nágena sama ebhistribhirlokaeh, that is, Parama Puruśa is unbiased. He is equal to everyone because He sees everyone in the same way. He sees an ant in the same way He sees a small mosquito. He understands an ant in the same way that He understands a mosquito. He does not make any undue fuss over a giant serpent (python or “elephant of the jungle”) because of its great size. He sees a python or “elephant of the jungle” in the same way that He sees an ant or a mosquito, and they also see Him in that same way. Nor does He make any special fuss over this universe, the three worlds of heaven, earth and hell, because of their vastness, and they also look at Him in the same way. In other words, everyone is equal to Parama Puruśa – a mosquito, ant, python, mammoth and even the three worlds. He remains with everyone equally through His ota yoga and prota yoga [individual and collective association of Parama Purnśa with jiiva]. He is impartial under all conditions.
summary: In Sanskrit the word pluśińa was more widely used than the word valmiikakiit́a.
He does not make any undue fuss over a giant serpent (python or “elephant of the jungle”) because of its great size.
He is impartial under all conditions.

paragraphs.text: In the opinion of biologists, ants first appeared on the earth approximately six million years ago. It is possible that they appeared somewhat earlier than this, but not later. In other words, after ants arrived on the earth, they passed through at least one, if not more than one, ice age, and have arrived in their present form having undergone one or more long hibernations. ( 3 )
summary: In the opinion of biologists, ants first appeared on the earth approximately six million years ago.
It is possible that they appeared somewhat earlier than this, but not later.

In other words, after ants arrived on the earth, they passed through at least one, if not more than one, ice age, and have arrived in their present form having undergone one or more long hibernations.

paragraphs.text: Bugs (kit́ibha): Kit́ibha: kit́i+bha+d́a = kit́ibha. The etymological meaning of the word kit́ibha is “that which looks like a kit́i”. In common usage, kit́ibha means “bug”. There are two reasons why a bug is called kit́ibha. Suppose you have returned very tired… It is already night … you are about to sleep. Then suddenly you notice a bug on your bed. Well, you might have immediately killed the bug. But you are left with the apprehension that since you have spotted one bug, there must be more bugs in the bed. You say to yourself, “I will lose my sleep for nothing tonight.” You are frightened by the bleak prospect of spending an agonizing night. The kind of fear that you experience on seeing the bug is similar to the kind of fear you have on seeing a rhino or a boar. So a bug is called kit́ibha, that is, like a kit́i [rhino].
summary: Bugs (kit́ibha): Kit́ibha: kit́i+bha+d́a = kit́ibha.
Well, you might have immediately killed the bug.
So a bug is called kit́ibha, that is, like a kit́i [rhino].

paragraphs.text: In ancient times people used to say that there is another reason for calling a bug kit́ibha. That is, if you look at a bug through a magnifying glass, making it fifty or hundred times larger than its actual size, you will see that it is a creature of horrifying appearance. Howsoever brave and valorous you may be, you are sure to be frightened by the terrible sight of the hugely magnified bug. That is why another name for bug is kit́ibha. ( 1 )
summary: In ancient times people used to say that there is another reason for calling a bug kit́ibha.
Howsoever brave and valorous you may be, you are sure to be frightened by the terrible sight of the hugely magnified bug.
That is why another name for bug is kit́ibha.

paragraphs.text: Large-sized scorpion: Khararomańa means “large-sized, dark and hairy scorpion” (in English scorpion, in Latin scorpio). Usually these scorpions live in the hills. They live in the openings between rocks or in large crevices in the hills. These dark-coloured scorpions are known as khararomańa. They are very venomous. In 1963 the present writer was once bitten by such a scorpion. Its sting is unbearably painful. Small babies might succumb to their sting. Once in the khirkhiriá section of the Rajmahal branch of Ramgarh hills [Jamalpur hills fall in the same hill range] there were plenty of these scorpions. In my boyhood days I used to watch these scorpions bristling together, removing slabs of stone. At that time, that particular hill was covered with forests. Later the hill and the forest came under control of the provincial government (state government). During the British rule, the forests were ruined. As a result such scorpions also quickly became extinct. In 1964 when I went there, I saw that the number of these scorpions was greatly reduced in the forests, and even removing the stone slabs I could hardly come across one or two such creatures. Their number must have been even further reduced, since there is no forest in that area now. In the plains adjacent to the hills, due to abolition of the zamindary system, the forests have been obliterated. Arrangements have been made for sanctuaries, only for the sake of preserving certain wild animals. However, since no preservation of these scorpions is possible, they will soon become extinct.
summary: Large-sized scorpion: Khararomańa means “large-sized, dark and hairy scorpion” (in English scorpion, in Latin scorpio).
In my boyhood days I used to watch these scorpions bristling together, removing slabs of stone.
However, since no preservation of these scorpions is possible, they will soon become extinct.

paragraphs.text: In this context, let me point out that these scorpions are the favourite food of long-beaked birds, such as cranes, adjutant storks and parrots (especially wild parrots or bon-tiyá), which attack them en masse and eat them up. ( 2 )
summary: In this context, let me point out that these scorpions are the favourite food of long-beaked birds, such as cranes, adjutant storks and parrots (especially wild parrots or bon-tiyá), which attack them en masse and eat them up.

paragraphs.text: The word kurpii means káṋkŕá biche [crab scorpion; it derives its name from the Bengali word káṋkŕá which means crab]. Its alternative Sanskrit name is briscika. The etymological meaning of the word brishcika is something of a crooked nature. Another meaning of the word is “something which is unbearable”. The Bengali word bichá or biche is derived from the word brishcika. There are several different species of scorpions in the world. The chief among them are teṋtule biche [a variety of scorpions as dark-coloured as a ripe tamarind seed] and káṋkŕá biche. Although teṋtule biche can be of different colours, it is mainly reddish in appearance. And when it lies quietly on the road, from a distance it looks like a ripe tamarind seed. Hence its name is teṋtule biche. In India, apart from a good number of white and yellow varieties of teṋtule biche, a genus of ink-black colour is also found. Many people call a white scorpion sarasvatii biche [Saraswati is a mythological Hindu deity, whose colour is supposed to be pure white], a yellow scorpion or sońá biche [golden-coloured scorpion], and the black scorpion or káli biche [dark-coloured scorpion like the dark-complexioned mythological Hindu goddess Káli].
summary: The word kurpii means káṋkŕá biche [crab scorpion; it derives its name from the Bengali word káṋkŕá which means crab].
The chief among them are teṋtule biche [a variety of scorpions as dark-coloured as a ripe tamarind seed] and káṋkŕá biche.

paragraphs.text: The biting power of all scorpions is not the same. The sting of some results in a heavy loss of blood, whereas in the case of others the loss is minimal. These scorpions are venomous no doubt, but the burning sensation that their bite causes is not entirely due to the venom; it is mainly due to loss of blood. A scorpion is far more venomous than a teṋtule biche. The way in which a scorpion moves resembles somewhat that of a crab. Hence it is called káṋkŕá biche. When a crab moves, it keeps its claws raised all along. This is because it moves with the thought that if it is attacked by an approaching enemy, it will launch a counter attack immediately. The same is the case with a scorpion. It also moves with its claws elevated, so that it can collide with an advancing enemy and pierce its sting into its body. In India, generally three types of scorpions are found: 1) pale-dark, 2) deep-dark, and 3) those dwelling on hills and mountains. The pale-dark variety is somewhat smaller in size, and its bite is less painful. In Bengal, this type of scorpion found in greater number. The deep-dark variety is larger in size, and its bite is extremely painful. If it bites a child, it can even cause the childʼs death. They are sometimes found to live in the holes between the leaves of banana trees. Those who incise date-palm trees are often attacked by this type of scorpion.
summary: The biting power of all scorpions is not the same.
The same is the case with a scorpion.
Those who incise date-palm trees are often attacked by this type of scorpion.

paragraphs.text: The hill scorpions normally dwell in hills in narrow openings between large-sized pieces of rock. Some of these scorpions have hair on their body. Their bite is very painful. The venom of scorpions is used in poison therapy. Its venom is also used in the preparation of homeopathic medicines. The old Sanskrit and Vedic name of scorpions is kurpii. The name brishcika is also quite old. Their Latin equivalent is ‘scorpio’. From ‘scorpio’ has come the English word ‘scorpion’. The word kaorpya means anything related to scorpions. You can call the venom of scorpions kaorpya viśa, and the medicine prepared from its venom kaorpya aosadha. You can also call a man of extremely crooked nature kaorpya kut́ila.
summary: The hill scorpions normally dwell in hills in narrow openings between large-sized pieces of rock.
The name brishcika is also quite old.
You can also call a man of extremely crooked nature kaorpya kut́ila.

paragraphs.text: Among the zodiac signs, next to Libra is Scorpio. It looks almost like a scorpion with its claws raised. ( 3 )
summary: Among the zodiac signs, next to Libra is Scorpio.
It looks almost like a scorpion with its claws raised.

paragraphs.text: Louse (ukun): Keshakiit́a (louse) is a type of insect which resides in hair and eats the fat at the root of the hair and the skin of the head. Literally, it means “louse”. The eggs of the louse are called niki and the adult lice are called dyáuṋgar. So you understand the meaning of the word “louse,” and you must be alert regarding these insects. In earlier times, to protect themselves from lice attack, people used to blend kerosene oil with coconut oil in equal proportions and apply it on the head. It was necessary to sit with oneʼs back to the sun for one hour in this condition before taking bath. That resulted in the disappearance of the lice in two or three days. Nowadays one can do the same or use [lice] shampoo once a month to protect oneself from the onslaught of lice. ( 4 )
summary: Louse (ukun): Keshakiit́a (louse) is a type of insect which resides in hair and eats the fat at the root of the hair and the skin of the head.

paragraphs.text: Gandhi bug: In the equatorial region there resides a particular type of insect which is known as gándhipoká, from whose body emanates a pungent smell. It tends to fill the adjoining areas with a foul smell, for which reason house lizards do not come near them – nor do other creatures that normally prey upon insects. In certain situations, these insects cause tremendous harm to contain crops. Of course, they are also beneficial to other crops.

paragraphs.text: Mosquito: The d́áṋsh [gnat] variety of mosquito (mashá) can drink excessive quantities of blood. After they drink an excessive quantity of blood they remain torpid for quite some time. Some are of the opinion that their stomach often bursts and they die as a result of drinking too much blood.

paragraphs.text: Rat: Kund + uń = kundu. The etymological meaning is “one whose nature is to lurk”. Suppose there are seven hundred rats in a room. A cat enters the room. The rats immediately know it; they understand the situation. Suddenly, from that very moment, they stop all movement, stop making any noise. Silence reigns in the room. It would be hard for anyone to know that seven hundred rats were lurking. So one colloquial meaning of the word kundu is a rat of any kind, whether a rat or a mouse. In Hindi a rat is called cuhá and a mouse is called cuhiyá. In Bihar the big ones are called muś, the small ones cut́ri. For a woodland rat or field mouse the word ákhu was common in old Sanskrit. In later times the word went almost completely out of use. Múśika or iṋdura refers to all kinds of rodents. Muśá was common in old Bengali. Now it has gone out of use.
summary: Rat: Kund + uń = kundu.
So one colloquial meaning of the word kundu is a rat of any kind, whether a rat or a mouse.
Now it has gone out of use.

paragraphs.text: There is a particular community that is known as “Muśáhara” because they eat rats. Generally in Bihar large rats are called muśá and medium-sized rats are called muśa. These words are not used in standard Hindi and Urdu, however. ( 1 )

Generally in Bihar large rats are called muśá and medium-sized rats are called muśa.
These words are not used in standard Hindi and Urdu, however.

paragraphs.text: As you well know, there are many species of iṋdur such as the mouse, the rat, the field mouse [marmot group], tree rat, etc. Some of them live in kitchens, some in storerooms, some in holes in the wall and some in tree hollows. They have many names according to their species and dwelling place: iṋdur, muśika, ákhu, kundu, and so on. The mole also has three main species in India. But they are all field moles; they live in burrows in the fields. The entrance to the burrow is towards the bottom and the burrow itself moves upward. So what happens is that during heavy rains when the field is on the point of being submerged, it is difficult for water to seep into the dwelling. If there is water at the mouth of the hole, they can easily come out and escape. Since it lives in a field, the moleʼs proper name is vasumitra. During the day the mole cannot see properly, so they mostly come out at night. Certainly you will hardly ever see a mole entering your house during the day. You see it at night.
summary: As you well know, there are many species of iṋdur such as the mouse, the rat, the field mouse [marmot group], tree rat, etc.
The entrance to the burrow is towards the bottom and the burrow itself moves upward.
Certainly you will hardly ever see a mole entering your house during the day.

paragraphs.text: The moleʼs burrow is also called kulaka. One proper name for the mole is kulakeya, in the sense of “kulaka-dweller”, kulakeyii in feminine gender. Do you not call “the mole” that type of firework which runs about hither and thither during Diipavali [light festival] just like a mole does, making a sharp hissing sound? This mole firework does not stay in a kulaka; it is kept in a box or in oneʼs pocket. The moleʼs hole is called kulaka, but do you know the name of the ratʼs hole? It is good that you do. If you do not know, then listen well. The word is kundubil. Kundu means “rat;” bil means “hole” or “opening”. The word bil is used in Hindi and in a few North Indian languages to mean “hole”. ( 2 )
summary: The moleʼs burrow is also called kulaka.
It is good that you do.
The word bil is used in Hindi and in a few North Indian languages to mean “hole”.

paragraphs.text: One who goes around all the time looking for or eating something or the other is karvva. Rats are always going around looking for food. If they do not find anything edible they will cut things with their teeth, thinking that after it is cut up it might turn into food. In this sense, the word karvva also means “rat.” Of course, karvva does not mean “mouse” (plural, “mice”). ( 3 )
summary: One who goes around all the time looking for or eating something or the other is karvva.
If they do not find anything edible they will cut things with their teeth, thinking that after it is cut up it might turn into food.
” Of course, karvva does not mean “mouse” (plural, “mice”).

paragraphs.text: Aromatic rat (gandhamuśika): You are already familiar with the word “hibernation”. You all know that there are cold-blooded creatures on this earth. They cannot move or function in cold weather. That is why they fall asleep for a long spell with the advent of winter. They feel drowsy two or three days before their hibernation starts. At that time, struggling against drowsiness, they move towards a safe shelter and lie down. Generally that shelter is under the ground, because they feel warm there. That warmth of the ground does not allow them to die. During this long spell of sleep, they consume the fat (in Bengali basá, carbi in Hindustani) accumulated in their body. At the end of winter, the lukewarm weather of spring creates a stir in their nerves and blood, and they awake. If someone kills them while they are in hibernation, they die, but their sleep does not break. That is why this hibernation is described in Sanskrit as himanidrá. After this long spell of sleep they emerge from their hole in the ground. Due to the reduced fat in the body, the upper layer of their skin slackens, just as happens with a fat person after a spell of sickness, or with a person who has crossed over from middle age into old age.
summary: Aromatic rat (gandhamuśika): You are already familiar with the word “hibernation”.
That warmth of the ground does not allow them to die.

Due to the reduced fat in the body, the upper layer of their skin slackens, just as happens with a fat person after a spell of sickness, or with a person who has crossed over from middle age into old age.

paragraphs.text: So, on waking from hibernation, these creatures shed the loose skin from their body. The skin they shed is called khosá, or outer skin, just like the outer skin of the coconut or the banana skin. In the language of Kolkata Bengali it is called kholá – that which can be removed. In Bengal both the words kholá and khosá are widely used. That which has to be removed, which cannot be kept on the body even though one might like to keep it, and the removal of which is indispensable, is called kholas in Bengali. So after getting up from hibernation these creatures shed their skin (kholash). The chaste Bengali or Sanskrit word for this kholash is nirmok. So it is said, “Snakes shed their skin in the spring.” When the old skin is shed, the inner skin that emerges is very thin and sensitive. At this time, the creatures cannot bear the scorching rays of the sun. So they come out of their hole only in the early hours of the night. Now, during the spring and summer seasons, there is a greater intrusion of snakes onto village roads. Since their skin has become sensitive, if anyone tramples upon them, they strike. So when moving about at night on the road during this period, one must carry some kind of light.
summary: So, on waking from hibernation, these creatures shed the loose skin from their body.
So it is said, “Snakes shed their skin in the spring.
So when moving about at night on the road during this period, one must carry some kind of light.

paragraphs.text: Be that as it may, these cold-blooded creatures in India are appreciable in number. At the end of Ashvin or Kárttik [end of autumn] they lie down to hibernate. Chief amongst those who indulge in this form of hibernation is a small creature of the rodent order that lives in the holes of the lower Himalayan mountain ranges. They are generally known as marmots. A strange odour emanates from their body. The chaste Bengali name for such aromatic rats is gandhamuśika. ( 4 )
summary: Be that as it may, these cold-blooded creatures in India are appreciable in number.
They are generally known as marmots.
The chaste Bengali name for such aromatic rats is gandhamuśika.

paragraphs.text: Otter (udbiŕála): Uda or udaka means “water”. The etymological meaning of udbiŕála is “that cat-like creature that lives in the water”. Its colloquial meaning is bhodaŕ [otter]. Some people have the notion that this otter [Mustelid family] is perhaps an aquatic creature, but it is not. It is a land creature like the crocodile and the fish-eating crocodile. It goes into the water to catch prey. It is a land-dwelling creature that breastfeeds its young. It sleeps and gives birth on land, and it normally lives in large holes near ponds and reservoirs. ( 5 )
summary: Otter (udbiŕála): Uda or udaka means “water”.
It is a land creature like the crocodile and the fish-eating crocodile.
It sleeps and gives birth on land, and it normally lives in large holes near ponds and reservoirs.

paragraphs.text: When the large animals of ancient times became physically incapacitated, they took refuge in a secluded place and died there in the normal course of events. According to some scholars, the bones and fat of these animals accumulated in those places. Some form of terrible whirlpools were created in the sea, in watersheds or large lakes, and due to that, the remains of the dead animals inside those whirlpools would drift out to sea and become the Sargasso Sea (Saraságar or floating islands of earth). They even floated into the ocean depths. Some scholars believe that those places where earlier saraságars were created from the remains of animal bodies now yield us oil [petrol] from under the earth. If such places, instead of being close to the sea, happened to be inside any land region, then the fat and other remains of these large animals would float out to the sea, whereas the bones would pile up in the form of hills. In the course of time, these hills of bones turned into limestone or dolomite.
summary: When the large animals of ancient times became physically incapacitated, they took refuge in a secluded place and died there in the normal course of events.
They even floated into the ocean depths.
In the course of time, these hills of bones turned into limestone or dolomite.

paragraphs.text: When this calcium-enriched substance was burned, it turned into a type of lime, which we call in spoken language páthure cuń [lime obtained by calcination]. When the shells of water-grown animals with hard skin (snails, oysters, conch shells, etc) are turned into a type of lime through calcination, we describe it in spoken language as kalicuń. In southern Bengal the whitewashing of houses is called kali pheráno [bringing new lime]. A commercial centre developed for this kind of lime along with matted coir ( 1 ) has come to be known today as Kalikátá [Kolkata] – in Oriya language Kalikatá. Another village near this place is also called Kalikátá. Whether it is lime produced by calcination or kalicuń, both are produced from the bones of animal bodies. Those who are averse to taking kalicuń in betel leaf [for chewing after a meal], thinking that it is produced from an animal body, should remember that the calcinated lime (páthure cuń) is also derived from animal bodies. Not only the leader of the elephant herd but all elephants belonging to herds in the forest used to go into such seclusion as death neared. Today elephants do not have permanent habitats. Fearing human beings, they move from one forest to another, hence they also have no fixed place to breathe their last breath. ( 2 )

paragraphs.text: Animals in the world have their different styles of movement. The ant moves quickly but keeps it eyes open for any sweets, sugar or other food morsels along the way. Usually nothing lying on its path escapes attention. Since it has a limited number of senses, it must perform the function of several senses using a sensitive nose.
summary: Animals in the world have their different styles of movement.
Usually nothing lying on its path escapes attention.
Since it has a limited number of senses, it must perform the function of several senses using a sensitive nose.

paragraphs.text: The tiger moves very cautiously, keeping its eyes on both sides of the path so as to take note of anything unusual happening. If it notices that certain objects are lying on its path which it did not see earlier, it will keep its eyes alert while moving towards it, and if it senses that things are unfamiliar and unsafe, it will shun that path. The tiger is a very clever animal. As it falls upon its prey and moves away with it, it runs very swiftly and leaps also. The movement of the cat may not be exactly like that of the tiger, but there are great similarities between them.
summary: The tiger moves very cautiously, keeping its eyes on both sides of the path so as to take note of anything unusual happening.
The tiger is a very clever animal.
The movement of the cat may not be exactly like that of the tiger, but there are great similarities between them.

paragraphs.text: The horse usually runs continuously. When taking a turn to the left or the right, it is hardly aware of propriety. The pig never moves in a disciplined manner; whatever food it comes across, it turns in that direction. The dog usually moves quickly. Although it runs in the direction of food, it does not at all lack alertness. The buffalo moves more slowly than the cow, while always fixing its eyes on the watershed. When it comes across any watershed, it does not care for any right or wrong and simply plunges into the water. The cow normally moves at a medium pace and habitually avoids mud, slime, water and sand very carefully. It does not like to come in contact with water, and does not like to bathe in water at all. The lion is fond of moving in leaps and bounds. It also loves to run. However, it has less intelligence. So for no real reason it runs and leaps and thereby endangers itself.
summary: The horse usually runs continuously.
When it comes across any watershed, it does not care for any right or wrong and simply plunges into the water.
So for no real reason it runs and leaps and thereby endangers itself.

paragraphs.text: Sheep move at a medium pace and prefer to move in a row. The first sheep in the row may keep its eyes on food but others in the row follow the beaten track blindly. This movement of sheep is called gad́d́áliká praváha [following the beaten track] or gad́d́ál > gad́hál > gáŕhol >gáŕol. The foolish person is sarcastically called gáŕol. Actually gáŕol means “sheep”. In northern India, those who tend the sheep are known as gad́heri.
summary: Sheep move at a medium pace and prefer to move in a row.
The foolish person is sarcastically called gáŕol.
In northern India, those who tend the sheep are known as gad́heri.

paragraphs.text: [The nature of people is somewhat like that of a flock of sheep. When one sheep falls into a ditch, the others will follow.]
summary: [The nature of people is somewhat like that of a flock of sheep.
When one sheep falls into a ditch, the others will follow.

paragraphs.text: In this world, there is a common trend. Just as one sheep runs ahead, the other sheep behind it follow suit. If the sheep ahead falls into a pit, the sheep behind it also fall into the pit. The ox loves to move haltingly. After moving forward a few steps, it stands still like a sculpted statue. If it happens to notice any food nearby, it will slowly move in that direction without caring what others might think. It does not even care to check whether someone may come chasing it. Its temperament is such that it appears not to care for anyone on this earth. Suppose you see an ox standing on the road. For your own safety, you are walking at a distance by the side of a drain on the other side of the road. The ox would not even bother to look at you; it simply would have no interest. However, if you are wearing a garland of marigolds around your neck, it will advance towards you. You might think it is coming to knock you down, and so you may run away. However, the ox is not coming to attack you. It is coming in your direction to snatch away the marigolds and gobble them up. The habit of the ox is to move step by step and then halt, rest a while, and then again move. Due to this strange habit it is called kramodbeg [graded tension]. This word is specifically used to describe an ox of bulky appearance. ( 1 )
summary: In this world, there is a common trend.
For your own safety, you are walking at a distance by the side of a drain on the other side of the road.
This word is specifically used to describe an ox of bulky appearance.

summary: Birds and Animals, Our Neighbours [a compilation]

paragraphs.text: Crocodiles develop friendships with sparrows and other tiny birds, while donkeys are friends with pigeons. On the sandy beds of rivers the crocodile rests and warms itself in the sun, keeping its mouth open while tiny birds enter its mouth and pick up bits of meat from in between its teeth, thus cleansing them. It is to be remembered that the crocodile does not use any kind of toothbrush or other instrument to clean its teeth. Likewise, pigeons sitting on the backs of donkeys pick lice and other insects and eat them. The donkeys feel comfortable with this and the pigeons also obtain their supply of food. Donkeys feel much better when the pigeons have picked the insects off their backs. That is why pigeons are the favorite birds of donkeys. For this reason, pigeons are also known as kharapriya. ( 1 )
summary: Crocodiles develop friendships with sparrows and other tiny birds, while donkeys are friends with pigeons.
The donkeys feel comfortable with this and the pigeons also obtain their supply of food.
For this reason, pigeons are also known as kharapriya.

paragraphs.text: I mentioned to you in connection with musk that the hormone secreted by the musk deer accumulates in its navel, and as it becomes stiffer, the intensity of its fragrance also increases. Ultimately when it becomes too stiff, the fragrance also becomes too intense. At this stage, overwhelmed and excited by the fragrance, the deer runs madly in search of the fragrance until finally, exhausted and worn out, it meets its death. Similarly the elephant, in a state of frenzy in certain situations, turns mad and after some time it dies. Of course, not all elephants turn mad, and those which do become mad do not live long in this condition. Among elephants, such deaths are not frequent, yet they do occur. Elephants that go berserk are not only dangerous for human beings; they are also dangerous for other elephants. Other elephants become frightened of them and stay far away. In normal conditions, elephants enter human localities in search of food. Their favorite food is green leaves and twigs, ripe maize, paddy and wheat. If they can procure food without any disturbance, they do not attack anyone. The villagers light fires and beat drums and tin pots; they do all these things not in fear but to avoid any kind of disturbance.
summary: I mentioned to you in connection with musk that the hormone secreted by the musk deer accumulates in its navel, and as it becomes stiffer, the intensity of its fragrance also increases.
Elephants that go berserk are not only dangerous for human beings; they are also dangerous for other elephants.
The villagers light fires and beat drums and tin pots; they do all these things not in fear but to avoid any kind of disturbance.

paragraphs.text: When an elephant goes berserk, it does not even think of food; it goes without food for several days and even goes without water. Its overheated brain urges it to break laws... to challenge restrictions. You all know that there are those who encourage people to break laws, and in fact incite them to do so. The consequences are never good. To quickly achieve independence during British rule, a class of political leaders started a civil disobedience movement (in Hindi, kánun toŕńá). Some of them used to say, “Our objective is not to break the law … our aim is to tear through the mist of darkness to reveal the truth … to snatch our freedom away from the clutches of evil; this is not a movement to break laws.” This is our urge, our search for truth… this is satyágraha [the movement for truth].
summary: When an elephant goes berserk, it does not even think of food; it goes without food for several days and even goes without water.
The consequences are never good.
” This is our urge, our search for truth… this is satyágraha [the movement for truth].

paragraphs.text: However, whatever name you may give to the rose, the rose is still a rose… The thresher still threshes paddy even while in heaven… this path of disobeying the law is the way to break the law… to challenge any regulation. Its results are never good. Today, following in this tradition, without any forethought, for the slightest agitation, for any dissatisfaction, people burn trams and buses which were purchased with the tax-payerʼs money… they burn down private and state buildings, destroying their own hard-earned wealth, and reduce them to ashes. Behind all these acts lies that old civil disobedience movement of those unruly people during the British rule – or what can be called in chaste language “satyágraha.” After careful analysis and discrimination, we should call it “durágraha” [movement for evil] and not a movement for truth. Rather it is a tool to destroy the present society.
summary: However, whatever name you may give to the rose, the rose is still a rose… The thresher still threshes paddy even while in heaven… this path of disobeying the law is the way to break the law… to challenge any regulation.
Behind all these acts lies that old civil disobedience movement of those unruly people during the British rule – or what can be called in chaste language “satyágraha.
Rather it is a tool to destroy the present society.

paragraphs.text: Those who, in the name of revolution or “leftism” kill innocent people, who are devoid of reason, and who, under the impetus of their confused, irrational philosophy lose their humanity, are also goaded and misguided by a similar type of psychology.
summary: Those who, in the name of revolution or “leftism” kill innocent people, who are devoid of reason, and who, under the impetus of their confused, irrational philosophy lose their humanity, are also goaded and misguided by a similar type of psychology.

paragraphs.text: Be that as it may, I have already said too much in the context of the elephant gone berserk. Nature does not approve of breaking laws. So long as there are rules and regulations, they must be observed. If they are found to be harmful, if they impede the progress of society, if they try to encircle, entangle and shackle the path of human progress at every step like a snake entwined about oneʼs legs, in that case, they must be smashed and razed to dust. New laws must be enacted and obeyed. Otherwise there will be anarchy; the law of big fish eating little fish will dominate society. The civil disobedience movement in India has left that kind of harmful impact on the Indian society.
summary: Be that as it may, I have already said too much in the context of the elephant gone berserk.

If they are found to be harmful, if they impede the progress of society, if they try to encircle, entangle and shackle the path of human progress at every step like a snake entwined about oneʼs legs, in that case, they must be smashed and razed to dust.
The civil disobedience movement in India has left that kind of harmful impact on the Indian society.

paragraphs.text: However, in the case of the musk deer, when it dies in this state of frenzy, usually, the navel of the deer is extracted from its body and used for therapeutic purposes. In ancient times, people believed that when a person developed breathing difficulties in the final critical stage [of life], the use of the navel hormone of the musk deer increases the body temperature and sometimes the person even survives. Whether the person survives or not, their life is prolonged, although only for a brief period; there is no doubt about it. The medicinal power and quality that makaradhvaja [aquaregia] has are also present to a somewhat greater extent in musk. It is very potent indeed.
summary: However, in the case of the musk deer, when it dies in this state of frenzy, usually, the navel of the deer is extracted from its body and used for therapeutic purposes.
Whether the person survives or not, their life is prolonged, although only for a brief period; there is no doubt about it.
It is very potent indeed.
