points.body: The root meaning of the word kot́arában is a forest where there are plenty of trees that have kot́ar [holes]. In common usage kot́arában indicates a forest of trees having less commercial value, or which are of limited use. Trees that have holes hardly serve any useful purpose. They cannot be used for manufacturing quality furniture. Their wood is also cheap. As mentioned, in common usage kot́arában stands for a jungle of commercially non-valuable timber; the trees of the Sundarbans are mostly of this variety. It is not that there are no good or valuable trees in the Sundarbans, but their number is very limited. However, the trees of the forests belonging to the Jalpaiguri region are mostly of good quality. Of course, there are some trees of non-commercial variety as well. Most trees of the Bankura and western Ráŕh forest areas are of the sal [Shorea robusta] species. The sal species are very valuable trees. Hence the annual financial return of a square kilometre area of forest in the Jalpaiguri region is eight to ten times that of an equivalent area in the Sundarbans. Again, the yearly financial return of a square kilometer area of forest in the Ráŕh region is about one and a half to two times that of the Jalpaiguri forest region. So long as the zamindary system was prevalent, the forests of the Ráŕh region were well-maintained and well-protected. With the abolition of the zamindary system, the forests of the Ráŕh ( 3 ) region – what to speak of Ráŕh, all government-owned forests in the entire state of Bengal – are on the verge of being demolished. The rainfall in the country is decreasing… floods are more frequent, and land erosion is increasing. The wealth of the forests is fast waning. With the dwindling number of birds and animals, the triangular balance and harmony among the trees, wild animals and human beings is about to be disrupted. The air is becoming polluted as the ratio of oxygen in the air diminishes. Toxicity in the environment is spiralling, with a resulting higher incidence of cancer, brain diseases, heart ailments and eye problems. The water table is sinking, and the capacity of storage tanks, wells and water reservoirs has been curtailed. Liveliness and emotional charm are gradually disappearing from human minds, and mental rudeness is magnified at a rapid pace.

points.body: Human beings are very cruel creatures. They eat wild animals, birds and deers after slaughtering them. But is this the end? Is this all? No, they show their extreme cruelty by butchering and eating even their domesticated animals and birds. For the sake of wealth and property, they kill innocent people. Due to their tyranny and acts of oppression, many innocent creatures have been obliterated from the surface of the earth, many green pastures and fields of grain have been transformed into deserts, and treasures of lush green grass have been converted into thorny cacti. points.title: Vultures are carnivorous birds

summary: Vultures are carnivorous birds.

points.body: Vultures are carnivorous birds. Yet it is found that they are not cruel or heartless. Usually, like eagles, they do not attack living humans or animals. Their habit is to eat the flesh of dead bodies. There was an incident in my childhood that I can still vividly recall. To the west of our locality there was a large field that bordered on a tributary of the Ganges. As the soil was not fit for cultivation, nothing was grown there. On the upper side of that fallow land was a mound upon which stood a large tamarind tree. A vulture lived in a nest in the tree. Beside the mound was the site for the disposal of carcasses. Cows used to graze in the field, along with a few horses and sheep. Once an elderly cow came there and fell flat on the ground due to utter exhaustion. The veterinary doctor came and said, “The cow has no chance of survival. She is likely to die in a few hours.” The owner of the cow was a very kind-hearted man. He tried to save the cow in various ways, but in vain. I noticed that so long as the cow was alive, she gently wagged her tail, even when her eyes were half-closed. There was no other symptom of life, or at least so it seemed to me. I also noticed that so long as her tail was wagging, the vulture remained patiently in the tree. It came to eat the cowʼs flesh only one hour after her natural death. Human beings are far crueler than vultures. Their hearts do not melt even when seeing the tears of innocent birds and animals. Just to gratify their sense of greed, they mercilessly slit the throats of animals with sharp knives and swords, thus depriving them of the right to live, and all the while preaching the hollow dictates of religion.

points.body: When any animal lies dead in a field of carrion, people will never bother to go near it. If under compulsion they go there, they will cover their nose with a handkerchief. But when any such smell from a distance enters the nostril of a vulture, it immediately rushes in that direction and easily traces the corpse. The vulture does not consider it to be a foul smell. That is why the rotten corpse is not harmful to the vulture. Yet if humans use carrion as their food, death is inevitable. The difference between congenial and uncongenial mental feelings in human beings occurs according to oneʼs self-created saḿskáras [psychic reactive momenta]. A person belonging to the Ráŕh region would feel like running away from the smell of dried fish. Yet there are places on this earth where the smell of dried fish would be highly coveted. Here the differences between people are due to their self-created saḿskáras. There are some people who slice off the flesh of dead animals lying in a field of carrion and cook and eat it at home. Once I saw vultures eating one part of the flesh of a dead cow, and a girl cutting off another part with a knife and filling a basket with it to take it home. Who knows whether she cooked and ate that meat herself or sold it to a restaurant? Was there any difference between the vultures and the girl as she sliced off the flesh of the corpse with one hand, while with the other hand she warded off the vultures? And yet she was a human being! There was not yet that particular foul smell coming from the corpse, yet there was indeed a bad smell. ( 3 )

points.prompt: Recall and explain from memory: According to many scholars, the first expression of creation took place not on land but…
summary: According to many scholars, the first expression of creation took place not on land but in water.

Without delving into a hair-splitting analysis of how far the author of the shlokas succeeded in his task, one can say that he attempted it with utmost sincerity.
points.body: According to many scholars, the first expression of creation took place not on land but in water. Living protoplasm, thoroughly drenched in carbon materials, appeared as a unicellular entity, as kaoshikii sattá, for the first time in water. It is in water that the unicellular entity or elementary cell evolved into multiple-celled entities or compound cells. Then, in the ascending phase of evolution, due to environmental needs, some of those creatures had to move onto land, while others found opportunity for development in water. Even in water they were born from eggs. On leaving the water, they turned into reptiles. Those reptiles, still oviparous, developed into higher forms of creatures. They evolved into mammals. Higher forms of these reptiles became winged creatures – vihauṋga, or birds. The quadruped mammals living on land learned to climb on trees and developed into shákhámrga [tree animals, that is, ape-men or proto-apes]. The ape-men, climbing further up the ladder of evolution, developed into Australopithecine …proto-human apes. [Some] mrga [quadruped land mammals], after further development, became known as shákhámrga. [Some] shákhámrga were the half-human or anthropoid apes (like gorillas, chimpanzees and orangutans). These anthropoid apes gradually developed into men with pigtails and sacred threads, into men with coats and pants or suits, and, in a further course of forward journey, into enlightened mahápuruśas [great personalities] wearing clothes. How these marine creatures slowly developed into evolved human beings, and from humans into superhumans, has been narrated in the shlokas of Dashávatára [“Ten Incarnations of Viśńu” – the god of preservation]. Without delving into a hair-splitting analysis of how far the author of the shlokas succeeded in his task, one can say that he attempted it with utmost sincerity.

This complete manifestation of Parama Puruśa, this complete development of Táraka Brahma, is the Kalki bháva of Viśńu.
points.body: But even this was not enough. The divinity in human beings, and their humanity, must be spread outwards to all the different corners of the universe. Exceeding the margins of all horizons, they will have to rush beyond the nebulae and stars, transcending the confines of the milky ways towards the limitless boundary of the universe. On the one hand, this path is beautiful, yet on the other hand it is full of struggles – a benevolent path but certainly not strewn with flowers. This is the greater humanity (mahámánava) or Neohumanism. This is the highest fulfilment of life and living. This is to be achieved through an all-out struggle against evil forces. These are creatures of primordial stage of creation in this expressed world. But all the creatures of this group are not of the same type – some are born from eggs, subsequently taking the form of larvae which undergo external metamorphosis and acquire their final forms as flying creatures. As they have an orderly growth divided into subsequent stages, they are called krimi in Sanskrit [the Sanskrit krama = “order”].

points.body: Once an egg is laid, the embryo starts developing under the impetus provided by the eggʼs contact with air, light, and heat from the environment. When the developing foetus is fully mobile, it pierces its shell and emerges into the outside world where it needs more heat than is normally present in the environment; so the mother bird or mother reptile helps the foetus develop by supplying it warmth from her own body. Of course, not all creatures hatched from eggs require this extra heat. In such cases, the mother abandons the egg once it is laid. In accordance with natureʼs law, it does not feel any instinctive affection for the egg. For those eggs which require extra heat, however, it is the law of nature that the mother feels an instinctive affection for the egg. If someone comes and takes the egg, she will often chase after them.

During that time some creatures were in an intermediate stage; for several hundred thousand years they continued to lay eggs, but at the same time they used to breast-feed their offspring in small amounts. Later, when they stopped laying eggs and started bearing their young, the amount of milk they fed their offspring increased.

The crocodile, fish-eating crocodile (mecho-kumiir), iguana (gosáp; in Sanskrit, godhá or godhiká; in indigenous Bengali, goháŕgil, goh, gosáp), girgit́i [a type of lizard], t́ikt́iki [a small house lizard], takśaka [a venomous snake] (the word guisáp is used in East Bengal), áiṋjuni [also a type of lizard] – all these egg-producing creatures have a similar nature; they differ only in their level of cruelty. The man-eating crocodile is extremely ferocious. The rest of these creatures are also ferocious with the exception to some extent of the iguana, which, despite being a meat-eater, has a somewhat timid nature. When they see people, they will flee if they have some place to run. The Indian iguana is predominantly of two types: the black iguana and the golden iguana, both of which share this timid nature.

Those who are permitted to take fish, such as Gaoŕiiya Vaeśńavas [Vaishnavites of Bengal], eat it as fish. I say once again, ciḿŕi is not a fish; it is a kind of insect from putrid water. There are ciḿŕi of different types, belonging to both sweet and saline water. Ciḿŕi of reddish hue are found in the estuaries and rivers adjacent to the sea. These shrimp are hard to digest and cause ailments to those who partake of them. Amongst the sweet water ciḿŕi available in Kolkata are lobster, bágdá ciḿŕi [another big-size ciḿŕi], kuco ciḿŕi, mocá ciḿŕi, kádá ciḿŕi, etc. [all smaller and still smaller varieties]. Although people of Kolkata do not eat them, in some parts of Bengal people also eat dried shrimp (shut́ki ciḿŕi). Like the salted hilsa, these dried shrimps are foul-smelling and rather bad for digestion. As some flying insects look like prawns, they are called ucciḿŕe (ur [flying] + ciḿŕe = ucciḿŕe). points.body: The water turtle is highly carnivorous. However, the water turtle also comes onto land in order to lay its eggs. It removes some sand or soft earth and lays its eggs in that depression. Afterwards it covers up the eggs and returns to the water. With the help of the internal heat of the sand or earth, the young break their shell and emerge. The moment the young ones are born, they run straight for the water. Normally most of the young turtles are eaten by birds or other carnivorous creatures before they can make it from land to the water. While the tortoise also lays its eggs underneath the sand or earth, it remains nearby, so fewer of its children die. The water turtle lays a great quantity of eggs, while in comparison the tortoise lays far fewer. People eat both kinds of turtle eggs. A perusal of old Bengali literature shows that the Bengalees of that time used to eat turtle eggs with bitter greens [a bitter vegetable green]. Not all water turtles are edible.

Those sharks that are large in size and live in the ocean are normally called háuṋgar in Bengali, and those sharks that live in coastal rivers, backwaters or estuaries, are called kámat́a in spoken Bengali. They are somewhat smaller in size than the háuṋgar. At one time there were a great number of kámat́as in the rivers of Midnapore, 24 Paraganas and Khulna Districts. Taking bath in those rivers was dangerous during that period. The oil of these kámat́a sharks has medicinal qualities. As the cod fish began disappearing, shark oil began to be used as a substitute for cod liver oil, and from that time began the annihilation of the kámat́a species. Nowadays the number of kámat́as has greatly diminished. ( 9 )

points.body: In ancient times any aquatic creature was called matsya or fish. The word makara means crocodile, but according to some, a makara is háuṋgar or kámat́a. If it belongs to the sea, it is called háuṋgar [big shark]; if it belongs to saline river water, it is called kámat́a [small shark]. But the háuṋgar or kámat́a is of course a fish – a fish with rows of sharp teeth that, because of its characteristics, is sometimes described as a water vulture. However, there cannot be any justification for calling the crocodile a fish. It belongs to the land, eats on the land, and sleeps on the land. It lives in cavities near any pond. No pond with its nearby cavities and land can be found in the ocean. That is why there is no crocodile in the ocean. Where would it find shelter? Where would it eat? Where would it sleep? Even then, since ancient times common people have called the crocodile makaramatsya [crocodile fish], from which in current Hindustani has come the word magaramaccha. In a village in Khulna, I have heard people calling shrimps ciḿŕi mách and crabs kákŕá mách [mách means “fish”], although there is no head or tail relation between the fish and the crab.

points.body: Similar is the case of dolphins (shishumár, porpoises), whales, seals and walruses; they do not belong to the fish category. They are not born from eggs; they are mammals. Yet many people wrongly term the whale and the seal as fish. This is certainly incorrect. In ancient times, dolphins were land mammals. Losing the battle of survival, they were compelled to take shelter in the water. Hence their lungs function like those of land animals. They develop respiratory problems if they remain too long under water. So at intervals, they swiftly float up to the water surface, breathe deeply, and then again dive to the depth.

points.body: Although whales are large in size, they were also originally land creatures. Due to fear of other gigantic, carnivorous land animals, the whales were likewise compelled to retreat into the water. Even today their way of breathing is different from that of other sea creatures. Their ways of eating are also different. They combine their eating and breathing. With mouths wide open, they dive deep into the water and swallow not only small but also many large creatures. At that time, both air and water enter their gullet. After some time, through a slit in their head, they spray the water up and outwards like a fountain. One can locate whales from their water spraying. In this manner, whale hunters come to know the location of whales.

points.body: Dugong: Stories circulate in certain parts of the world about sea creatures called mermaids. The lower part of their (dugongsʼ) body below the navel is like that of a fish; on its upper part there are wings and fins for moving ahead and steering through the water. Its facial appearance is similar to the walrus. It is a kind of mammal, hence this creature has teats above the navel. Generally it keeps the lower part of its body under water and will bring the upper part above the surface of the water for a short while. It then immediately dives back into the water. Since it has teats above the navel, people at a distance used to wrongly perceive it as a woman. In fact, these creatures are like whales and walruses – a type of mammal living in the water.

points.body: It is said that these creatures have excessive emotions or sentiments. The word kaeshik is applied to them; it means inordinate articulation of anger, shyness, hatred, affection, love, attachment or disaffection. In their welling up of emotions, people cry out in joy, which they cannot restrain with the help of their nervous system. Though unwilling to express hatred, they often fail to suppress it. Thoughts stirred by feelings of love, affection, compassion and attachment are suddenly articulated when people become unable to confine those feelings to the subterranean currents of their hearts. Probably later they think that they should not have said such things. They realize that it was not proper for them to have expressed themselves. This expression of emotion varies from creature to creature, from human to human, and even varies in the mode and trend of expression. The general name for this form of expression is kaeshik. Under the influence of kaeshik, human beings often commit suicide. Being goaded by kaeshik [the urge for emotional expression], they climb high mountains, sail through space and kiss the soil of the poles.

points.body: A long time ago, in eastern Indonesia, a man killed an innocent dugong. The dugong does not have the strength or intelligence to fight against human beings. After some days it was found that about fifty to sixty dugongs had helplessly flung themselves onto the seashore. Since they are marine creatures, when they sprang out of the water and dashed themselves onto the land, they all died immediately. The local people then understood that for their murder of one innocent dugong, fifty to sixty dugongs, in an emotional, silent protest, had made a sacrifice of themselves. ( 2 )

In common usage, it means a salt-water porpoise [the same suborder as the dolphins]. Although uśaka means salt-water porpoise, in colloquial Sanskrit the word is used to mean any kind of porpoise – fresh-or salt-water. Another name for the porpoise is shishumár.

points.body: Zoologists say that life first evolved in water. Different water animals, driven by the urge for self-preservation, became land animals and birds. All water animals of those days were oviparous. Hence, all animals which later became land animals or birds were all oviparous in the primary stage. Those that became land animals were in their initial stage reptiles, for example, the dinosaur, coctatius [such as alligators and crocodiles], etc. The ancient dinosaurs and coctatius were all oviparous. Those of their direct descendants that still exist on earth in the form of different species – the crocodile, lizard, chameleon and snake – are all oviparous. Those that evolved from water animals into flying animals (i.e., birds) are all oviparous.

points.body: When reptiles, in a transformed state after becoming land animals, gave up crawling on their chests and learned how to move on their hind legs or on four legs, they abandoned their oviparous character and became mammals. During the intermediate stage of their evolution into mammals, for a certain period they retained some of the characteristics of both oviparous animals and mammals. For example, some of them were oviparous, yet at the same time were mammals. Some were not oviparous and also were not mammals. On certain isolated islands today, such intermediate-stage animals still exist. The duckbill [platypus], living in certain South Pacific islands, belongs to this category. They belong to the cat family, are oviparous and yet are mammals. However, due to natural law, these animal species are not expected to survive on the earth much longer. Certain land animals glide through the air and fly with the help of webbing on their hands and body. They are simultaneously land animals and oviparous mammals. Although they can fly, they are not really birds. Examples are bats, titmice and flying squirrels.

points.body: Even after leaving behind their reptilian characteristics upon becoming land animals and mammals, some of them again returned to the water for self-preservation. Although they are now aquatic animals, they still show many characteristics of land animals. Of these, some familiar names are the whale and the porpoise. They are aquatic animals, but they do not belong to the fish group. They are not oviparous, and their young ones suck milk from their motherʼs breast. Many mistake whales for fish. Whales are whales; they are not fish. The walrus and seal are not fish either. Although the prawn, octopus, lobster and tortoise are partly aquatic and partly terrestrial, they are not fish. They are oviparous.

points.body: The coelakanth, the ancestor of the fish group, is in no way similar to the prawn, octopus, tortoise and lobster. Yet they share one similarity; they are all oviparous. Octopuses are akin to spiders in many respects. Hence although the octopus is an aquatic animal, some say that one species, after becoming land animals, might have been transformed earlier into spiders. This type of fish we call jiiyal [“that which can be kept alive in a vessel of water”]. Some examples of this are nyát́á, kai (in Maethilii kavai), shiuṋgii (shruṋgiká), mágur (madgur), etc. If they could survive for a few million more years, they would be transformed into land animals. If the deer, while quenching its thirst by the river bank, catches the eye of a crocodile or vice-versa, sometimes it happens that the deer trembles, frozen in fear to the spot, and the crocodile slowly advances and grabs it. In this manner, the fish-eating alligators [mecho kumiir] are able to catch fish and other water animals that move with relatively greater speed. The crocodile and the alligator, although they submerge into the water for their prey, live in cavities near the riverbed. Due to the mesmerizing power of their eyes, they not only get hold of agile water and land animals and eat them, they are also able to catch and eat air-borne creatures.

In India the iguana or go sáp is divided mainly into two classes: the dark iguana (krśńa godhiká) and golden iguana (svarńa godhiká). points.body: In ancient times, people believed that this lizard-like creature or go sáp ran after cows to suck the milk from their udders, and when they failed to get milk, they bite the cowsʼ udders, which caused ulcers to form. The cows became blind and even died due to the impact of the venom. Since these reptiles ran after the cows, they were called godhá>gohá >goh. At certain places they were called goh, gohágil or go sáp. Go sáp means “the snake that is associated with cows”. As indicated earlier, this reptile is much larger in size than the chameleon, and even more heavyset. In ancient times, people used to eat these iguanas after roasting them in the fire. Even today some groups of people do this. In the middle era of Bengali literature, the poet Kavikauṋkan narrates that pregnant women in Bengal used to eat roasted iguanas.

points.body: In physical appearance, dark skinned iguanas are larger in shape. In some areas of the Sundarbans, iguanas are so large in appearance that from a distance they may be mistaken for crocodiles. Of course, like the crocodiles, they belong to the reptilian order. Ranging from huge crocodiles to alligators, man-eating crocodiles, fish-eating crocodiles or ghaŕiyáls, chameleons, house lizards or tiny lizards that lie hidden in the corners of rooms, all belong to the same order of reptiles. They are born from eggs and all are carnivorous. The manner in which they grab their prey is quite similar. They all possess the capacity to create a vacuum in their palms. They can all lash with their tails during flight. Their ancestors, the coctatius, had thorny backs, the remnants of which we can still see on crocodilesʼ back. By nature they are very cruel. Those species living on land, such as iguanas, chameleons, house lizards and small lizards living in rooms, are afraid of human beings, but their amphibian relatives such as crocodiles, fish-eating crocodiles and ghaŕiyáls are not afraid of people. Sometimes, though, they run away at the sight of people in self-preservation.

points.body: For the amphibian species, raw turmeric is as good as poison. Even for those that live on land, raw turmeric acts like poison. Since they move on their breasts, they are all reptiles. Long, green-coloured iguanas are found in Southeast Asia and Japan in great numbers, but in the Sundarbans there are only a small number; they are also called salamanders. The hide of this variety of iguana is very soft, smooth and comfortable. For this reason, during the British rule [of India] iguanas were killed and nearly obliterated. Later during the same regime, certain restrictions were imposed on the killing of these creatures. But by then, substantial harm and loss had already been caused to the iguanas. Like the water snakes (d́hoṋŕá, d́hyámná and jald́hoṋŕá), its population has also declined. Though iguanas primarily eat the eggs of birds, they also eat their own eggs. In this regard, their habits are somewhat similar to those of snakes.

There is a misconception that people die if bitten by an iguana. However, it is a wrong notion. Of course, since it is a carnivorous animal, its bite does have a poisonous effect. The notion that the iguana bites and does not let a person go until the clouds burst is also not correct. Although a small creature, its cries are very loud and shrill; it sounds like a bird calling from a distant tree. In this regard it is similar to the hedge cricket and cricket.

points.body: House lizard (t́ikt́iki): The house lizard or t́ikt́iki of Bengal is generally lean in appearance and makes a t́ikt́ik sound. Since they make a t́ikt́ik sound, they are called t́ikt́ikis. In the Auṋgiká language they are called t́ikt́ikiá. In northern Bihar and the eastern part of Uttar Pradesh, house lizards are large in size, white in appearance and are dumb. The people of this region call the house lizard bichaoti, and in Hindi they call it chipkali. In their habits, the house lizard is no exception to other lizards. As they create a vacuum in the curves of their feet, they can move quickly along the walls. While moving in this way, if they lose this vacuum grip, they fall down. The connection between the house lizard and its tail is very slender. That is why, when somebody presses down on their tail, they run away leaving it behind. They develop another tail after a few days. ( 5 )

points.body: You might have noticed house lizards sitting on a wall. How do they remain like that? Below the feet of most of lizards is a pad. By placing that pad on the wall, they create a vacuum, and thus remain fixed on the wall. However, when they move quickly on the wall, they cannot retain that vacuum. So they wait and move slowly, because if they move too fast, sometimes they slip to the ground.

points.body: You may have also noticed cockroaches. They are called telápoká in Bengali. Since they drink oil, they are called taela [oil] páyiká [that which drinks oil] in Sanskrit. From this word taela páyiká has come the Bengali word telápoká. Cockroaches are a favourite food item of house lizards. In Asia there are approximately fourteen types of cockroaches that are able to fly, but the house lizard cannot do so. The lizard order cannot fly. Nevertheless, they are all very ferocious. You may have noticed a house lizard sitting on the wall fixing its gaze on a cockroach, and the latter is quite mesmerized and has lost the power to fly. Since its nerve cells have stopped functioning, it is unable to fly with the help of its nerve fibres. Then the house lizard slowly moves forward. It moves slowly because it will fall down from the wall if it tries to move fast. The benumbed cockroach remains at that very spot, and the house lizard then slowly swallows it. After it has been partially swallowed, the cockroach becomes restless, but by then it is too late for it to escape from the mouth of the lizard.

Id́ápalli stands for the village of the Iid́ává community. So, although the proper name of Bhát́páŕa is Bhat́t́apallii, it is not a Sanskrit word. If we want to consider Bhat́t́apallii as a Sanskrit word, the meaning of Bhat́t́apallii would be Bhat́t́a or pandit, with pallii meaning house lizard (t́ikt́iki); that is, it will mean “pandit house lizard”. points.body: Crocodiles (krkalás group): I have said before that in Sanskrit, the krkalás group of reptiles refers to the coctatius sub-order. In the ancient world, this group of animals appeared on earth several thousand years before the appearance of humans. Their ancestors were much larger in size than present-day crocodiles (kumiir). This group appeared after the appearance of dinosaurs. The primitive dinosaurs were graminivorous. However, later they split up into branches: one remained graminivorous and was bigger in size, and the other a little smaller in size. They came to have mixed food habits, meaning they were graminivorous as well as carnivorous – both vegetarian and non-vegetarian. These carnivorous dinosaurs evolved into the ancestors of the prehistoric lizards.

points.body: There are various justifications for this hypothesis. Dinosaurs could not climb trees or move across steep hills. They had to move along the plains like human beings and cows (Zebu indica). Yet those animals belonging to the prehistoric lizards could climb trees and even up steep rocks because under their feet they had soft pads by which they could create vacuums and adhere to walls. This krkalás group of animals later split into two groups: one group comparatively large, hard-bodied and thorny, and the other comparatively soft and free from thorns on their body. Those without thorns, such as the go sáp or iguana, the girgit́i or chameleon, gui sáp or takśak, lived on land. Those with thorns habitually remained on land. To get hold of their prey, they went down into the water and, in that case, became “animals of the water”. Amongst them are crocodiles, alligators, etc.

points.body: By nature, the thorny variety of these reptiles is very ferocious. Their mode of catching prey (i.e., catching both land and aquatic animals) is quite similar. They attack their prey even when well-fed. If they are not capable of eating their prey, they leave it to rot in a secluded spot and return to consume it some days later. This reptile, fixing its gaze for a long time on its prey, scrutinizes which part of the preyʼs body it will eat first. Due to gazing at the prey for a long time, sometimes tears trickle from its eyes. Observing this, people wrongly think that it is weeping in grief over its prey. No, this is not the case.

points.body: Creatures belonging to the krkalás group are all born from eggs. Almost all mesmerize their prey and then attack. By nature and habit, because they are somewhat dirty, excessively carnivorous and drink little water (those that live in water, such as crocodiles and alligators, hardly drink any water), their teeth are weak and worm-ridden, and due to being excessively carnivorous, a foul smell emanates from their bodies. In earlier days, in the Burdwan district in the River Gáuṋgur (Devidaha) and on the borders of Birbhum-Burdwan-Murshidabad in the River Kuey (at the confluence of Bakreshvar and Kopái rivers), there were plenty of crocodiles. Crocodiles also remain in the lower rung of the Rupnarayan River, in some areas of Tamluk sub-division, and in the Shyampur region of Howrah. At one time in Midnapur district, the Rasulpur and Digha rivers were full of crocodiles of the saline water. In those days the rural people of Midnapur and 24 Parganas never crossed the rivers without spears in their hands. All those narrow rivers were called kháŕi (estuary) in ancient Bengali. The water of these estuaries was invariably saline.

points.body: In assessing the present situation, crocodiles still remain in India. However, they are almost on the verge of extinction. There were also crocodiles in that part of Hazaribag district through which the Damodar River flows; they are now present only in limited numbers. Just as tigers eat people today, in those days crocodiles would swoop upon and catch human beings in their grip. It was a regular, everyday phenomenon. I heard a story regarding the crocodiles of the southern part of Midnapur. Once a certain co-wife was having a meal with banana, curd and ciŕá [pressed rice]. The news reached her that her counterpart (second co-wife) had been caught by a crocodile. If the second co-wife died, then she (the first co-wife) would become impure as per the social code and would not be allowed to finish her meal. So she continued to wolf down her meal. Some examples of these life forms are snakes, frogs, marmots, etc. Some species of the scorpion order are also reduced to this state. These creatures that go into hibernation cannot move during the winter; they are affected by a particular kind of drowsiness. They expend the fat collected in their body during this period in order to preserve the body. The heat generated by their fat keeps them alive. At the end of winter, with the touch of the refreshing warm spring breeze, they regain their power of movement. At that time they are still quite weak. Their outer skin becomes very loose because, with the consumption of fat, the external cover of the body shrinks to a certain extent.

points.body: At the end of winter when the warm season begins, like all other creatures in hibernation the snake also awakens. At that time, in comparison to its body, the outer skin is very loose. The snake then sheds its own skin. So, that discarded skin serves temporarily as its cover (kholas). In proper Bengali it is called nirmok (nir + muc + ghaiṋ suffix), or slough. When it sheds this slough, the light skin underneath is exposed. Neither sunlight nor daylight can be endured by this newly exposed skin. That is why, during this period, the snake comes out after dusk and its nature becomes sensitive and ferocious. ( 1 )

points.body: Snakes are cowardly by nature: Although we consider snakes as very venomous creatures, they are in reality very cowardly by nature. They are always engrossed in protecting themselves. They are always restless in apprehension of the mongoose, that is, neuls (nakula > naula > neul; barjiká > bajjiá > beji. In Bengali both beji and neul are accepted names). Furthermore, snakes are always on the alert for peacocks coming from any direction. Out of the urge for survival and self-preservation, they are continuously aggressive and hissing. Except in a few instances, they will run away given the opportunity, instead of giving chase. When the snakeʼs tail is trampled upon, it bites out of fear of death. When it sheds its skin, for some time it remains very sensitive and excitable because of its new, thin skin, and as a result it bites at the slightest provocation. Except for black cobras, most snakes will usually take the first opportunity to run away. Since black cobras have excessive venom, they are by nature hot-tempered. That is why they are fond of comparatively cold environments, despite being tropical creatures. When snakes live in cold countries, they are non-venomous.

Many people call the old snakes that have shed their tails a vástu sáp [house snake]. Since they dwell in our houses, they are called vástu sáp. We have to remember that even black cobras belong to the larger group of gokśurá class. In English they all belong to the cobra suborder. Even the largest, most venomous snake, candracuŕa is called “king cobra” in English. This gokśuro or gokśura is generally known in the western part of Ráŕh as kharish. points.body: During British rule, a census revealed that Burdwan district had the highest number of deaths from snakebites. One can easily surmise that the highest number of snakes was prevalent in that district. Generally the snakebites occurred near ponds. The reason can be easily understood. Since Burdwan is a western district [of Bengal], summers were long and the rainy season was likewise prolonged. Being the land of sticky, clayish soil, there are plenty of ponds. In the sandy, soft earth the snake pits are readily filled with rain water. Yet it does not happen in sticky soil. The pits remain undisturbed for a longer period. For this reason, snakes thrived there. Since certain circumstances have changed, the number of snakes in that district has diminished substantially. Nevertheless, the eastern part of Burdwan district continues to have a significantly larger snake population.

This is because it is a region having excessive rain, heat and humidity. In this regard, Bengal is also the land of tigers that likewise prefer dense forest and exceedingly long summers followed by abundant rain. In ancient times in Bengal, except for the periphery of Ráŕh, there were few lions, but tigers thrived because it was the land of dense forests. Only along the periphery of western Ráŕh did lions and tigers live. Today tigers are on the verge of extinction, and there are no remnants of lion species in Bengal. The lions of Ráŕh have been extinct for the past two hundred years. There may be one or two lone survivors. However, if at all they exist, they are barely visible.

points.body: The overindulgence of Manasá worship or devotion to the goddess Manasá is found only in the snake-infested regions of India. You will notice that, because people who relied on gods and fate, tried to safeguard themselves, Manasádevii emerged. However, in all countries there are always some practically minded people. People noticed that nakul (neul or beji, in English “mongoose”), keráńi pákhi [a bird of the woodpecker subfamily] and peacocks are very adept at killing snakes. The nakul kills snakes but has little interest in eating them. Unless compelled to do so, it does not eat snakes. Human beings who eat snakes generally sever the head and eat the rest of the body. Keráńi pákhi both kills and eats the snake, yet it hardly relishes eating it. However, the peacock both kills snakes as well as relishes eating them. More than male peacocks, the female peacocks are adept at killing as well as eating snakes. In ancient times people worshipped the goddess Manasá, but in pursuit of pragmatism they kept mongooses and peacocks as pets. They were more interested in keeping peacocks than mongooses as pets, because mongooses kill snakes only when they encounter them. In contrast, peacocks consider snakes as their food, and hence actively seek them out in their resting places and kill them. Those pet peacocks that were adept at killing snakes and trained for this work were called garavrata in ancient times. ( 3 )

points.body: Python: You all know that because of the differences between non-venomous and venomous snakes, snakes are of two kinds. The large-sized snakes are mostly non-venomous. Also, venomous snakes are not equally venomous. Compared to other venomous snakes, the black cobra is by far the most venomous. They are divided into álkeut́e, kálkeut́e, gharkeut́e, gáckeut́e and other species: gokhro snakes (gokśurá, cobra; in Ráŕh Bengali called kharish) are divided into káligokhro, padma-gokhro, cakra-gokhro and other species. These gokhros are less venomous than the keut́e (black cobra). Apart from this, in [India] the other venomous snakes are laud́agá, sháṋkhámut́i, dumukho, biściti, etc. In America there is the rattlesnake (jhumjhumi sáp). In Southeastern Asia, among the venomous snakes the largest in size is the shauṋkhacuŕa (king cobra). They prefer humid forest areas. In the Sundarbans, sometimes a king cobra of fifteen to sixteen feet length can be found. In Burma, Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand, king cobras of twenty-four to twenty-five feet length are found. These snakes are very venomous. Snake venom is used in preparing different kinds of medicines.

points.body: Now let us come to our discussion on pythons. Pythons are large-sized, non-venomous snakes. In English we call it python, in Bengali, mayál. A python can easily swallow a goat. That is why it is called ajagar. All creatures belonging to the snake species maintain certain fixed habits. One of them is hibernation. Many cold-blooded creatures go into hibernation during the winter for a prolonged sleep. For several months they lie almost unconscious. Even if their limbs are chopped off, their sleep remains unbroken.

points.body: In [India] primarily snakes, frogs and ucciḿŕe hibernate in winter. Marmots (a rodent) that reside in cold countries, and a few in the Indian Himalayas, have the longest period of hibernation. As mentioned earlier, during this hibernation they consume their reserved energy. As a result of the reduced fat reserve in the body, when their sleep is broken with the arrival of spring, they appear very lean and thin. For this reason, their outer skin becomes very loose. They then have no alternative but to shed that old skin. When the warm breeze touches their body, snakes shed this outer crust. The inner skin of the snakeʼs body then becomes very sensitive. So the mood and temperament of the snake is very much on edge. Pythons are no exception to this rule. Of course, they do not hibernate for a long period. You all know that snakes have so many different names – bhujaga, bhujauṋga, bhujauṋgama, áshiibiś, ahi, phańii, etc. Their body functions like hands, and they are able to move with its support. Hence one of their names is bhujaga. Both bhujauṋgama and bhujauṋga have the same meaning. Generally pythons do not have venom. Therefore, the word áshiibiś [poisonous] is not applicable, as the word does not refer to non-venomous snakes. Usually non-venomous snakes do not have any hood [phań or phańá]. So also is the case with pythons. So they cannot be called phańii. ( 1 )

points.body: Cobra and black cobra: You already know that cobras (gokhros) and black cobras (keut́es) are different species of the same subfamily of snakes. Black cobras are slender, blackish and refuse to stay in houses; they live in forests and jungles and on the outskirts of inhabited land. Although they are cold-blooded, their temperament is very hot. Their body does not emit a sweet aroma but rather a pungent smell, which may be due to their temperament and nerves. This particular pungent smell often emanates from the body of an ordinary man. A different kind of pungent smell emanates from the body of a courageous man. Then again, if the courageous man is of pious nature, the smell emanating from his body is somewhat like the piquant smell of marigold blossoms. If the man is only of pious nature, the smell emanating from his body is like the drenched earth after the first shower of rain. Belonging to the same family as the black cobras but of a different species are the cobras. The difference in temperament between the cobra and the black cobra is that cobras prefer to stay in peopleʼs houses, especially in derelict houses. Although they live in forests and jungles and next to ponds, they are very fond of abandoned houses. The venom of the black cobra is more potent than that of other cobras, but less than that of the largest – the king cobra shauṋkhacuŕa.

points.body: Cobras on their own do not bite anyone. But if someone tramples upon them without realizing it, they bite in self-defence. Due to advanced old age, when they are bereft of their tails, they find it difficult to move. At that stage they no longer react to any creature or bite it. They live on ripe bananas, insects, milk and fatty items. In rural areas they are called vástu sáp [house-snakes]. Some people do not kill them. Whatever may be the case, no intelligent person should knowingly allow venomous creatures to live in their house – Sarpena saha grihe na vása – whatever you may or may not do to your enemies, you must not under any circumstances live with them in the same house. Some people keep the house-snake somewhere in the corner of their house, and feed it milk and ever ripe bananas. We proverbially say, “Nourishing the snakes with milk and bananas.”

points.body: You must have also heard about kálasarpa. The black cobra is a sub species of gokśura [Cobra de capello]. A gokśura is called gokhro in the Kolkata region. In the Ráŕh region, both the names – gokhro and kharish – are prevalent. [As told little earlier] Gokśura has many species and subspecies – kaligokhro, padmagokhro, shauṋkha gokhro, etc., are examples. The keut́e or black cobra has several species and subspecies, such as kálakeut́e, álkeut́e, etc. A black cobra generally lives outdoors in fields away from human habitation. Kálakeut́e generally lives away from human habitation in forests, bushes and shrubs. Since the body of álkeut́e is very warm [in comparison to other snakes], it usurps rat holes on the sides of embankments in the rice fields [ál in colloquial Bengali] and lives there. When it feels very hot, it keeps its body submerged in water, keeping only its head above the water. Although álkeut́e is short, thin and as venomous as any snake of the cobra family, its temper is always very hot. If any person walking on the ridge inadvertently disturbs its peace, it at once rushes out and bites that person. But other snakes do not rush out to bite; they bite only in self-defence. Álkeut́e, kálakeut́e and common keut́e – all three – cannot stand heat. Many times they lie entwined along the rail lines at night when the rails are somewhat cold. On hearing the sound of a coming train, other snakes flee the rail lines, but the ill-tempered keut́e does not. Possibly it thinks, “Whom do I fear enough to run away from?” Accordingly it remains on the line. So most of the snakes that are run over by trains in the summertime, are keut́es. The Sanskrit name of this keut́e is krśńagokśura or kálasarpa.

Snakes live primarily in tropical countries, particularly where there are adequate wet lands. Generally lions, giraffes, and certain types of deer and golden iguana live in larger numbers in the desert areas or in areas where the surrounding natural colours are grey or sandy. Their enemies, their hunters and their prey cannot recognize them because their colour merges with the colour of their surroundings. This is called prákrtik varńavibhránti [“natural camouflage”].

points.body: Snake venom therapy: You may perhaps know that on the basis of the principle Sama samaḿ shamayati [“poison controls poison”], the noble Hahnemann devised his theory called homeopathy, which is an invaluable treasure in human intellectual research. If this knowledge is properly utilized, new kinds of research could take place not only in the world of therapeutics, but in other realms of knowledge as well, and humanity would move boldly forward in different spheres of universal wisdom. The use of snake venom in human medicine has existed since the pre-Aryan age – it was very much prevalent at the time of the Mahábhárata. As in homeopathic medicine, the snake venom is used [such as cobra or Naja], so also other kinds of venom, such as bee-venom (Apis indica) were used. Still other kinds of poison are used today in medical treatment. We can assume that there would be further use of poisons in the future. In ancient India, the use of poison as medicine was widely prevalent. People benumbed with poison were saved or revived by the use of snake venom. When the Kaoravas poisoned them, the benumbed Pandavas, particularly the middle one, Bhimsen, recovered after being treated with snake venom. In those days, the venom of snakes, scorpions, spiders, and honey bees were all used as medicine. This method of treatment using poison acquired great importance and recognition in Kerala. In the royal family of Cochin, several kings and princes won fame in the use of this kind of therapy. ( 5 )

Of course, it is said that there is an exception in the case of kat́kat́e vyáuṋga [frogs making harsh sounds]. It is said that even the female of this species croaks. The garud́a bird is normally seen during the autumn in the fields of autumn crops in North Bihar. They come from cold countries on the other side of the Himalayas. When the seeds are sown in the fields, they come and dig them out and eat them. The common people call them garud́a birds. They drive them away by scaring them, but they do not kill them. They do not even eat them. Garud́a birds are not large in number. Sometimes only one will arrive in a village during a particular year, and may be none in another year. From a distance it can be mistaken for a human being. In height it looks like an ordinary person. Once I saw such a bird in a field of black grams on the northern bank of the Buŕigańd́ak River in the Khagariya District of North Bihar. On another occasion I saw such a bird in wintertime in a field of lentils near Rátábáŕi in the Karimganja district of Assam. The word khecara will also apply to these birds. ( 1 )

points.body: The derivative meaning of the word garud́a is, that which drenches from beginning to end. The Puranic name of the bird Garud́a of which you have heard – why is it so named? Has it from its very birth been drenching the heaven, earth and the netherworld? Yes, according to theologians, it has continued to drench all these spheres with devotional feelings. The Puranic legend concerning Garud́a says that the wife of sage Káshyapa laid several eggs. In due time, when the eggs burst, innumerable infant snakes crawled out. Having so many offspring, his wife, Kadru, was very delighted. With a great sense of glory and pride, she looked at her co-wife, Vinata. Vinata had given birth to only two eggs. The two eggs took a long time to burst. Seeing the great fortune of her co-wife Kadru and her own misfortune, she lost her mental balance. She forcibly burst open one of her eggs. A crimson-coloured male figure emerged. That newly born man told Vinata, “You have forcibly burst the egg in an untimely manner. Hence it will not be possible for me to remain on this earth. I am leaving. I will be the charioteer of the sunʼs seven-coloured, horse-driven chariot.”

points.body: Thus the light that appears in the sky on the threshold of the sunrise, is known as Aruńa, the first child of Vinata. The first streak of light of the risen sun at bráhmamuhúrta ( 2 ) [daybreak] is also called aruńa, and hence, the first rays of the sun seen at bráhmamuhúrta are also called aruńa. In English this colour is called crimson. The morning suffused with this sunlight is called the crimson dawn. To distinguish the variety of red colours, some people describe the colour of the morning sky as crimson red. No, the phrase “crimson red” is not correct; it should be “crimson colour”. Yes, it is truly a unique variety of the colour red.

points.body: The word garud́a means “one whose job is to drench others”. According to the Puranic legend, after coming out of the eggshell, Garud́a told his mother Vinata that his firm resolve was to preach the glory of the Lord. Since by remaining at home on earth it would not be possible for him to fulfil his vow, he would have to move out into the vast expanse of the cosmos. As the mount of Lord Náráyańa, he would go around the world and throughout the universe preaching the glory of the Lord. He would drench the minds of all creatures of the world with tender feelings of devotion. So it was proper to name such a being as Garud́a, whose job was to drench all beings with devotional feelings from birth until death. This entire Puranic story was allegorical. Garud́a represents the devotee of the Lord, and Náráyańa the Supreme Lord. The mind of the devotee is the váhana [mount or vehicle] of the Lord. Devotees want to attain supreme fulfilment by drenching the mind of universal humanity with devotional feelings. Here the word váhana is not used in the literal sense of a physical vehicle. It is in the metaphorical sense of the carrier of the Lordʼs glory. In that sense, the name Garud́a is justified.

They are larger in size than the ganders and flamingos of India. Monkey-eating eagles are quite large in size and have terrific strength. They can swoop down on a monkey and lift it up. If the monkey is too large and cannot be lifted, then, with the thrusts of its wings and claws, and tearing it apart with its beak, the eagle forces it into submission and often eats [the monkey] while it is still alive. Eagles are mostly dark grey or grey in colour. A limited number of eagles are golden in colour. Once upon a time in Great Britain golden eagles abounded. These medium-sized birds were a source of great pride for Britain. During the reign of King Henry VIII, the people of France and Italy used to come to Britain to see the golden eagles. However, that standard of glory is no more. Nearly a hundred years ago, the last surviving golden eagle was shot dead by a cruel hunterʼs bullet. With that event, the era of the golden eagle came to an end.

In India vultures always maintain their unique custom that they will never eat any animal alive. As long as it sees that the tail of the dying cow is moving and stirring, the vulture will not fly down from the tree and put its beak on the animal. Only after making sure that the cow is dead will it begin feasting on its flesh. Eagles and other birds belonging to this family are not guided by such psychology. They attack even living birds and animals. However, they maintain nobility in distinguishing between edible and non-edible prey, which the Indian vultures do not maintain. Almost all dead animals are food for the vultures but are not for the eagles.

In ancient times three varieties of this bird were found in India – krśńa shakuni, svet shakuni and the raktakańt́ha shakuni [the red-throated vulture]. Krśńa shakunis [black vultures] refer to those that we see even today. Svet shakunis [white vultures] are rarely found; raktakant́ha shakunis are even rarer. points.body: Whether it be tropical or cold countries, some species of vultures are sure to be found. Vultures of tropical countries are mostly of the Indian variety. They build their nests on the upper part of tall trees, primarily of banyan trees. While other birds build their nests with bits of dry grass and straw, vultures never do so. Their nests are somewhat open; however, for the protection of the eggs, straw is added. They lay their eggs in sparse quantity. The eggs are a light blue colour, quite large in size. The mother vulture cannot properly hatch her eggs. Instead, they break open with the heat of the sunlight. When vultures go to a distant dung-heap, during their absence salamanders come and eat up the eggs. Some say that due to eating too many of these eggs, the salamanders or iguanas often die. The body of the vulture bristles with different kinds of worms. These worms are found even in their nests.

points.body: Among birds, vultures are very sharp-sighted. Their beaks are extremely hard and can even pierce stones. The strength of their beaks is very close to that of a bird called banrui. They eat the flesh of animals by slicing them neatly with their beaks. Even when eating rotten flesh, they do not get food poisoning. Vultures are natureʼs self-created scavengers. In Bengali it is said, “On land the vulture, in water, the shark”. In Sanskrit the verb shak means “do”. The sentence “He can do it” is sah shaknoti in Sanskrit. With the suffix ktin we obtain the word shakti. In translating the word “battery” we have the verb shak, and adding lyut́ to it, we have the word shakan. With the verb shak and with the suffix uń we derive the word shaktu, meaning fried gram-powder, which gives strength when eaten. Shaktu > shattu > shátu > chátu. From the verb shak we derive the name of the bird shakunta. ( 5 )

They are the old inhabitants of northeast China, Siberia, Russia and Tibet, but due to the oppressive cold in those lands during wintertime it becomes impossible for them to sustain themselves. It is extremely cold, and moreover there is a scarcity of food. Thus they come to India and other hot countries during the winter and remain there for a few months. During this time they lay their eggs, and after their young are somewhat grown they teach them how to fly and how to gather food. Then, when the hot winds begin to blow, they return to their homeland. They return to the exact place they came from, and every year they again return to the same place. By attaching a marker to their legs or through other means, their incredibly- developed intuition and ability to recognize places has been verified. Great crowds of [these flamingos] gather during winter in the Kolkata Zoo, Sandeshkhali of 24 Paraganas, and Bharatpurʼs bird sanctuary. points.body: Parrot, Cockatoo: You surely must be aware of the fact that talking birds are by common consensus divided into two groups: one group is called shuk, and the other group is known as sárii or sáriká. These two groups of birds are talking birds. The beaks of the birds, called shuk, are thick at the source and thin or pointed at the end; they are curved. The beaks of shuks are generally red in colour. Of course, there are some birds of the shuk group whose beaks are not exactly red in colour. Our family birds like t́iyá [parrot], ban-tiyá [wild parrot], candaná [a kind of parrot having red streaks around its throat] and kákátuá (cockatoo) all belong to the shuk group. They appear to be green, yellowish-green or white in outward appearance. Owls do not come out in the day time. Yet, they are similar in appearance to the shuk birds. Owls, however, are not talking birds. Shuks are called sugá in Urdu. The exquisitely red beak of the shuk became sweet indeed in the poetʼs imagination. When looking at the lush red colour of palásh [Butea monosperma] blossoms in the spring, a question arose in the poetʼs mind as to whether it was really a flower or the red beak of the shuk bird. Speaking in Sanskrit, the poet asked, “Was it shuk?” “Kiḿ Shuka?” So from Sanskrit the flower came to be known as kiḿshuka.

Its original habitat was eastern India, especially Ráŕh and Orissa. Millions [of these birds] thrived in the forests of Midnapur, Bhanjabhum, Bankura and Birbhum. The parrot, the wild parrot, the wild myna or pied myna belong to the shuk category of birds. Of course they cannot talk like the mynas. Mynas also have a well developed vocabulary. points.body: Our familiar birds – the bábui (weaver-bird, báyá ciŕiá in Urdu), t́unt́uni (tailor bird in English, in Urdu julhá-ciŕiyá), bulbuli (in English nightingale, in Urdu bulbul) – they all belong to the sárii group. Those of you who are familiar with Vaeśńava literature must have heard or read the narrative of Shuk-Sárii called Krśńakathá related to Rádhá and Krśńa. Among the talking birds of Bengal, the candaná belonging to the shuk group and the myna belonging to the sárii group are more gifted than other birds. During the last fifty years, thousands of birds have been exported abroad from Tripura, Midnapur and Bhanjabhum. India is becoming devoid of myna birds. I am drawing the attention of everyone to this development. Candaná are normally very limited in number. Their numbers are continuing to diminish. Perhaps they are also being secretly exported abroad.

points.body: There was a time when most people belonging to the middle class along with wealthy families used to keep birds as pets in their houses. They normally kept myna or candaná as pets. These two kinds of birds are very calm and quiet. Cockatoos are also talented talking birds. However, they are comparatively larger in size. Their attitude is quite aggressive. That is why they are kept chained to a stand. During the Moghul period even the parrots and candaná were kept chained to a stand. Today they are simply kept in cages. The number of birds is rapidly diminishing. Due to a dearth of money, householders are giving up many of their luxurious habits. Like the dodo birds, these other birds are also awaiting their final days. ( 2 )

An entity which speaks its own language and also utters the words of others, that is, speaks various words, is known as harabolá [capable of mimicking various voices]. The word har [various] comes from the Persian language. In between the house myna and myna there is a bird species that the villagers of Burdwan district call guye myná or guye nyákŕá [wild myna]. These can also be trained to talk. Normally people do not keep wild mynas as pets, but they do keep other mynas. In Sanskrit mynas are called sáriká. Among the more familiar birds of Ráŕh are mynas, red-throated parrots and cockatoos.

points.body: Among the birds belonging to the parrot order, there are cockatoos of different colours – light-green, yellowish, with specks in the throat – candanás of normal appearance and green, hefty parrots, wild parrots and the green-coloured magpie robin (doyel) of Bengal, which are commonly seen in northern Bengal and rarely seen in southern Bengal. Of this group, candanás prefer to stay away from human localities; cockatoos prefer to stay in a humid environment at a distance from such localities. Wild parrots remain in the forest and fly over human localities. They rarely rest at any particular spot. Magpie robins live close to settled habitats, always moving in search of insects. They are very cruel and ferocious in nature.

points.title: Pigeon: By kapota we mean pigeon
points.prompt: Recall and explain from memory: Pigeon: By kapota we mean pigeon
summary: Pigeon: By kapota we mean pigeon.

points.body: Pigeon: By kapota we mean pigeon. From the word kapota comes the word kabutar, and from the word párávat is derived the word páyrá. Kapotaraka > kaotara > kautar > kabutara. By adding the suffix kan to kapota we form the word kapotaka. The word kapota refers to any aircraft, but the word kapotaka means pigeon and nothing else. The etymological meaning of grha kapota is any domesticated pigeon. In common usage it refers to house pigeon or golá páyrá. In ancient times, the people of Ráŕh had boundless affection for birds and animals. To prevent people from flaying the skin of dead animals, they even used to dig pits near the path by their home to bury the corpses of dead animals [cows and other animals] so that no one could come to flay their skin secretly or carry away their flesh by digging them out. To prevent hawks and greedy persons from killing the pigeons, local people, while constructing their mud homes, used to insert clay pitchers at a slant in the wall. Pigeons could use the pitchersʼ opening as an entrance to reach their nests inside. I do not know if this is done nowadays, but they used to do it earlier. Since pigeons lived in homes, they were called grha kapota [domesticated pigeons] or golá páyrá. They were so called because they used to live on the paddy corns of the corn bin in houses. ( 1 )

points.title: Ka means “water”, pota means “ship”
points.prompt: Recall and explain from memory: Ka means “water”, pota means “ship”
summary: Ka means “water”, pota means “ship”.

The feminine form of kapota is kapotii; another meaning of kapotii is “a small, ocean-going vessel”.
points.body: Ka means “water”, pota means “ship”. That which does a shipʼs work at the time of crossing a large reservoir, lake or sea is kapota. That is its etymological meaning. The colloquial meaning of the word kapota is ghugu [“dove”] and páyrá [“pigeon”]. In olden days, when roads were not well-developed, people used to send messages to distant lands with the help of trained pigeons or doves. Generally a letter was attached to one of the birdʼs limbs. Once those trained doves or pigeons arrived at their destination, they would then carry back a reply. This system of mail delivery with the help of these birds was prevalent for many years on the battlefield. Pigeon post was even used in some places in India during British rule. From this word kapota or kapotaraka we obtain the word kabutara (in Mymensingh Bengali, kaetara). However, for “pigeon” the word páyrá is better than the word kabutara, because páyrá has come from the Sanskrit word párávata. Párávata refers only to “pigeon” and not to “dove”, but kapota means both “pigeon” and “dove”. The feminine form of kapota is kapotii; another meaning of kapotii is “a small, ocean-going vessel”.

points.body: People scatter kernels of grain in front of pigeons, or on their usual path, for them to eat. This scattering is called “pigeon feeding.” At the end of autumn, when the paddy fields are somewhat muddy, seeds are scattered in those paddy fields where it is not possible to sow seeds for the winter season, or where, due to lack of water, those seeds will not sprout in the dead of winter even if sown. These sprout and grow into plants in the spaces between the paddy. When the paddy is harvested, the tops of these plants are also cut. As a result, more branches grow, and at the end of the cold season they yield a generous amount of flowers and pods. This type of seed-scattered crop is called the “pyra crop” [pigeon-harvest]. Small lentils, gram or blackish-coloured small gram [also called t́hikre cholá], pea [blackish-coloured, small pea, also called t́hikre mat́ar], rapeseed, khesári or teoŕá (triput́ii or triput́iká – Lathirus sativas) – these crops are generally produced as part of the pyra crop. In most parts of Bihar, the pyra cropping is called páyruyá. On land where there is no system of irrigation, or where the soil becomes hard or cracked at the end of winter, the produce from the pyra cropping is of great benefit to the farmers. Moreover, this pyra crop increases the soilʼs fertility and productivity. As for the surplus, the stalks, pod husks and chaff make excellent bird food and cattle fodder. If mustard is planted, it yields oil cake which can be used as both fertilizer and bird food.

points.body: Peacock: The peacock (mayúr) is a special bird of India. Its original habitat is Southeast Asia. The male peacock can spread its tail and dance; the female peacock has no tail and never dances. It is also ugly to look at. It generally prefers a dry climate, and cannot lay eggs in a humid environment. There may be peacocks in damp forest areas, but for laying eggs they move away to distant drier climates. In Bengal, rather in eastern India, there are few peacocks in the forest areas due to excessive rain. In the Bankura and Purulia districts of western Ráŕh, some peacocks are found in the forests because of the dry climate. Due to the dry climate in western India, especially in Rajasthan and Gujarat, peacocks abound.

points.body: There are generally three different types of peacocks: (1) Our very familiar, colourful peacocks, (2) yellowish peacocks, and (3) white peacocks from Burma and Thailand (Shyámdesh). White peacocks can somehow tolerate a humid environment. Another name for peacock is shikhii. The call of the peacock is known as keká. Hence the word keká means peacock. In ancient times the peacock was a favorite food item for human beings. Emperor Ashoka did not entirely forbid the butchering of peacocks in his kitchen, even after his transformation into Dharmáshoka [non-violent or Buddhist Ashoka].

By adding the suffix kan to the verbal root kae, we obtain the word káka, whose etymological meaning is “one who shouts in an ugly manner”. points.body: There are many colloquial meanings of the word káka, the ordinary crow that we commonly see. According to biologists, the crow is not a very old bird. This half-carnivorous bird (it has an equal fondness for both vegetarian and non-vegetarian food) is renowned for its intelligence. In Bihar it is said, manukhme (one writes it as mánuś but pronounces it manukh) naová, ciṋŕai me kaová. [“Among humans the barber, and among birds the crow.”] That is, among human beings, the most intelligent are the barbers; among birds it is the crow. Their solidarity is also praiseworthy.

Their voice is extremely harsh… something like ka, ka, ka (kka). Their beaks are a little longer and harder than those of general crows. The colour of white crows is not exactly white; rather, it is grey. In ancient times, white crows used to be called báyasa. Nowadays báyasa means any type of crow. In northern India crows are called kaová, and jackdaws are called kág. In Auṋgiká language, jackdaws are called dṋáŕkaová. In the language of Ráŕh, Bengal, they are called ko or koy.

points.body: The second meaning of khat́akhádaka is byághra (vi – a – ghra + a = byághra) or tiger. That is, an animal whose sense of smell is very strong. If a tiger gets a promising scent, it easily locates the prey and pounces on it. Just as a crow is termed a khat́akhádaka due to the strength of its beak, so also a tiger is called a khat́akhádaka by virtue of its strong claws and teeth. Another characteristic of the tiger is that, simply by supposition, it makes a calculated leap so as to fall exactly on its prey.

In this connection, we should remember that although the Bengali word háṋs has come from the Sanskrit word haḿsa, in Sanskrit the word haḿsa does not refer to any particular species of duck; it refers only to the swan (rájhaḿsa). For swan there is another word in Sanskrit, marál, which is now known to belong to the flamingo group. For different species of ducks (háṋs) familiar to us, the Sanskrit name is keraba; for the swan, marál or Haḿsa. In Sanskrit the use of the word rájhaḿsa is very limited; rather, it is hardly used. For duck, the word keraba is used, and for another variety of duck, that is, for the Chinese duck (ciiná patiháṋs), the Sanskrit word is krśńa-keraba or piuṋgal keraba. points.body: Primitive Mammoth: In English, the word for aerávat is mammoth. You certainly describe a large meeting as a “mammoth meeting”. This mammoth was a prehistoric animal. Their descendants are the elephants. In the world today, among the various elephant species the largest one is the African elephant. It is somewhat lacking in intelligence, but is quite huge in height. It is surmised that the primitive mammoth was twice the size of these African elephants. Their tusk was quite long. This huge animal, lacking in intelligence, became extinct nearly half a million years ago. Fossils of this creature have been found in certain areas of Bankura and Purulia. Others have even been found in the eastern part of Ranchi district in the Suvarnarekha Valley. In any case, from what we have come to know thus far, after the primitive dinosaur, these mammoths were the largest creatures to appear on earth. In other words, they were the “second-order” animals in the animal kingdom. Still, it must be remembered that mammoths and dinosaurs did not belong to the same period. Dinosaurs were more primitive than mammoths. In addition, among dinosaurs, the huge-sized dinosaurs (mainly vegetarian) were more primitive than the smaller (mainly non-vegetarian) dinosaurs. ( 1 ) It is surmised that since they were food for the smaller dinosaurs, these huge mammoths became extinct long ago. The smaller-sized dinosaurs became extinct during an Ice Age, most probably under the cover of snow.

points.body: Nature of elephants: Fools can be divided into several groups: “absolute fool”, “ignorant fool”, “blatant fool”, “solid fool”, “elephant-fool” (hastimúrkha), and some people even say “cow-fool” (go-múrkha). The word gańd́a-múrkha means someone whose foolishness has reached down to their cheeks and might come out of their mouth any moment. The solid-fool (niret́-múrkha) is one who is stock full of stupidity with no room to spare. Some people think that the elephant is a large creature but its intelligence is not comparable to its large body. That is why they call some fools hastimúrkha [fools like elephants] when their intelligence is not commensurate with their size. However this expression is not wholly correct. Certain species of elephant have lower intelligence, but not all of them are unintelligent. In fact, some have sharp intelligence. Although the elephants are descendants of ancient mammoths or aerávat, still they cannot be classified into one species at present. The African elephants are quite tall but their heads are comparatively smaller; they have less intelligence and are not amenable to human control.

points.body: Some people think that the sour wood apple (kaed-bel) is a non-Indian fruit, imported from overseas. No, this is not correct. It is a local fruit belonging to a number of Southeast Asian countries. Its Latin name is Feronia elephantium or Feronia elephantinum. Some people might think, “Why is the name of an elephant associated with the fruit called kaed-bel or sour wood apple?” The general consensus of the people of Southeast Asia is that this is a favorite fruit of elephants. Elephants eat this fruit intact, and when the entire fruit comes out in its excreta, one can observe that the elephant has digested the entire core of the fruit, while from the outside it appears that the fruit is intact. That is why the object that appears outwardly intact but is inwardly hollow is called in Sanskrit Gajabhukta kapitthaka [like the hollow wood apple eaten by the elephant]. Elephants eat these fruit intact. They think that the whole fruit tastes very delicious. Elephants do not have the intelligence to realize that taste lies in the taste buds of the tongue; once the food goes past the tongue, there is no difference between sweetmeats and cow dung. In comparison to their size, elephants have low intelligence.

points.body: Herd instinct of the elephant: Like the human being, the lion, the crow and other kinds of birds and beasts, the elephant also has a strong herd instinct. If the herd does not have an unquestioned leader, it breaks up in internal feuds and its security is affected. Hence you can see that when a crow is killed by someone or meets an unnatural death, thousands of crows gather together and raise their voices vociferously in their own language to protest against such an atrocity. At that time, even the most valiant retreat to safety. Those who are against hero worship in human society or are against showing respect to leadership, those who oppose individual superiority, should understand that if such individual recognition is accorded to an honest personality, it helps to guarantee the longevity of human society. If that recognition is misplaced, it becomes harmful. Human beings have advanced in knowledge, science and learning. Since by nature human beings are collective-living creatures, they must find out, irrespective of time and place, a true universal leader who should be given full recognition in the greater interest of collective welfare. Otherwise for the ever-feuding human society, there is no scope for optimism.

points.body: From the Cretaceous to the Oligocene, Miocene and Pliocene periods, mammoths were among the great animals that appeared on earth, and were the predecessors of elephants. Leaving aside those belonging to the reptilian class, all these large animals were herd creatures. They had similarity or uniformity in one respect: their old and physically incapacitated leader used to leave the herd and go to a secluded place, very much like people of ancient times when they became superannuated. In their extreme old age, those ancient people used to leave the society and go into váńaprastha [seclusion]. Living in the forest, they would devote themselves to worship, meditation, and to writing books. They no longer had direct social commitments.

points.body: At the very end of old age, when they became physically incapacitated, they turned into Bhikśus [renunciates]. They had no further social obligations or mundane responsibilities. They had nothing to do except to worship the Lord in seclusion. Those who lived in isolation in forests (váńaprastha) looked after these Bhikśus. points.body: People once believed that if water fell from the star Sváti [the fifteenth of the twenty-seven zodiacal stars], pearls would be produced. Similarly, there was a belief that during the dark fortnight of the moon, if water fell from the Sváti star onto the head of an elephant, jewels (gajamáńikya or gajamoti or maoktika) would form on its head. When this jewel is produced, the elephants turn mad and finally die. In reality, this elephant jewel or gajamoti is something else. Compared to other animals, elephants develop more tumors (arbud) on their head. If any one of these tumors grows too large, the elephant becomes mad and eventually dies. These tumors sometimes become so hard that they cannot be broken or sliced. The common people call it gajamoti or elephant jewel. In English a shrub-like tamarisk is called Thuja, which in Sanskrit is called arbudágni. This shrub-like Thuja neutralizes the tumor. From the Sanskrit word arbud has come the Bengali word áb.

points.body: Thuja is an effective medicine in the treatment of tumors. If elephants are fed the leaves of shrubs like tamarisk on any night during the dark lunar fortnight in the month of Fálgun, Caetra or Vaeshákh [the last two months and first month of the Bengali calendar], they can be cured of this mental malady. Hence you should understand what this term gajamoti means. Whether it be from the growth of a tumor that impairs the brain of the elephant, or whether it be from the rupturing of its [facial] veins due to the scorching heat of the sun, this state of madness is known as gajamoti. In searching for the source of this fragrance, the deer dart about wildly, and after some days turn mad and meet their death.
