points.body: Sundarbans deer (kákara deer): The word kákara has come from the Sanskrit word kokad́. One meaning of kokad́ is the medium-sized deer of slightly red colour of the forests in wet and salty regions. The kákara deer of the Sundarbans belongs to this group. Due to its cry that sounds like kákar … kákar … in Bengali, it is called kákar hariń [kákara deer]. The máyá hariń of the Sundarbans is not a different species of deer. It is the female gender of this kákara-deer. It looks slightly different from its male counterpart. In using the expression meye hariń [female deer] in ancient Bengali, they often used the expression máiyá hariń. This very expression has turned into máyá hariń [legendary deer]. People of ancient Bengal never consciously slaughtered the female deer. Even in the case of ritual sacrifice, it was not the custom to slaughter the female deer. Probably for this very reason, the people of the Sundarbans in those days did not kill the máyá hariń [female deer].

points.body: Goat-like deer (chágal pani): One of the meanings of kokad́ is “very small sized deer”, resembling a goat in appearance. They prefer to live in sparse forests. By nature and temperament they are very quiet and timid. They run away at the sight of humans even from a distance. There was a time when lakhs [hundreds of thousands] of these deer used to roam all over India, as did the krśńasár deer. A few years ago, because of human short-sightedness, the krśńasár deer was on the verge of extinction, but given some recent safeguards, their numbers are now rapidly increasing. Yet for the small-sized deer (kokad́), no such magic wand has been offered for their survival. For this reason they are about to become extinct. Only a limited number can be found in the forests of Assam, and a very few in the Dalma hills and adjoining areas in western Ráŕh. In the Assam region they are called chágalpani, in Rárhii Bengali they are described as mrgii. Due to their sentient nature, people generally look upon them as sacred creatures, which one should neither slaughter nor allow to be slaughtered. Yet, sinful humans are continuing to kill them surreptitiously, and this innocent creature is forced to face the critical question of survival. ( 8 )

points.body: Bison or wild buffalo: In the ancient world wild buffaloes (mahiś) ranged wherever there were forests of tall, wild grass. In todayʼs world, bison are chiefly concentrated in the northern part of America where there are forests of tall grass. The number of bison is rapidly dwindling in other countries of the world. In those areas of Ráŕh where the rhinoceros once lived, and beside large lake areas called baŕa [big] Hizal and chot́a [small] Hizal in Murshidabad district (West Bengal), huge numbers of wild buffalo once roamed. They do not look like domesticated buffaloes. Their mouth is a little lower than that of domesticated buffalo. Their horns are bigger and very strong. Their back is somewhat elevated. Their forelegs are comparatively smaller than the hind legs. Domesticated buffaloes cannot run fast and hence they yield plenty of milk; wild buffaloes run very fast and hence give less milk. Domesticated buffaloes rarely get angry, but wild buffaloes are angry nearly all of the time. Once in Birbhum, some parts of Murshidabad, Sahebganj, Rajmahal and Gadda, there were vast stretches of wild jungle grass called sábui. People used to prepare ropes, sleeping cots, swings, slippers, and so forth out of this sábui grass. Today good quality paper can be made from this grass. At one time wild buffalo used to roam the bushes of this grass in Ráŕh. I have already said that the number of wild buffaloes is rapidly diminishing. There is no such buffalo in Ráŕh now. ( 9 )

points.body: Kangaroo: There are differences with regard to self-confidence between humans and animals. Just as all humans are not equally self-confident, similarly amongst animals and birds the degree of self-confidence is not the same. Suppose a particular person says that they will surely perform a particular task. Another person then comes and discourages and threatens that person. The person loses their self-confidence and gives up. Yet there are other people who, after declaring their intentions and determination, will not bother about other peopleʼs discouragement and threats of obstruction. However, in the event of severe stress and torture, they break down internally. There are still other people, however, who believe in “do or die” and continue with this kind of firm determination. One must understand that their determination and self-confidence are as hard as kaśt́ipáthar [a hard stone]. They emerge victorious and give inspiration and momentum for others to work alongside them on the path of advancement. They not only lay down the foundation for humanity but also help in tirelessly building up the edifice of human wisdom with all their heart and soul. They are the symbols of the human soul, and the vanguard and pioneers of human existence.

points.body: Although most countries of the world have horses, and those countries have differences in their climate and environment, horses belonged in the beginning to the same species – mostly residing in central Asia. On the other side of the Atlantic, in Máyá Dviipa [America] there were no horses in ancient times, as was also the case in Australia. Today, however, horses have spread all over the world. Of course, certain environmental changes have affected them. The Burmese pony has remained outside these main groups [of horses]. We call it t́át́t́u in Bengali. Earlier the pony was not recognized as a horse . . . it was considered a different animal species. During the last three hundred years it was recognized as a horse. In Bengali, instead of ghoŕá [horse], it is presently called t́át́t́u ghoŕá [pony].

points.body: Nowhere in the world is land cultivated with the help of elephants. However, in central-eastern Asia and in certain parts of northwest India, horses were used for the cultivation of land, and it is still done in some of those regions. In Europe the soil was cultivated with the help of horses, but they are no longer considered suitable for that task today. Tractors and power tillers are replacing them. Thus horses are found unsuitable for tilling land. It is true that compared to horses and cattle, tractors are more useful and powerful, but they do not offer any fertilizer in the form of excrement. That is why chemical fertilizers have been invented. Slow-moving, horse-drawn carriages and cattle carts have been replaced by taxis and omnibuses. So like the elephants, and along with cattle and camels, horses are nowadays considered redundant; their days in our lives are numbered. Maybe in a short time children will have to visit zoos to watch them from close quarters. If there are no more horses, there will also be no need for battle horses in our lives.

points.body: A long time ago, in Kolkata, the palanquin bearers went on strike to raise their fares. At that time most of the palanquin bearers were Oriya people. The fare was one paisa per mile; they demanded one and a half paisa per mile. The Britishers then living in India were opposed to such a hike in fare, and instead designed a type of carriage by tying horses to palanquins. Such a palanquin carriage drawn by horses came to be known as pálki-gáŕii, juri-gáŕii, or bagi-gáŕii. The word pálki comes from the English word ‘palanquin’. The word bagi comes from the English word ‘bogey’. Ravindranath Tagore and his family members, indeed all the aristocrats of Bengal, used to go by phit́an to the gaŕer mát́h [open air Kolkata meadows] in the morning and evening to enjoy the open air.

points.title: In ancient times, any covered, one-wheeled or two-wheeled carriage drawn by one or two…

summary: In ancient times, any covered, one-wheeled or two-wheeled carriage drawn by one or two horses and used in war was called ratha [chariot].

points.body: In ancient times, any covered, one-wheeled or two-wheeled carriage drawn by one or two horses and used in war was called ratha [chariot]. The sound ra is indicative of a start or movement, and the tha is indicative of a halt. The word ratha has emerged from these sounds. In northern India the modified version of this ratha is called táuṋgá. The word táuṋgá has come from the Sanskrit word tauṋgan. In ancient times, just as human beings moved about in rathas, so also their so-called mythological gods used to go to battle in chariots. During the Buddhist era there were rathayátrá [chariot festivals] centering on gods and goddesses. Even today in different parts of India these rathajátrá festivals are held. Such festivals are very old. The medieval king of Bengal, Matsyendranath – who in later years became the great yogi Matsyendranath – went to Nepal on a ratha to dispel the prevailing drought there. This journey of Matsyendranath by ratha later turned into the rathayátrá of Lord Jagannatha. In the Buddhist age in Bengal, ratha of Dharmarájiká or Dhámrái became very famous in Dacca and Comilla district.

points.body: History of the horse-drawn chariot: The chariot is one of the most ancient carriages. Donkeys, horses and cows were amongst the domesticated animals kept by human beings in the past. The characteristic feature of these animals was that donkeys were very proficient in carrying luggage, but once they were tied to carriages, their capacity for work diminished. So although there might still be carriages drawn by donkeys in some parts of the world, they are seldom popular. Although ponies are quite capable of carrying goods, they are not as efficient as donkeys; but once they are tied to carriages and fitted with blinkers, they work quite efficiently. Donkeys and cows are not restless like horses. They are not predisposed to wayward movements. So when drawing carriages, they are never made to wear blinkers. In contrast, when cows are tied to the grinding tree of an oil-mill, they feel restless after some time and try to run from one place to another. Hence when fastening them to a grinding tree, blinkers must be put on the cows. They cannot carry goods on their back and often try to shake them off. When tied to carts, they work very efficiently; but if there is mud or slush on the road, the feet of the cows become stuck. Even their heels become stuck in the sand. Because of this, cows cannot pull a carriage properly on the sand. That is why in Rajasthan and other desert areas, though carriages are drawn by cows in the towns and villages, outside the towns and villages they are drawn mostly by camels. Carriages drawn by camels used to ply the route between Burdwan and Katwa, before the narrow-gauge railway came into existence.

points.body: In the more frequented areas of Bengal, on the roads and lanes, cows draw carriages quite easily; but if there is mud or slush on the road, then people are compelled to use buffaloes instead of cows. It happens on agricultural land as well. On soil that is full of mud and slush, it is easier to plough with the help of buffaloes. Cows, buffaloes and camels are large animals. Cows have greater strength than human beings. Hence, to keep them under control, ropes are inserted through their noses by piercing them (in eastern India it is called natha [controlling rope], and in northern India nákel). The Zebu indica is physically smaller in appearance and by nature quiet and calm. So there is no need to apply natha to their nose.

points.body: Among the luggage-bearing animals, human beings first became acquainted with horses, next with donkeys, and then with cows and camels simultaneously. Horses yield very little milk. The mule does not yield any milk. The donkey gives a modicum of milk but that milk does not yield any butter. The milk yielded by a female donkey is very much like that of a woman. So a motherless child can be fed on the milk from the female donkey, and this is also done. Camels offer less milk than cows of better breeds, but they do yield a good quantity of milk. Of course, there is very little butter in that milk. In certain parts of India, cowʼs milk is adulterated with camel milk.

points.body: Secondly, the buffalo requires a much larger quantity of food than the cow. When it does not yield any milk, it has to be fed at considerable expense to the owner. Thirdly, the buffalo must spend quite some time during the day submerging itself in water, as otherwise its body becomes emaciated, and it begins bleeding and abruptly dies. The women of the household can milk the cows, but in the case of buffaloes, let alone the women of the household, not even all the men can milk them. For this a milkman has to be called. Human beings learned to keep buffaloes at home much later. In fact, there is something inherently wild in the buffalo.

points.body: People first invented horse-drawn carriages; carriages drawn by cows came much later than horse-drawn carriages. In ancient times there were constant feuds between different groups of people. There was hardly a day in peopleʼs lives when group clashes did not take place. To move from home or village to the battleground, people were compelled to use horse-drawn carriages. In its earliest stage the shape of this carriage was like that of a ratha. The horse was urged to move forward with the rrr…. sound and was made to stop with the sound tha … tha …That is why the carriage came to be known as ratha. In those days, when there were no battles, just as soldiers indulged in horse racing, so also they participated in chariot racing or ratha-racing. However, those chariots were built in a lighter style and used in a specific manner. They were called krd́á-ratha [sports chariots]. In the later period, for the purpose of competition, whatever ratha, carriage or animal came to be used, they were given the common name of ‘sports carriage’ – whether it was a ratha or boat, horse or camel. ( 2 )

The psychology of the horse is that whenever it is on the verge of engaging in strenuous labour, it lets out a shrill cry so as to reduce the strain. When it is unable to drag its four feet, its physical exhaustion becomes quite evident. In earlier times there was a popular notion that dark-coloured horses had the greatest capacity to undertake labour. Hence they were considered to be the smartest and most agile. In Hindustani they are called chaltápurjá. So in those days the black horse fetched the highest price in the market place. On the battlefield, if at the front [line of battle], the horse rider or charioteer was found to use black horses, the white horse or horses of the rival side ran away in panic. So the enemy party, after seeing the black horse of the opposing side, often retreated from battle. Black horses had such esteem in those days.

points.body: Donkey: Donkeys (gádhá) have been under human control since very ancient times. Both horses and donkeys came under human control nearly 15,000 years ago. Although much is made of horses in the Vedas, there are comparatively very few references to donkeys. The reason is that at the primitive stage of human civilization, horses were the prime mounts. Donkeys are not quick moving. So as transporters, their position was far behind that of horses. They could not draw carriages as effectively as horses. However, being more docile than horses and less expensive to maintain, the donkeys and mules (father: male horse and mother: she-ass) have long been used for transporting goods.

points.body: Since ancient times, the Aryans and Mongols have used horses and horse-drawn carriages on the battlefield. Since they are slow-moving, donkeys were never used in battle. Of course, the donkey is more suitable than the cow and the horse for transporting goods. In comparison to donkeys, mules can carry still more goods. But the mule is relatively rare, since it is not a natural born creature. This means that it cannot be found in the forest. For drawing carriages, donkeys are not as adept as cows, but donkeys are more efficient in carrying luggage. For this reason, when there is no need of haste or speed, donkeys have been utilized for carrying goods. Even today people do so. Almost all over India there was the practice of keeping donkeys. In parts of Gujarat, Kutch and Rajasthan, hordes of multi-coloured donkeys could be seen that were not easily amenable to control. Nevertheless, they were quite swift. That is why human beings had little interest to keep or maintain such donkeys. For some natural reasons, since the last century those multi-coloured donkeys have been on their way towards extinction. The use of donkeys for carrying goods was common in India since ancient times, and it is still practiced there. But the use of donkeys for carrying luggage and drawing carriages was not so extensive. Today it is rarely seen. Previously, however, there were carriages in India drawn by donkeys.

The original habitat of the donkey was the dry desert region of western India, Afghanistan, Baluchistan, the northern part of Russia and Persia. When they live in forests they move about in herds. The colour of their body is quite varied – red, blue, violet, yellow, brown and gray. Unlike the wild horse or the zebra, which is not amenable to human control, the donkey is different. The gray-coloured or brown-coloured donkey is readily amenable to domestication and is quite mild-natured. It carries luggage in silence; but when luggage beyond its capacity of endurance is heaped on its shoulders, it quickly sits down. Then the owner, understanding the predicament, reduces the weight of the luggage.

The nutritional value of donkey milk is far less than that of the cow or the horse. It also yields less butter. Yet in qualitative terms, the milk of the donkey is as good as the milk of a woman. So for an orphaned infant, the milk of the donkey is a good alternative to motherʼs milk. In English, the slow-moving, wide-eared, braying creature is called donkey. Its sound, behaviour and activities work according to the drift of its individual flow, regardless of whether that pleases someone or not. The donkey has similar behaviour. points.body: Mule: Mules have greater capacity to carry goods than donkeys. Compared to donkeys, they are swifter animals. Even in drawing carriages they are more proficient than donkeys. In physical appearance they have greater affinity to horses, but in their habits they are akin to donkeys. Since they have to make movements up and down across the fields, it is not possible for them to develop udders. Hence for this reason, amongst mules there is no gender distinction; it can be said that they are all eunuchs. Since mules have a tendency to travel uphill, they are also called khesara. From this word khesara has come the word khaccara [mule].

points.body: There has been many a storm in the tea cup among modern pandits over the exact nature of the Go-medh yajiṋa. One group of scholars opined that, as the horse was killed and sacrificed in fire during the Ashvamedha yajiṋa [the same was the case with cows in Go-medh yajina]. Since that time the name of the fire came to be hutáshana. The word huta means “that which was sacrificed in fire”, and ashan stood for eating. Hutáshana means “that which eats up anything offered to it as a sacrifice”. Hence, in a wider sense, hutáshana means “something that accepts as food anything offered to it”. Whatever is offered to fire is accepted and consumed by it. Since fire eats up anything offered to it, another name for fire is hutáshana or hutásh. Of course, since in any yajiṋa the use of fire was essential, the other names of fire became játaveda, hutáshana, pávaka and sarvabhuka. Fire has several other names according to its uses.

points.body: The word má stands for ‘tongue’ and the word aḿsa means the sequel. So máḿsa means the sequel of ‘tongue’, that is, speech. Go means sense organ. That is why the meaning of the go-máḿsa is anything derived from our speech or the sense organ tongue. So consumption of go-máḿsa [cow flesh] is not eating the flesh of the cow; it refers to control of the expression of our vocal cord or of speech.

Yet it is true that in agricultural society, cows occupied an important place. That importance is related to our needs. For that reason, there should be control over cow slaughter. Those who are opposed to animal slaughter or violence to animals should be vocal against not only cow slaughter but also against slaughter of other animals like buffaloes and goats.

points.body: When they were in the wild, they had ample ability to run, just as the goat, which could also run. To save themselves from attack by ferocious animals in the forest, they needed both mobility and speed. Due to their rapid movement, their milk udders were small, very much like those of deer today, or those of antelope. With large udders, it is not possible for animals to run rapidly. We might guess that in ancient times the cow and goat gave less milk, very much like the deer and antelope of today. Even now the cow species that gives a plenteous quantity of milk is very slow moving. For any movement it takes them a long time.

points.body: Of course, the enhancement of their capacity to yield more milk has come as a boon to human beings. People have come to be proud of this “White Revolution”. However, if one thinks of the welfare of this animal species, it has been harmful to them. Even if the calf is allowed to drink all the milk in the udder, it would not be able to do so. And by carrying this extra quantity of milk over a long period, the [mother] cow becomes physically weak. By yielding excessive milk the buffalo does not suffer physically as much as the cow, since it is physically bulky. Still, if their production of milk is excessively increased, their health is bound to suffer, just as to overnourish one particular organ of the human body enhances its power at the cost of oneʼs general health.

points.body: Of course, today there is no alternative but to enhance the supply of cowsʼ and goatsʼ milk because of the increasing demand of human beings. I also understand fully that one day in our science laboratories synthetic payasa [milk] will be produced. (I am avoiding the use of the word dugdha for ‘milk’, which is secured by milking the cow. Since we do not get synthetic milk by milking in the laboratory, I am using the word paya or payasa). At one time the horse was used as sophisticated mounts. The importance of the horse as a domestic animal has come to an end. Similarly, with the invention of the tractor, power tiller and synthetic milk, the necessity for cows will also come to an end. You might say that for the sake of eating meat, people will have to keep cows. However, I am not thinking along those lines. I believe that, with the advancement of human intellect, emotional sensitivity and rationality, human beings will be more inclined towards Neohumanism, they will develop indifference towards eating flesh and will give up their carnivorousness. ( 2 )

summary: Milk is derived from milking the cow, camel or buffalo.

points.body: Milk is derived from milking the cow, camel or buffalo. According to Puranic accounts, the kapilá cows did not require any milking; once they were worshipped, milk flowed endlessly from their udders. However, in the case of the earthly cow, milking is required. Giving milk to the baby is nothing strenuous for the mother, or for any other mammal. Still, milking is always a strenuous job for all, even for the milkman. It is very difficult to milk an animal whose udder is very stiff. In the village of Burdwan I saw that women milked the cows, but for milking the buffaloes they had to call the milkman. Very often even men with fragile health are unable to milk the buffaloes.

points.title: In ancient times when cows were not yet brought under human control or when people were…
points.prompt: Recall and explain from memory: In ancient times when cows were not yet brought under human control or when people were…
summary: In ancient times when cows were not yet brought under human control or when people were not yet able to bring the cow from the wild in the forest to a domesticated condition, they had first kept horses.
Although it offered very limited service, human beings had to take the responsibility of feeding the horse.
It was the men who did the heavy jobs while women did the milking.
points.body: In ancient times when cows were not yet brought under human control or when people were not yet able to bring the cow from the wild in the forest to a domesticated condition, they had first kept horses. The horse is a swift-moving animal, and a swift animal gives less milk. So for the sake of milk, no one keeps a swift animal. In those days people did not cultivate with the help of the plough and the bull. They kept the horse to ride and to use in battle field. Ancient human beings procured food for the horse and used it as a mount. It did not serve any other purpose. Although it offered very limited service, human beings had to take the responsibility of feeding the horse. Occasionally they felt irritated, yet they could not do without the horses. They called the horse ashva (ash + bun), which means “that which works on the strength of food”. When humans came in contact with the cow, they learnt to cultivate with the help of the cow. The cow is a slow animal, for which reason she gradually came to provide more milk. After domesticating the cow, humans also learnt to milk it. It was the men who did the heavy jobs while women did the milking.

summary: The word duhitá means “the milking women”.
It would be relevant to point out that, although milking the buffalo is quite difficult, tending the buffalo is not at all difficult.
If there is one food which has all the good qualities of many different foods, then it must be milk.
points.body: The word duhitá means “the milking women”. People had not yet learnt to bring the buffalo under control; may be they had not conceived of the idea. The buffalo always seeks a wet place or a pond. The Áryanyavraja or present Iran [where Aryans first arrived in their journey towards India] is a dry and hard country. Although cultivation is marginally satisfactory, it has very little wetland. It would be relevant to point out that, although milking the buffalo is quite difficult, tending the buffalo is not at all difficult. If you put the buffalo into a wetland, it will look after itself – the whole day. Scrub it well and bathe it in water; that will be good enough. After coming in contact with the cow, people learnt almost immediately about all the qualities of milk. If there is one food which has all the good qualities of many different foods, then it must be milk.

For this reason, it is suitable only for people in the age group of 16-40, and not for young people or even for older people.
In the milk of the camel or the goat, there is hardly any fat content, due to which it also has less nutritional value.
points.body: After coming in contact with cowʼs milk, people then came in contact with buffalo milk. After coming in contact with the camel and the sheep and tasting their milk, they came to learn that whatever good qualities are present in cowʼs milk, they are also present in buffalo milk, and perhaps in even greater quantity. However, the fat content in buffalo milk is around 1¼ percent to 1½ percent more than in cowʼs milk. For this reason, it is suitable only for people in the age group of 16-40, and not for young people or even for older people. In Bihar, even where buffalo milk is available in larger quantity, babies and elderly people are fed on cowʼs milk. Sheepʼs milk, in which the fat content is less, is not fully nutritious. In the milk of the camel or the goat, there is hardly any fat content, due to which it also has less nutritional value.

points.body: The milk of the donkey is considered to be as good as [human] motherʼs milk. So for a motherless baby cowʼs milk is good, but for a baby of more than two years, it is less nutritious. The clarified butter prepared from buffalo milk (bhaesá-ghee), if taken in large quantity, can cause stomach upset or dysentery. However, the clarified butter prepared from cowʼs milk normally does not do any harm. So to prevent any constipation arising out of regular intake of sunned rice, in ancient times people used to take it with clarified butter prepared from cowʼs milk. Since milk, especially cowʼs milk, has the power to offer vitality, and in addition has healing powers, it is called gadáhva. In the grass, especially in the variety called dudhiá, the vitamin content is sufficiently adequate. Graminivorous animals acquire their vitality through this grass and thus supply ample milk. The sap of the grass prevents blood poisoning, helps mitigate the oozing of blood and helps to heal the wound. Out in the field, in the event of accidental bleeding arising from any injury, if this grass is chewed and pasted on the wound, the bleeding stops in a short while. Grass, especially the green durbá grass [Cynodon sp.], has this healing power. ( 3 )

points.body: Uh means the upper side. Suppose there are many cows in an area. The most gifted among them, in all respects, is called gaboh. The native cows of India (Zebu indica) are smaller in shape and give less milk; but their milk is sweet and pleasant smelling. The cows of western India are larger in size and give more milk, but their milk has hardly any sweetness or nice fragrance. By this criterion, if the best cows are chosen from amongst all those in India, they would be the patniiá cows. When compared to common, indigenous cows, they are a little larger in appearance. Indian cows have a hump on their shoulder, which European cows do not normally have. The patniiá cows also have no hump. They give more milk and by nature are calm and quiet. They truly belong to the gaboh category.

points.body: Next to these, the best variety of Indian cow is the Sirhindii cows of the western part of Haryana. In this region there is an upland plateau, which is a large water barrier; the rivers and canals on its eastern side flow down and into the Bay of Bengal, and those water bodies to the west flow down into the Arabian Sea across the Sindhu River basin. As it is an upland area, it is called Sirhind or “the head of India”. The cows of Sirhind are larger in size and give more milk. They are called Sirhindii cows.

points.body: Aside from this, in the north of Sindhu there is a semi-desert region that belonged to the former Bahawalpur Kingdom; now it is a district of the Sindh province of Pakistan. The Bahawalpur cow is rather large in size and gives more milk. (The people of Bengal wrongly call this Bahawalpuri cow as the Bhagalpuri cow.) However, the amount of butter in the milk is less than that of Sirhindii cows. There is little taste in the curd made from the milk of the Bahawalpuri cow. Still, for other milk products the Bahawalpuri cow is very profitable. Then there is the Gujarati cow of western Punjab. The cows of Gujarat district adjoining Gujranwala and Sialkot districts of Punjab [Pakistan] are of higher quality; but when they are brought to eastern India, they do not reproduce well. They lose their health because of the humid climate. In certain areas of India like Rajasthan, Gujarat and Kutch, there are some worthy local cows or gabohs.

points.body: In southern India in the Krishna River basin of Andhra Pradesh, some good quality cows or gabohs are found. From their milk a high quality of butter oil is produced. The butter of their milk cannot be preserved for a long period; but the butter oil can be preserved for quite some time, like that of other cows. Once in the districts of Nadia, Bagri, Murshidabad and Malda there were some “quality” local cows, but in the absence of proper care and attention, they are now practically extinct.

points.body: In the Damodar basin of Hoogly and Burdwan districts there were once some excellent Bengali cows (Indian zebu of Banjalitis breed). If proper attempts are made even today, their breed can still be saved. These cows (of the Kriśńá variety) give fragrant and tasty milk. Even today in certain villages, after a proper search one can find one or two such dark-coloured or Krśńá type cows along with their calves. ( 4 )

points.body: You must have seen cows that chase people or kick them if one tries to milk them. This kind of bad-natured cow is called a márkáńd́á cow in some places. This márkáńd́á cow is called karat́a. If this márkáńd́á cow is fed fodder mixed with mustard chaff before dawn, then its affliction will be alleviated, that is, its temper will be calmed. Often this kind of cow kicks its own calf and chases it away, that is, she does not allow it to drink her milk. In order that these calves do not die for want of nourishment during infancy, they can be fed pure roasted gram flour dissolved in water; then their life can be saved. ( 5 )

points.body: Buffalo: You all know that the buffalo (mahiś) is not that civilized, domesticated or gentle a creature as the cow is. It is not even as responsible as the cow is. While drawing the carriage, it sometimes runs straight to any bog or pond it comes across, dragging the carriage along with it. If it observes that its owner is not that alert and observant, it may not return home at all. The cow is different.

Shyambabu brings the cow home and entertains it; the women of the house smear its horns with vermillion and worship it, feed it with mustard oil cakes, sliced paddy hay and other delicacies. However, taking advantage of the open gate due to the ownerʼs carelessness, the cow slips away and returns to the house of its original owner miles away. Many villagers are acquainted with such events. I have told you long ago about a rhyme in western khat́t́á [mixture of Bhojpuri, Magahii and some other local sub-dialect] dialect:

points.body: The wild buffalo, which is called ‘bison’ in English, has a somewhat low front and raised back. They are normally calm and quiet by nature, but become furious when angry and refuse to be domesticated. The gabalas I have spoken about are not like bison; they look like domesticated buffaloes. Indeed they are. Compared to domesticated cows, they give less milk. Their udders are dry and smaller in size. ( 6 )

It does not like anyone to sit on its back.
points.body: Let us compare the horse, the cow, the buffalo and the mule – these four animal species. There is a difference in their nature and appearance. The horse is swift. Its cry is shrill-sounding like ci – hi – hi, chi – hi – hi, chi – hi – hi. The horse cannot carry much luggage. It has a greater capacity to pull than to carry. So instead of putting more luggage on its back, its is made to pull chariots (rathas), carriages etc. It feels uneasy if more than one person rides it. If while moving along, the horse comes across one road that goes uphill, another that goes downhill and another that goes straight on flat land, it will choose the path that goes straight ahead on flat land. The foal must be fed from its infancy on tender green grass. It cannot receive full nourishment from its motherʼs milk. The cow, whether of the zebu, Bos indicus, or any other species, makes the usual sound of hámbá – a – a – hámbá. It has horns, but they are very weak. When there is a battle between the bulls, their horns break. The cow very much dislikes to carry any luggage on its back. It does not like anyone to sit on its back.

points.body: The horse submits to some extent when it is given a bath, but the cow sees a tiger when it is taken to water. It always wants to keep away from water. When someone found in a bad situation is cornered, people will say, “Give the cow a good wash”. Since the cow is slow moving, it has great capacity to provide milk. Not only is the calf nurtured on its motherʼs milk, but there is always an extra supply of milk, in fact more than double the quantity of milk the calf requires for its sustenance. Thus if the requisite milk for the calf is left aside and the excess milk is consumed by human beings, there is no question of depriving anyone.

points.body: The buffalo came into human contact much later. The horse came into contact with humans the earliest; next came the cow, and then the buffalo. The horn of the buffalo is slightly circular. It has strength; hence it does not break easily. Sometimes with the help of its horns it is able to resist attack. The tiger is not at all afraid of the cow, but it treats the buffalo with a certain regard, although it is not afraid of it. If luggage is put on the back of the buffalo, it scarcely takes note and even endures the load. In northern and western India, people in rural areas move about on the back of buffaloes for miles and miles together.

points.body: One of my boyhood friends was a reputed zamindar from a place in Bihar. Let us assume that his name was Chandra Kanta Sinha. Once one of my distantly related nephews told me, “Uncle, please write a letter to Chandrakantajii in my favour, which will help me in accomplishing some work easily.” Accordingly, my nephew went to Chandrakantajii with my letter. Chandrakanta was not at home at that time. He was also a professor of Philosophy at a nearby college. My nephew thought that he must have gone to the college to teach his classes, so he went in the direction of the college. Almost taking him by surprise, Chandrakanta met him on the way. He was riding on the back of an indigenous buffalo towards the college four miles away. Of course, even then he had a voluminous Philosophy book in hand. My nephew asked him, “Uncle, is everything alright?” Chandrakantajii replied, “Yes, yes, you had better come along and sit beside me.” I did not ask my nephew what happened after that.

points.title: Apart from this, whatever the cow can do, such as tilling the soil or drawing the cart,…

points.body: Apart from this, whatever the cow can do, such as tilling the soil or drawing the cart, the buffalo can do it all. In muddy soil the cowʼs feet get stuck and then it cannot till the field or draw the carriage properly. The buffalo can do this all very well. Compared to the cow, the buffalo is much more slow-moving. That is why in comparison with the cow it gives far more milk. However, the difficulty with the buffalo is that when it finds the road splitting into one going ahead on flat land, one rising uphill and one going downhill, it chooses the road going downhill. If it finds any slough or pond beside the road, it goes down to the water right along with the plough and the yoke or the covered carriage, dragging everything along behind. At that moment the buffalo hardly remembers that there is a hefty man sitting in the carriage. When tilling dry land belonging to someone, if it comes across water on the adjoining land, it does not hesitate to enter that land along with the plough and yoke. Due to its tendency to go downhill or towards any water body, it is called kasara, kásara or kesara. When the road goes in three different directions, the donkey, the horse and the cow all choose the road going on flat land, but the buffalo chooses the road going downhill; the camel prefers the dry road, and the mule chooses the road going uphill. For military purposes, and in the hilly regions for commercial and transportation purposes, people have used the mule more often since it likes to move uphill.

summary: When a person living in a particular country is nourished by the land and water, the beauty and flavour, the flow of life and vitality of that country, and if they come to address that country as their mother, it is not a grammatical error or desecration of history, or great sacrilege.
It is simply a kind of veneration that is offered here due to someone caring like a mother.

points.body: When a person living in a particular country is nourished by the land and water, the beauty and flavour, the flow of life and vitality of that country, and if they come to address that country as their mother, it is not a grammatical error or desecration of history, or great sacrilege. Even the affectionate father holding the daughter in his lap caresses her as he would his mother, though everyone knows that the tiny girl is none other than his own daughter. If by drinking the milk of any creature a person receives nourishment, what is wrong if they address the animal as their mother? Does it really turn the animal into their mother? It is simply a kind of veneration that is offered here due to someone caring like a mother. Yes, it is true that human beings do not take only cowʼs milk but also the milk of the camel, goat and buffalo. So if we offer veneration, we have to also do the same to the camel, goat and buffalo. Yes, to make much ado of the cow as mother is not desirable, because it will appear ludicrous, and if someone thinks that they can worship the cow, smearing it with oil and vermilion they can worship it, while the buffalo can be slaughtered and with its blood one can even take a ritual bath, then it would be an intellectual betrayal. Their attitude cannot be appreciated. ( 7 )

points.body: Domestic pig: That which multiplies in huge numbers or is counted in big numbers is called kot́ija. In that sense, various kinds of viruses or insects such as shyámápoká [Green leaf-hoppers] can be called kot́ija; but in the derivative sense it means “pigs” and “plantain trees”.

points.body: Among the domesticated animals, pigs (shúkara or shor or baráha) multiply very rapidly. Expenses incurred in maintaining pigs are also minimal. That is why since ancient times, poor people have invariably shown interest in keeping pigs. No other animal meat is as cheaply available. Pigs are very dirty creatures and are also fond of eating dirty items. In most countries of the world pigs are domesticated because they are easy to maintain. In India, people primarily belonging to the scavenger caste keep pigs. Others also keep pigs and many of them eat their meat as well. Except for those who are forbidden by religion, many people have been trading in pig meat since ancient times. When Englishmen came to Bengal, they used to dry pig meat (at that time the scientific method of de-hydration had not come into practice) and export it. It is said that pigs were even exported alive. The place from which the Portuguese came to collect pigs, just adjacent to Kolkata, is still known today as Baranagar or Barahanagar. Barabani of Burdwan district and Barabazar of Manbhum district, however, do not derive their names from the export of pigs. In the forest areas of those places, many wild pigs or baráha used to roam. That is why those localities came to have such names. In ancient India only the shúdras (lower caste people) were permitted to eat pig meat (pork). The kśatriyas had permission to eat pork during the time of battle. The practice of eating the meat of wild boar was prevalent among all people except Brahmans.

points.body: The population growth rate of wild boars is not similar to that of domesticated pigs. Besides this, living in the wild they are constantly struck down and ravaged by an uncongenial environment. Carnivorous people say that the meat of the wild boar is far more delicious than that of domesticated pigs. Wild boar meat is also very dear to the tiger. Of course, the huge tiger does not normally attack the wild boar, because one would not be sure who would win the battle and who would die. Normally the large tiger attacks the calf of the boar, just as the boar attacks the calf of the tiger. Although the wild boar is normally a vegetarian, it has a tremendous weakness for tiger meat and buffalo meat. The wild boar, having an angry disposition (such a creature is called kaopin in Sanskrit), is frequently carried away by rage and meets with a premature death. Some people think that wild boars for generations have been converted into domesticated pigs. But no, this is not correct. Domesticated pigs and wild boars are two different kinds of creatures, although they both belong to the pig genus.

By temperament the rhinoceros is calm, but the wild boar is hot-tempered. For human beings, the wild boar is more dangerous than the rhinoceros. Carnivorous people say that the meat of the rhinoceros is as tasty as that of the wild boar.

points.body: The one-horned rhinoceros of the Sunderbans has become extinct due to human greed for its meat. Of course, killing the rhinoceros is not as easy as killing the wild boar. The hide of the rhinoceros is impenetrable, but that of the wild boar is extremely tender. The rhinoceros is feeble-eyed, while the wild boar is keeneyed. Although a rhinoceros is not amenable to human control, if well treated it tries to make friends with people, especially with children. The wild boar, however, is always ready to attack any other creature. It has been noticed in the Sundarbans that when the number of wild boars and Sundarbans deer has reduced, the number of tigers has also either reduced or they have invaded human settlements. In any case, due to their rapid growth, pigs have come to be known as kot́ija. However, this word would apply better to domesticated pigs and not to wild boars. ( 8 )

points.body: Yak (Camrii): In Tibet and adjacent areas, the yaks, called cámrii, are available both in the wild and domesticated state. Their milk is very similar to cowʼs milk, except that it has a bad odour. The wool of the yaks is lengthy and handsome. Many a time the attractive appearance of a human being or an animal winds up being the cause of that creatureʼs death. The impressive hide of the deer or its horns is often responsible for its death; the wings of the bright green insect are often responsible for its death; once the feathers of a peacock were considered to be the cause of its death. Similarly, the handsome hair of the camrii is often considered to be the cause of its death. It is said: Kesheśu camriiḿ hanti, meaning, “for its hair a yak is killed”.

points.body: In English camrii is called yak. The female yak is called giripriyá. Some people firmly believe that the ox on which Lord Shiva used to roam around the world was no ordinary ox, but a male yak. Apparently the male yak is somewhat ferocious looking. At least, people of the plains would become frightened at its initial appearance, although there is no reason to fear it. It is very calm and quiet by nature. On its own it never attacks anyone; and even when attacked, it does not normally retaliate. It fights only when its life is in danger. Its lengthy, beautiful hair, when tied around a stick, is known as cámar. In ancient times, ritually blessed persons used to be fanned with a cámar.

points.body: Usually, on reaching the five different stages of life, one had to pass through certain rituals called abhiśek. The first was at the early stage of childhood on the occasion of játakarma or naming ceremony; the second was during the sacred thread ceremony; the third was the marriage ceremony; the fourth was upon ascension to the throne or when being crowned as the crown prince; and the fifth was when, by the grace of the Guru, one received initiation into higher spiritual practices. This kind of spiritual initiation at the directive of the Guru was called Sámrájya Diikśá [initiation of universal sovereignty]. On this occasion, at the directive of the Guru, one of his junior disciples used to fan his senior disciple with the cámar. These five stages combined were called Paiṋcábhiśek [five-fold initiation]. On these occasions, there was the practice of using conch shells, five lamps and the cámar. Yes, Kesheśu cámriiḿ hanti – for the sake of its hair, the yak was killed by humans. ( 9 )

The job of tilling is now being done by power-tillers and tractors. The bullock cart is going out of use; the use of the horse-carriage is now as good as nil. For the sake of milk, people will probably keep cows for some time to come. After the discovery of synthetic milk, people will give up keeping cows at home, since for tilling and milking cows will no longer be necessary. For use in oil mills, bullocks have already become redundant.

points.body: Just as the necessity of cows will disappear in future, the necessity of horses also has almost come to an end. I surmise that in some dayʼs time, the horse will turn into an animal in the zoo. However, there was a time when the word ‘carriage’ was inalienably linked up with the horse, and along with the carriage they would invariably use the expression ‘horse-carriage’ (ghoŕá-gáŕii). In the field of speed, the horse was in such high demand! In the past, on the roads and resting places, on highways, in big towns and at road crossings, there was an arrangement for keeping large cisterns for quenching the thirst of horses and for bathing them by the roadside. In our own city of Kolkata, at various places there were such big cisterns filled with water. The black gram that was kept as fodder for the horses was soaked in these cisterns. In the Buddhist and even post-Buddhist eras, such large cisterns filled with water were prevalent on the roads and city thoroughfares. ( 10 )

points.body: Dog family and cat family: You all know that our familiar carnivorous animals are divided into two families: the cat and the dog families. Animals belonging to the cat family have round faces with whiskers (even the tigress and the female cat have whiskers). They are not at all inclined to live as a family. They have sharp intelligence and courage, but they display their courage by applying intelligence; that is, they do not like to endanger themselves by simply making a show of their courage. Animals belonging to the cat family have little tolerance towards other animals. Animals belonging to the dog family (in Sanskrit kukkura or kukura; in Bengali kukur) have long and pointed faces; some of them even live in families (such as the lion). They have average intelligence. They thrust themselves into dangerous situations to display their courage. They are quite generous in nature and even make sacrifices.

points.body: In the dog family, the largest animal is the African lion, now on the verge of extinction. The lions of Ráŕh became extinct about one hundred years ago. The Gujrat lion, the lion of Girnar or the Gir lion, both male and female, have no mane. In another lion species, only the males have a mane and not the females. (In Sanskrit and Bengali a lion is called siḿha, in Persian babar, in English lion, in Latin leo). Apart from this, there is the wolf in northern India called lákŕá bágh (in Sanskrit called brka, in English known as wolf). Then there are different species of dogs and jackals. Amongst these familiar animals, the smallest is the fox.

points.body: Among the feline species the largest of them all is the kudo bágh or Royal Bengal Tiger of the Sundarbans. In Bengali it is called bágh, in Sanskrit byághra or shárdul, in Persian sher and in English tiger. There are black tigers, then jaguars of South America, gulbághás or panthers, cheetahs, and chitra byághras or leopards. Then there are also hyenas, which are called huŕárs, huńd́árs, begoyás, gobághás, in Sanskrit tarakśu. Smaller than this is the civet cat (bhám), the pole cat (khat́t́ásh, in spoken Bengali kát́t́ash), wild cats and our own domesticated cat.

points.body: Both animals of the cat and dog families are carnivorous; they do not eat uncooked vegetarian food, although they sometimes eat cooked food. What is interesting is that although there are large and small varieties of dogs, they are not of any distinct subspecies. Its father is a wolf and its mother is a female jackal. Such is the identity of the dog. That is why, while seeking primitive fossils, I have come across the fossils of wolves and the fossils of jackals, but no fossils of the dog. In their early stage, all animals belonging to the dog family look very much alike. As they grow up, differences in their appearance become prominent; their cry also becomes distinct from other animals. Alsatians are very close to wolves. Domesticated wolves (they are not easily amenable to human control) and Alsatians have very little differences. They have a very powerful sense of smell and can easily differentiate between various kinds of scents. Hence in the task of apprehending criminals, they help human beings to a great extent. Both the dog and cat families of animals make distinctive sounds. ( 1 )

points.title: The dog is a sharp-snouted member of the canine family, and the tiger is a round-snoute…

Some people are of the opinion that while the dog no doubt belongs to the canine family, it is not an original species but rather a cross-breed – the wolf is its father and the jackal its mother; this was the ancient conception.
points.body: The dog is a sharp-snouted member of the canine family, and the tiger is a round-snouted member of the feline family. There is an inherent hostility between these two. According to biologists, members of the canine family are sharp-snouted, carnivorous, swift runners, make noise when they run, and have a strong sense of smell (the Alsatian is an exception). They also display a great deal of affection towards their young. The largest animal in this group is the maned lion, native to Africa. In addition, there is the medium-sized, maned Indian lion, the maneless Indian lion or gurjar lion, the wolf (brkabyághra), Alsatian, ( 2 ) the ordinary domesticated Indian dog, the wild Indian dog, the jackal (shrgála), the fox (ulkámukhii), and so on. In addition there are many kinds of short-haired and long-haired dogs differing in variety and from country to country. Some people are of the opinion that while the dog no doubt belongs to the canine family, it is not an original species but rather a cross-breed – the wolf is its father and the jackal its mother; this was the ancient conception.

points.title: Although dogs live in groups, different members of the canine family do not mix with ea…

points.body: Although dogs live in groups, different members of the canine family do not mix with each other. For example, wolves and lions are not on good terms with each other. Wolves will chase a dog if they see one and will kill it, regardless of whether they eat it or not. Dogs will also chase jackals if they see them.

points.title: The tiger, however, is a different family of animal, a feline

summary: The tiger, however, is a different family of animal, a feline.

points.body: The tiger, however, is a different family of animal, a feline. Members of the feline family do not remain in groups. They are extremely greedy and self-seeking. points.body: There are many similarities and dissimilarities between tigers and lions – both carnivorous animals. Judging from circumstances, the tiger must have come to India from the direction of China, while the lion must have been the original inhabitant of India. The tiger loves rain-affected regions and dense forest areas. It even likes slightly salty water. The lion is fond of land with scanty rainfall and bushy forests. It does not like salty water. Both tigers and lions are courageous animals. In physical strength, the Royal Bengal tigers of the Sundarbans are far more powerful than the African or Ráŕh lions. The lions of Gujarat are more powerful than certain types of tigers and weaker than others. Whether weak or powerful, all lions are courageous, and all tigers are valiant. Both tigers and lions have qualitative distinctiveness. Both are good looking. The tiger is much more intelligent than the lion. If tigers moving in the forest notice that some tree branches have been chopped off, they will suspect that enemies are lurking nearby. If it finds that a goat has been kept tied up in a secluded spot in the forest, it might feel tempted to attack, but it will not go forward and fall upon its prey immediately. Glancing all around, it will advance surreptitiously and run away with the goat. It runs away so fast that even the hunters are stunned. However, the lion has somewhat of a devil-may-care disposition: “Let the enemy come, I donʼt care; surely no one can beat me in physical strength,” is how the lion feels. Without looking around, and even risking its own life, it will fall upon its prey – the goat. It is not as greedy as the tiger or the wolf, especially when its stomach is full. It does not normally attack anyone without reason but it will counterattack someone who charges first. Compared to the tiger, the lion is more compassionate. Not only for its own progeny – which even the tiger feels – it has been found to have affection even for the offspring of other animals. Evidence of this behaviour has been documented.

points.body: The damp areas of the Sundarbans are very congenial for tigers, but not for lions. The lion can hardly endure the salty water of that area. While the dry climate and sweet water of Ráŕh are quite congenial for lions, they are not at all congenial for the tiger. Hence in ancient times, although tigers were primarily concentrated in Bengal, both tigers and lions lived in Ráŕh. That is why the Puranic gods and goddesses have both tigers and lions as their mounts; the mount of the tiger god of the forest (Dakśiń Ráy) is naturally a tiger, and the mount for the goddess Rájrájershvarii is a tiger on the back of an elephant. Meanwhile, the mount of the Puranic goddess Durgá is a lion.

points.body: The tiger, having a round face, is an animal of the cat family. Animals of both the dog family and the cat family have a very powerful sense of smell. However, animals of the dog family have to concentrate in order to track a scent. To understand where the milk or fish or meat is, the dog has to apply its mind, and only then does it pick up the scent; but animals of the cat family spontaneously get the scent through their nose. The cat does not have to apply any special faculty to know where in the house the milk or fish is located. The scent wafts towards it, and the cat is compelled by natural law to run in that direction. If the housekeeper drives it away, even then the cat remains drawn by the scent, voluntarily or involuntarily. We say that even after a beating, the cat forgets after some time and returns. Whether the cat received a beating or not, it is a particular scent that draws it back. Among the animals of the cat family, the tiger also has a very powerful sense of smell. The derivative meaning of the word byághra is “one who has a very strong sense of smell”. The number of tiger species is quite large. ( 1 )

points.body: After construction of the dam on the Damodar River, in Ráŕh and in South Bengal the Jalangi, Mathabhanga, Ichamati, Kumar, Bhaerava, Nabaganga, Garai, Madhumati, Shivsa, Rupsa and Citra Rivers all dried up. As a result there was a severe onslaught of malaria in the region. Once known for its wealth and clamour of human beings, once resounding with the notes of birds, the then Banagram of Jessore district turned into a forest, having fallen victim to all-engulfing malaria. Due to fear of malaria, many people left their hearth and home and settled in and around Kolkata on the bank of the Bhagirathi. Not only Banagram, but three other sub-divisions r– Magura, Jessore-Sadar and Jhinaidaha – were reduced to the same plight, except for the Narail sub-division of Jessore. People moved away, and in their place came pole cats or Kat́t́ásh, herds of them. So there was a popular saying: “Kat́t́ásh is the king of Banagram and the lion of the forest.” ( 2 )

points.body: Civet cat (gandhagokul): The gokul [cat] that emits a sweet smell [gandha] is called gandhagokul [civetcat]. You know that certain creatures possess certain kinds of smell, good or bad. This is nothing but the secretion of hormones from certain glands. The glandular secretions of the musk rat emit a bad smell. While moving, the musk rat emits a foul smell particularly from the secretion of its lymphatic glands, which distresses the human nose. Due to differences in their hormones, the pungent smell that emanates from a tigerʼs body does not exude from the body of a cat. This smell can be perceived to a very small degree from the body of a wildcat (ban-beŕál). You will scarcely notice this in a khat́t́ásh (or kat́ash). Yet you would notice an odour in a similar but comparatively smaller creature such as the bhám. Though smaller than tigers, hyenas have this bad smell about them. Certain animals with testicles emit a foul smell from the secretion of their glands, but not when their testicles are removed. So the good or bad smell indicates the smell derived from the glandular secretion of hormones. Male goats with testicles have a severe foul smell; but goats without testicles have no foul odour at all. People who consume too much of onions, garlic and meat, which are difficult to digest, emit a bad smell from the secretion of certain glands. Hence excessive intake of onions, garlic, hard-to-digest meat and certain vegetables invariably causes a bad smell in human beings.

points.body: Those who are careful about taking food and do not allow profuse sweating will not generate a bad odour from their body. Of course, sweat itself has no smell, but when it remains on the body for more than 45 minutes, a bad odour develops. The moment the bad smell starts to develop, it is advisable to mop the sweat from the body with a towel or piece of cloth, or wash it off with water. On the other hand, persons who do yogic exercises or take part in devotional singing of kiirtana continuously for a long time secrete certain hormones from specific parts of their anáhata cakra [fourth psycho-spiritual plexus], vishuddha cakra [fifth plexus] and ájiṋá cakra [sixth plexus]. Such secretions emit a sweet fragrance similar to jasmine or ripe jackfruit (although not exactly comparable). So, devotees or yogis generally have a sentient aroma. One of the signs of pure love for God is the emanation of a sweet fragrance from the body of a devotee. When a person even in seclusion tries to feel the spiritual proximity of Parama Puruśa, they can feel the presence of a sweet fragrance wafting across the nose. This is in fact nothing but the sweet-smelling hormones secreted from their glands and concentrated at the tip of the nose. Although a biological phenomenon (related to bio-psychology), it can only be looked upon as the grace of the Supreme.

points.body: The Royal Bengal Tiger of the Sundarbans, the black tigers and jaguars of South America, the panthers and the leopards, all belong to the cat family. Of course, the original cheetahs became extinct about fifty years ago. Smaller than these cheetahs are the gobághá or hárols or bigobá, in English they are called hyenas and in Sanskrit tarakśu. These gobághá or hyenas are smaller in size than normal tigers. Hence they are afraid of adult humans. Next to them [in size] are the bháms. Smaller than bhám cats are the pole cats (khát́t́ás ) and even smaller are the wild cats (bon-beŕál), our known kuṋdo beŕál, domesticated cats (the tomcat and the female cat – meni beŕál). Beginning with the Royal Bengal Tiger up to the civet cat, they are all very similar in appearance and nature. They emit a very foul odour from their body. The kat́ás, bon-beŕál and kuṋdo-beŕáls are smaller in size. In addition, they eat food other than meat. Among its various traits are its keen intelligence and its powerful sense of smell. It is able to ascertain which animals are found in each direction by checking the wind.

points.body: Although they are much stronger than humans, they are much less intelligent, and they know this. So if they catch a human scent in the wind, they prefer not to tread that path. However, if they happen on a person unexpectedly, they will attack them out of a sense of self-preservation. Some can no longer struggle with other animals in their old age, and therefore kill and eat human beings because humans cannot run from them or match them in physical strength. It is very easy for them to kill humans, so those karvara tigers who become man-eaters in this way, and remain so for a long time, undergo some physical changes. Graminivorous animals usually have hooves and are without paws, while carnivorous animals have paws for feet. Graminivorous animals have sparkling white teeth which are carefully arranged. points.body: Among graminivorous animals, particularly those creatures belonging to the zebu species (or bison genus) had an ability to store food in their appendix. This developed during ancient times, when they lived in a volatile situation, unsure of obtaining food at all times. Apes, humans and goats all developed this capacity. Cows and buffaloes also did, and they still do today. As life becomes more and more secure, the necessity for this appendix also diminishes. This has happened to humans, apes and certain other animals. During leisure time, by regurgitating food from the appendix, these animals make it fit for digestion with the help of saliva. In English this is called rumination or chewing the cud; in Bengali it is called románthan or jábar kát́á. Carnivorous animals do not have this capacity, because the meat they have eaten quickly decomposes and develops a foul odour. It cannot be used for rumination or for chewing the cud.

points.body: In ancient times, those land-dwelling, graminivorous animals without horns or claws for self-preservation began to climb trees in search of safe refuge. For those animals, just as the necessity for using hooves came to an end, they now felt the need for using their forelimbs to catch hold of tree branches. They used their hind legs partly for clutching and partly for running. They used their forelimbs for clutching branches of trees as well as for other tasks. In ancient times, the forelimbs were earlier called kara, and later hasta. Australopithecines, creatures of the ape family, and human beings are all equipped with kara. In fact, they have four limbs; but human beings are not quadrupeds because their forelimbs are used for clutching objects.

points.title: In order to climb trees and to leap up, the creatures of the ape family required a tail
points.prompt: Recall and explain from memory: In order to climb trees and to leap up, the creatures of the ape family required a tail
summary: In order to climb trees and to leap up, the creatures of the ape family required a tail.

points.body: In order to climb trees and to leap up, the creatures of the ape family required a tail. However, for the more intelligent [members] of this family who no longer needed to leap as much, the importance of the lymphatic gland diminished and their tails dropped off. This superfamily of creatures – the apes – gradually split into two family lines. Both families had well-arranged teeth and no canine teeth. Both had an intestinal appendix, but one family had a tail and the other was tailless. Those with tails, belonging to the ape family, are called monkeys – in Bengali bánar or bádar, and the females bánarii or bádarii, in Urdu bandar, and the females bandariá. The tailless monkeys had greater intellectual development than those with tails. They also evolved into two different classes: one ordinary and the other more developed. Of the ordinary tailless apes there were again three distinct genuses; 1) gorillas, 2) orang-utans (in Malay language it means “men of the trees”) and 3) chimpanzees. Today the developed, tailless apes are known as humans. The word “man” stands for “mentally developed ape”.

points.body: The ape family: Ku+d́ikhin = kikhi. The verbal root ku is used in many senses. One meaning is grinning and grimacing. So the etymological meaning of the word kikhi is “one who grimaces”. One speciality about the suffixes d́ikhin and kvan is that the last phoneme of the verbal root can alternately be i. For example, if you add the suffix kvan/kvas to the verbal root kan, the resulting word will of course be kańva, but it can also be kińva. Similarly, if you add the suffix d́ikhin, it can be both kukhi and kikhi. But the kukhi form is not prevalent. In common usage, the word kikhi means monkey. On the slightest occasion, either due to fear or excitement, a monkey grimaces with clenched fists. So it is called kikhi. This habit of the monkey is prehistoric. Although the ancestors of human beings and monkeys are the same, they were separated at least one million years ago. So a human being also, when frightened or excited, clenches the fist and grimaces. A small child keeps its fist clenched most of the time, and the habit of grimacing also remains predominant in childhood. ( 2 )

points.body: The lifespan of these insects is normally about a fortnight. Yet, after investigation it has been noted that unless there is any serious damage to their bodies or life, they can live up to two months. During the late autumn, however, due to the excessive mists, they die out. They usually lay their eggs on the upper part of grass blades. The eggs remain there for about a year. Many animals grazing in the fields eat up these eggs along with the blades of grass. Sometimes the scorching rays of the sun dry up the grass and kill the eggs. During the floods, these eggs, still attached to the blades of grass, float towards the sea. Of course, the eggs are numerous; in fact, there are millions and millions of eggs. So many of them may die [along the way], but not all. With the sprinkling of rain these eggs come to life again. At the end of the rainy season, the baby shyámápoká come out of their eggs and move about independently. They do more harm than good to humans. Yet they are food for many small-sized birds and other creatures. In that sense, they help to a great extent in maintaining the ecological balance in the world.

points.body: Pauṋgapál (locust) is a peculiar kind of insect. Generally it appears only in desert areas on occasion, when sultry weather abounds. You know, the heat of the desert is usually dry. Surely you must be aware of the fact that the heat of Jodhpur is much more intense than that of Kolkata. Yet the Kolkata climate, because of greater humidity, causes people to sweat profusely. Due to this perspiration, excessive salt exudes from the body and this weakens the power of activity. More than Kolkata, in East and North Bengal this sultriness is even more intense. So according to the theory of East and Wet ( 2 ) [humidity factor], the people of East and North Bengal are less industrious than those of Ráŕh. Again, the people of Assam suffer more from humid climate than those of East and North Bengal. That is why the people of Assam are far less industrious. Although the heat of Jodhpur is more intense than that of Kolkata, there is hardly any humidity. That is why there is less sweating and therefore less fatigue. While staying in Rajasthan, I personally experienced this. In any case, even in this desert region, if there is one percent increase in humidity, the locusts increase by the millions. In fact, locust eggs lie in a dormant state for several years in the desert, and once it becomes humid they bloom into life. This happens not only in Rajasthan, in Thar (Sindh), in the northern desert regions of Gujarat, but also in Persia (Iran), Baluchistan, Sahara and Gobi. Even in the deserts of South America such phenomena occur to some extent.

points.body: Though locusts are very close to grasshoppers as a suborder of insects, there is hardly any similarity in their nature or habits. The habitat of grasshoppers, especially their birthplace, is the extensive sandy beds of large rivers. They cannot, however, live far from a humid environment. They live in verdant fields and eat green leaves. Thus as a natural camouflage, their colour is deep green. Similarly, locusts are insects that feed on leaves of grass. However, because they are born in deserts, their colour is different. Bengal is far away from deserts, and so there are scarcely any locust attacks in Bengal. In assessing their nature and habits, the primary difference between grasshoppers and locusts is that grasshoppers do not live in groups, while locusts always do so. When they fly together in the millions, their dark shadow overcasts the sky. Whatever region they fly over finds its vegetation destroyed. These shalabhá or locusts are food for human beings in certain regions of the earth.

So, one of the literal meanings of kośanáyaka is the Apis indica type of bee. In India there are three types of bees (maomáchi): rock bee, bush bee and Apis indica. Rock bee is a large bee species that produces honey in large quantities. They have large honeycombs, normally on banyan trees or other large trees. Sometimes the honeycombs are so large that they break apart, and the honey oozes out and drips onto the ground. The honey produced by the rock bees is somewhat pungent. It is known as ugraviirja [inducing vitality]. points.body: In a human body that has reduced vitality, so long as there is no blood-consuming disease, ten drops of this particular honey, if consumed in the morning along with the leaves of krśńa-tulasii [black basil] on an empty stomach, will yield excellent results. However if a person has blood dysentery or any ulcer in the body, then one must not take it. The honey must be sucked [or licked], not swallowed. That is why in Indian ayurvedic science it is called avaleha.

points.body: Bush bees are small-sized bees. They are ancient inhabitants of India. Instead of building honeycombs on trees, they prefer to build them on the walls of mud houses. In the villages of Ráŕh Bengal, when ants make their home in mud houses built with clayish soil, if the bush bees find an opportunity to occupy them, they build their choicest and most beautiful honeycombs there. We obtain minimum honey from such individual honeycombs; but the honey is well-refined and pleasant in taste and scent. On the other hand, it is lower in vitality than any other honey. Good quality neem honey (obtained from the neem flower) is produced by these bees. It is surmised that they are the original bees of Ráŕh Bengal. They do not sting readily. Even when they sting, there is hardly that unbearable pain which is caused by the sting of rock bees.

points.body: Apis indica are the original bees of India. They are medium in size and live in medium-sized trees. Some trees produce floral nectar in plenty, and these bees build their honeycombs there or in neighbouring areas. If there is no fear of enemies, they build their honeycombs on the lower branches of trees. They are found all over Bengal; but they are mostly seen in large numbers in southern Bengal; especially in southern Ráŕh. They can fly for a long distance. Their stings cause severe pain. They prepare good honey from mustard flowers. At one time physicians preferred honey produced by these bees in the preparation of ayurvedic medicines. The very name Apis indica denotes their identity as the original bees of India. In Ráŕh they normally build their honeycombs in areas adjacent to rivers or at the confluence of rivers, mostly on trees of medium height. In the Sundarbans at the end of winter, they are the first to come forward to begin building their honeycombs. The wax of these honeycombs is quite pliable and soft. There was a time when it was sold at a very high price. Another good name of these Apis indica bees is kośanáyaka. ( 1 )

points.body: White ant: Ui [white ant] is a native Bengali word. In North India, diimak is used; on the Bengal and North India border, diiyaṋk or diiyáṋ is used; in English ui means “white-ant”, and in Sanskrit valmiikakiit́a or pluśińa is used. In many parts of Bengal, a is used in place of ra, and ra is used in place of a. For this reason ui are called rui nearly everywhere in southern Bengal. The mushroom that grows on anthills is called rui-chátu [ant-mushroom]. This tiny creature belonging to the ant group increases its numbers at an extremely fast rate. They cannot see anything in the sunlight. Their sense of touch also diminishes when exposed to sunlight. Thus they build little tunnels out of the earth to protect themselves from sunlight and use them to move around in because their sense of touch and other senses come to life in the darkness of these tunnels. Under certain conditions, the different branches and sub-branches of these tunnels that they construct right and left become visible as a mound or hillock. In spoken Bengali we call this ui-dhibi, in English “anthill”, in Sanskrit valmiika. An anthill was built around the entire body of a sage who remained motionless for many days during the practice of his austerities. At the time that he sat for meditation, he was known by the name of Ratnákara. The people gave him the name Válmiiki because at the time that he finished his penance and rose from his seat, his body was encased in an anthill.

points.body: In Sanskrit the word pluśińa was more widely used than the word valmiikakiit́a. Sama pluśińa sama mashakena sama nágena sama ebhistribhirlokaeh, that is, Parama Puruśa is unbiased. He is equal to everyone because He sees everyone in the same way. He sees an ant in the same way He sees a small mosquito. He understands an ant in the same way that He understands a mosquito. He does not make any undue fuss over a giant serpent (python or “elephant of the jungle”) because of its great size. He sees a python or “elephant of the jungle” in the same way that He sees an ant or a mosquito, and they also see Him in that same way. Nor does He make any special fuss over this universe, the three worlds of heaven, earth and hell, because of their vastness, and they also look at Him in the same way. In other words, everyone is equal to Parama Puruśa – a mosquito, ant, python, mammoth and even the three worlds. He remains with everyone equally through His ota yoga and prota yoga [individual and collective association of Parama Purnśa with jiiva]. He is impartial under all conditions.

points.body: Bugs (kit́ibha): Kit́ibha: kit́i+bha+d́a = kit́ibha. The etymological meaning of the word kit́ibha is “that which looks like a kit́i”. In common usage, kit́ibha means “bug”. There are two reasons why a bug is called kit́ibha. Suppose you have returned very tired… It is already night … you are about to sleep. Then suddenly you notice a bug on your bed. Well, you might have immediately killed the bug. But you are left with the apprehension that since you have spotted one bug, there must be more bugs in the bed. You say to yourself, “I will lose my sleep for nothing tonight.” You are frightened by the bleak prospect of spending an agonizing night. The kind of fear that you experience on seeing the bug is similar to the kind of fear you have on seeing a rhino or a boar. So a bug is called kit́ibha, that is, like a kit́i [rhino].
