points.body: Large-sized scorpion: Khararomańa means “large-sized, dark and hairy scorpion” (in English scorpion, in Latin scorpio). Usually these scorpions live in the hills. They live in the openings between rocks or in large crevices in the hills. These dark-coloured scorpions are known as khararomańa. They are very venomous. In 1963 the present writer was once bitten by such a scorpion. Its sting is unbearably painful. Small babies might succumb to their sting. Once in the khirkhiriá section of the Rajmahal branch of Ramgarh hills [Jamalpur hills fall in the same hill range] there were plenty of these scorpions. In my boyhood days I used to watch these scorpions bristling together, removing slabs of stone. At that time, that particular hill was covered with forests. Later the hill and the forest came under control of the provincial government (state government). During the British rule, the forests were ruined. As a result such scorpions also quickly became extinct. In 1964 when I went there, I saw that the number of these scorpions was greatly reduced in the forests, and even removing the stone slabs I could hardly come across one or two such creatures. Their number must have been even further reduced, since there is no forest in that area now. In the plains adjacent to the hills, due to abolition of the zamindary system, the forests have been obliterated. Arrangements have been made for sanctuaries, only for the sake of preserving certain wild animals. However, since no preservation of these scorpions is possible, they will soon become extinct.

points.body: The word kurpii means káṋkŕá biche [crab scorpion; it derives its name from the Bengali word káṋkŕá which means crab]. Its alternative Sanskrit name is briscika. The etymological meaning of the word brishcika is something of a crooked nature. Another meaning of the word is “something which is unbearable”. The Bengali word bichá or biche is derived from the word brishcika. There are several different species of scorpions in the world. The chief among them are teṋtule biche [a variety of scorpions as dark-coloured as a ripe tamarind seed] and káṋkŕá biche. Although teṋtule biche can be of different colours, it is mainly reddish in appearance. And when it lies quietly on the road, from a distance it looks like a ripe tamarind seed. Hence its name is teṋtule biche. In India, apart from a good number of white and yellow varieties of teṋtule biche, a genus of ink-black colour is also found. Many people call a white scorpion sarasvatii biche [Saraswati is a mythological Hindu deity, whose colour is supposed to be pure white], a yellow scorpion or sońá biche [golden-coloured scorpion], and the black scorpion or káli biche [dark-coloured scorpion like the dark-complexioned mythological Hindu goddess Káli].

points.body: The biting power of all scorpions is not the same. The sting of some results in a heavy loss of blood, whereas in the case of others the loss is minimal. These scorpions are venomous no doubt, but the burning sensation that their bite causes is not entirely due to the venom; it is mainly due to loss of blood. A scorpion is far more venomous than a teṋtule biche. The way in which a scorpion moves resembles somewhat that of a crab. Hence it is called káṋkŕá biche. When a crab moves, it keeps its claws raised all along. This is because it moves with the thought that if it is attacked by an approaching enemy, it will launch a counter attack immediately. The same is the case with a scorpion. It also moves with its claws elevated, so that it can collide with an advancing enemy and pierce its sting into its body. In India, generally three types of scorpions are found: 1) pale-dark, 2) deep-dark, and 3) those dwelling on hills and mountains. The pale-dark variety is somewhat smaller in size, and its bite is less painful. In Bengal, this type of scorpion found in greater number. The deep-dark variety is larger in size, and its bite is extremely painful. If it bites a child, it can even cause the childʼs death. They are sometimes found to live in the holes between the leaves of banana trees. Those who incise date-palm trees are often attacked by this type of scorpion.

The venom of scorpions is used in poison therapy. Its venom is also used in the preparation of homeopathic medicines. The old Sanskrit and Vedic name of scorpions is kurpii. The name brishcika is also quite old. Their Latin equivalent is ‘scorpio’. From ‘scorpio’ has come the English word ‘scorpion’. The word kaorpya means anything related to scorpions. You can call the venom of scorpions kaorpya viśa, and the medicine prepared from its venom kaorpya aosadha. You can also call a man of extremely crooked nature kaorpya kut́ila.

points.body: Louse (ukun): Keshakiit́a (louse) is a type of insect which resides in hair and eats the fat at the root of the hair and the skin of the head. Literally, it means “louse”. The eggs of the louse are called niki and the adult lice are called dyáuṋgar. So you understand the meaning of the word “louse,” and you must be alert regarding these insects. In earlier times, to protect themselves from lice attack, people used to blend kerosene oil with coconut oil in equal proportions and apply it on the head. It was necessary to sit with oneʼs back to the sun for one hour in this condition before taking bath. That resulted in the disappearance of the lice in two or three days. Nowadays one can do the same or use [lice] shampoo once a month to protect oneself from the onslaught of lice. ( 4 )

points.body: Rat: Kund + uń = kundu. The etymological meaning is “one whose nature is to lurk”. Suppose there are seven hundred rats in a room. A cat enters the room. The rats immediately know it; they understand the situation. Suddenly, from that very moment, they stop all movement, stop making any noise. Silence reigns in the room. It would be hard for anyone to know that seven hundred rats were lurking. So one colloquial meaning of the word kundu is a rat of any kind, whether a rat or a mouse. In Hindi a rat is called cuhá and a mouse is called cuhiyá. In Bihar the big ones are called muś, the small ones cut́ri. For a woodland rat or field mouse the word ákhu was common in old Sanskrit. In later times the word went almost completely out of use. Múśika or iṋdura refers to all kinds of rodents. Muśá was common in old Bengali. Now it has gone out of use.

points.body: As you well know, there are many species of iṋdur such as the mouse, the rat, the field mouse [marmot group], tree rat, etc. Some of them live in kitchens, some in storerooms, some in holes in the wall and some in tree hollows. They have many names according to their species and dwelling place: iṋdur, muśika, ákhu, kundu, and so on. The mole also has three main species in India. But they are all field moles; they live in burrows in the fields. The entrance to the burrow is towards the bottom and the burrow itself moves upward. So what happens is that during heavy rains when the field is on the point of being submerged, it is difficult for water to seep into the dwelling. If there is water at the mouth of the hole, they can easily come out and escape. Since it lives in a field, the moleʼs proper name is vasumitra. During the day the mole cannot see properly, so they mostly come out at night. Certainly you will hardly ever see a mole entering your house during the day. You see it at night.

points.body: The moleʼs burrow is also called kulaka. One proper name for the mole is kulakeya, in the sense of “kulaka-dweller”, kulakeyii in feminine gender. Do you not call “the mole” that type of firework which runs about hither and thither during Diipavali [light festival] just like a mole does, making a sharp hissing sound? This mole firework does not stay in a kulaka; it is kept in a box or in oneʼs pocket. The moleʼs hole is called kulaka, but do you know the name of the ratʼs hole? It is good that you do. If you do not know, then listen well. The word is kundubil. Kundu means “rat;” bil means “hole” or “opening”. The word bil is used in Hindi and in a few North Indian languages to mean “hole”. ( 2 )

If they do not find anything edible they will cut things with their teeth, thinking that after it is cut up it might turn into food. In this sense, the word karvva also means “rat.” Of course, karvva does not mean “mouse” (plural, “mice”). ( 3 )

points.title: Aromatic rat (gandhamuśika): You are already familiar with the word “hibernation”
points.prompt: Recall and explain from memory: Aromatic rat (gandhamuśika): You are already familiar with the word “hibernation”

Due to the reduced fat in the body, the upper layer of their skin slackens, just as happens with a fat person after a spell of sickness, or with a person who has crossed over from middle age into old age.
points.body: Aromatic rat (gandhamuśika): You are already familiar with the word “hibernation”. You all know that there are cold-blooded creatures on this earth. They cannot move or function in cold weather. That is why they fall asleep for a long spell with the advent of winter. They feel drowsy two or three days before their hibernation starts. At that time, struggling against drowsiness, they move towards a safe shelter and lie down. Generally that shelter is under the ground, because they feel warm there. That warmth of the ground does not allow them to die. During this long spell of sleep, they consume the fat (in Bengali basá, carbi in Hindustani) accumulated in their body. At the end of winter, the lukewarm weather of spring creates a stir in their nerves and blood, and they awake. If someone kills them while they are in hibernation, they die, but their sleep does not break. That is why this hibernation is described in Sanskrit as himanidrá. After this long spell of sleep they emerge from their hole in the ground. Due to the reduced fat in the body, the upper layer of their skin slackens, just as happens with a fat person after a spell of sickness, or with a person who has crossed over from middle age into old age.

points.title: So, on waking from hibernation, these creatures shed the loose skin from their body

points.body: So, on waking from hibernation, these creatures shed the loose skin from their body. The skin they shed is called khosá, or outer skin, just like the outer skin of the coconut or the banana skin. In the language of Kolkata Bengali it is called kholá – that which can be removed. In Bengal both the words kholá and khosá are widely used. That which has to be removed, which cannot be kept on the body even though one might like to keep it, and the removal of which is indispensable, is called kholas in Bengali. So after getting up from hibernation these creatures shed their skin (kholash). The chaste Bengali or Sanskrit word for this kholash is nirmok. So it is said, “Snakes shed their skin in the spring.” When the old skin is shed, the inner skin that emerges is very thin and sensitive. At this time, the creatures cannot bear the scorching rays of the sun. So they come out of their hole only in the early hours of the night. Now, during the spring and summer seasons, there is a greater intrusion of snakes onto village roads. Since their skin has become sensitive, if anyone tramples upon them, they strike. So when moving about at night on the road during this period, one must carry some kind of light.

points.body: Be that as it may, these cold-blooded creatures in India are appreciable in number. At the end of Ashvin or Kárttik [end of autumn] they lie down to hibernate. Chief amongst those who indulge in this form of hibernation is a small creature of the rodent order that lives in the holes of the lower Himalayan mountain ranges. They are generally known as marmots. A strange odour emanates from their body. The chaste Bengali name for such aromatic rats is gandhamuśika. ( 4 )

points.body: Otter (udbiŕála): Uda or udaka means “water”. The etymological meaning of udbiŕála is “that cat-like creature that lives in the water”. Its colloquial meaning is bhodaŕ [otter]. Some people have the notion that this otter [Mustelid family] is perhaps an aquatic creature, but it is not. It is a land creature like the crocodile and the fish-eating crocodile. It goes into the water to catch prey. It is a land-dwelling creature that breastfeeds its young. It sleeps and gives birth on land, and it normally lives in large holes near ponds and reservoirs. ( 5 )

points.body: When the large animals of ancient times became physically incapacitated, they took refuge in a secluded place and died there in the normal course of events. According to some scholars, the bones and fat of these animals accumulated in those places. Some form of terrible whirlpools were created in the sea, in watersheds or large lakes, and due to that, the remains of the dead animals inside those whirlpools would drift out to sea and become the Sargasso Sea (Saraságar or floating islands of earth). They even floated into the ocean depths. Some scholars believe that those places where earlier saraságars were created from the remains of animal bodies now yield us oil [petrol] from under the earth. If such places, instead of being close to the sea, happened to be inside any land region, then the fat and other remains of these large animals would float out to the sea, whereas the bones would pile up in the form of hills. In the course of time, these hills of bones turned into limestone or dolomite.

points.body: When this calcium-enriched substance was burned, it turned into a type of lime, which we call in spoken language páthure cuń [lime obtained by calcination]. When the shells of water-grown animals with hard skin (snails, oysters, conch shells, etc) are turned into a type of lime through calcination, we describe it in spoken language as kalicuń. In southern Bengal the whitewashing of houses is called kali pheráno [bringing new lime]. A commercial centre developed for this kind of lime along with matted coir ( 1 ) has come to be known today as Kalikátá [Kolkata] – in Oriya language Kalikatá. Another village near this place is also called Kalikátá. Whether it is lime produced by calcination or kalicuń, both are produced from the bones of animal bodies. Those who are averse to taking kalicuń in betel leaf [for chewing after a meal], thinking that it is produced from an animal body, should remember that the calcinated lime (páthure cuń) is also derived from animal bodies. Not only the leader of the elephant herd but all elephants belonging to herds in the forest used to go into such seclusion as death neared. Today elephants do not have permanent habitats. Fearing human beings, they move from one forest to another, hence they also have no fixed place to breathe their last breath. ( 2 )

The tiger is a very clever animal. As it falls upon its prey and moves away with it, it runs very swiftly and leaps also. points.body: The horse usually runs continuously. When taking a turn to the left or the right, it is hardly aware of propriety. The pig never moves in a disciplined manner; whatever food it comes across, it turns in that direction. The dog usually moves quickly. Although it runs in the direction of food, it does not at all lack alertness. The buffalo moves more slowly than the cow, while always fixing its eyes on the watershed. When it comes across any watershed, it does not care for any right or wrong and simply plunges into the water. The cow normally moves at a medium pace and habitually avoids mud, slime, water and sand very carefully. It does not like to come in contact with water, and does not like to bathe in water at all. The lion is fond of moving in leaps and bounds. It also loves to run. However, it has less intelligence. So for no real reason it runs and leaps and thereby endangers itself.

This movement of sheep is called gad́d́áliká praváha [following the beaten track] or gad́d́ál > gad́hál > gáŕhol >gáŕol. The foolish person is sarcastically called gáŕol. Actually gáŕol means “sheep”. In northern India, those who tend the sheep are known as gad́heri.

points.body: In this world, there is a common trend. Just as one sheep runs ahead, the other sheep behind it follow suit. If the sheep ahead falls into a pit, the sheep behind it also fall into the pit. The ox loves to move haltingly. After moving forward a few steps, it stands still like a sculpted statue. If it happens to notice any food nearby, it will slowly move in that direction without caring what others might think. It does not even care to check whether someone may come chasing it. Its temperament is such that it appears not to care for anyone on this earth. Suppose you see an ox standing on the road. For your own safety, you are walking at a distance by the side of a drain on the other side of the road. The ox would not even bother to look at you; it simply would have no interest. However, if you are wearing a garland of marigolds around your neck, it will advance towards you. You might think it is coming to knock you down, and so you may run away. However, the ox is not coming to attack you. It is coming in your direction to snatch away the marigolds and gobble them up. The habit of the ox is to move step by step and then halt, rest a while, and then again move. Due to this strange habit it is called kramodbeg [graded tension]. This word is specifically used to describe an ox of bulky appearance. ( 1 )

points.body: Crocodiles develop friendships with sparrows and other tiny birds, while donkeys are friends with pigeons. On the sandy beds of rivers the crocodile rests and warms itself in the sun, keeping its mouth open while tiny birds enter its mouth and pick up bits of meat from in between its teeth, thus cleansing them. It is to be remembered that the crocodile does not use any kind of toothbrush or other instrument to clean its teeth. Likewise, pigeons sitting on the backs of donkeys pick lice and other insects and eat them. The donkeys feel comfortable with this and the pigeons also obtain their supply of food. Donkeys feel much better when the pigeons have picked the insects off their backs. That is why pigeons are the favorite birds of donkeys. For this reason, pigeons are also known as kharapriya. ( 1 )

points.body: I mentioned to you in connection with musk that the hormone secreted by the musk deer accumulates in its navel, and as it becomes stiffer, the intensity of its fragrance also increases. Ultimately when it becomes too stiff, the fragrance also becomes too intense. At this stage, overwhelmed and excited by the fragrance, the deer runs madly in search of the fragrance until finally, exhausted and worn out, it meets its death. Similarly the elephant, in a state of frenzy in certain situations, turns mad and after some time it dies. Of course, not all elephants turn mad, and those which do become mad do not live long in this condition. Among elephants, such deaths are not frequent, yet they do occur. Elephants that go berserk are not only dangerous for human beings; they are also dangerous for other elephants. Other elephants become frightened of them and stay far away. In normal conditions, elephants enter human localities in search of food. Their favorite food is green leaves and twigs, ripe maize, paddy and wheat. If they can procure food without any disturbance, they do not attack anyone. The villagers light fires and beat drums and tin pots; they do all these things not in fear but to avoid any kind of disturbance.

” This is our urge, our search for truth… this is satyágraha [the movement for truth].
points.body: When an elephant goes berserk, it does not even think of food; it goes without food for several days and even goes without water. Its overheated brain urges it to break laws... to challenge restrictions. You all know that there are those who encourage people to break laws, and in fact incite them to do so. The consequences are never good. To quickly achieve independence during British rule, a class of political leaders started a civil disobedience movement (in Hindi, kánun toŕńá). points.body: According to ancient Puranic legend, on the western bank of the spot where the Náráyańii and Gańd́aka rivers met the Ganges River, a huge elephant and a huge turtle, symbolizing Hari [Lord Krśńa] and Hara [Lord Shiva] respectively, fought a duel. The people came there to organize a big fair annually on the full moon day in the Bengali month of Kárttika [in October during autumn]. Humans, birds and animals dear to Lord Shiva all crowded there together. In order to attract more people, shops were set up for buying and selling food items. People used to gather there in large numbers. Various animals from different parts of the country and abroad, such as elephants, camels, horses, cows, buffaloes, goats and sheep, were brought together at the fair. No other such fair was known to be held anywhere in the world until that time. That fair at the Hari-Hara ground continues to be held even today on the autumnal full moon day.

The spot falls under the jurisdiction of Sonepur Police station in Chapra district of Bihar. To the south of this place flows the river Ganges, and the ghat is popularly known as Pahleja Ghat. points.body: [As mentioned earlier], for a long time this has been the largest animal fair in the world. Now I am told that in Russia, near Moscow, a similar large animal fair is held. That fair is known to be even larger than the fair on Hazipur fairground nowadays. It is very likely because, with the abolition of the zamindary system, there is hardly any customer for elephants, although there are a few sellers. Few elephants are brought for sale. Is it only because of this? Even if the zamindary system had remained, the import of elephants would still have declined, because elephants are fast being replaced by four-wheeled jeeps. Yet is this the only reason? The elephant consumes every week twenty maunds ( 1 ) of branches, twigs and leaves of trees. During their stay in the forest, an elephant spoils about sixty maunds of such vegetation per week. Every week the elephant has to be provided with eight maunds of rice and half a maund of clarified butter. A mahout has to be employed to tend the elephant. Lest the elephantʼs head turns hot, it has to be regularly bathed in water. The jeep has no such problems. Other than expenses for petrol or diesel and occasional servicing, no other incurring expenditure is involved in its maintenance.

points.body: The import of horses has also declined; those who once used them for transport are now using jeeps, motorcycles, scooters, etc. There is now hardly any use for horse-drawn carriages. In its place have come petrol-operated cars and even cars operated by electricity. So the demand for horses and elephants has declined. The use of camels has also decreased, although not by much. As before, the people of northern India use the camel for tilling the soil even today. Whereas for tilling the land one requires at least two bullocks, only one camel will do the same job. And the camel also offers milk. Furthermore, the camel is also the ship of the desert. So the utility of the camel prevails almost as much as before. I say ‘almost’, because for drawing the plough there is increasing use of tractors. Whatever the case might be, the importance of the Hari-Hara fair has noticeably diminished. Yet the glamour of the fair is still there. On account of this animal fair at Hari-Hara grounds, the railway platform of the Sonepur station was once the longest platform in India, probably in the world. Now I learnt that the platform of the Kharagpur station of the South Eastern Railway has wrested that glory. This is quite likely. ( 2 )

points.body: Although they uttered the prayer Sarvaḿ khalvidaḿ Brahma [“Let everyone live in happiness”], yet in the name of religion they committed animal slaughter. They did not oppose the slaughter of innocent animals; in fact, they even supported it. This is quite regrettable. Maybe in those days the mindset of the people was such that the time was not yet ripe for reflecting about animals, birds and plants. Yet there were certain restrictions on animal slaughter. Animal slaughter and meat eating were not permitted on every religious occasion; female animals could not be slaughtered. Domesticated animals could not be slaughtered without giving them the opportunity to give battle. Fish could be caught in a net but could not be caught by using fishing bait or by tempting them with food. Those who did not observe these restrictions were called kut́aka. Forests where animal slaughter was forbidden were known as mrgadáva or sanctuaries (nirbhaya kánan, just as one near Varanasi adjacent to Sarnath was Rśi-pattan Mrgadáva; in the Prákrt language it is called Iśi-pattan Mrgadáva). Those who secretly killed any animal in these protected areas (mrgadávas) were also known as kut́akas. Those who took to this secret killing of animals – their nature was known as kaot́akika. For the word kaot́akika in its etymological sense, one could even use the expression kaot́ika.

How, by doing harm to someone or putting an end to someoneʼs life, can the [so-called] glory of sacrifice be attained by human beings? It is beyond our common understanding. points.body: Growth in the animal population takes place in three ways. First mammals grow in the motherʼs womb in a membrane (placenta), and after attaining their full size they become restless in the womb and are born with the placenta tied to the navel. The nurse severs the link between the navel of the baby and the placenta, which we can describe as analogous to the shell of an egg. Just as the interior of the egg is covered with a shell, the embryo of the mammal similarly remains encased in a placenta. In spoken language this placenta is called phul (in Nepali language the egg is called phul). The life of a child-bearing woman is endangered if the placenta takes a long time to come out of the womb, after the birth of the child. After the placenta comes out of the womb, it is either burnt or buried in the ground [in traditional societies.] For the proper extrication of this placenta, there are certain homeopathic medicines. In ancient Indian therapeutics, certain instruments were recommended or used for extricating the dead baby from the womb, for bringing out the placenta, or for bringing out the live baby from the womb; they were called garbhashauṋku.

That which comes out of the motherʼs body as milk essence, which is a metamorphosed form of motherʼs blood, is termed as stan – root verb + yat suffix = stanna. Stan + ac = Stan [breast] means “the motherʼs milk which provides essential calcium for the nutritional well-being of the baby”. Be it formula milk, milk from the midwife, powdered milk, or the milk of the female donkey – none is comparable to the motherʼs milk. So, those who deprive the baby of motherʼs milk do maximum harm to the baby. How much humans or animals are indebted to their mother becomes evident from the fact that right from the earliest stage in the womb, the blood and vitality of the baby comes from the motherʼs body. points.body: The transformation from oviparous creatures to mammals has led to significant complexities in the animal body. In some countries of the world there are animals which are midway between the oviparous and the mammal stage. The (duckbill) platypus is such a creature. Closely related to the cat; the duckbill (platypus) lays eggs, yet it is a mammal. Bats are much closer to mammals than the duckbill (platypus). They give birth to young ones, which remain in an immature state after birth. Akin to the bat order – perhaps its sub-order – is the vampire [bird; Geospiza nebulosa or sharp-beaked finch] and the titmouse (cámciká). These two belong to the same order. Whether they are oviparous or mammalian, the progeny of all creatures remain helpless after birth for some time. The home for these helpless babies is the “lying-in-room” or “birthing room”. The newborn child is entirely helpless – frail and helpless (árta or átura). That is why the birthing room is called the room for the helpless; in colloquial Bengali it is called áturghar (áturálaya) or “sick-room”.

For instance, there are biological disparities existing in the society, which are being encouraged by certain selfish persons. The biological disparity between human and animal, between human and plant, between animal and plant – that disparity must not be there. Just as my life is dear to me, so the lives of created beings are also equally dear to them. It is the birthright of human beings to live in this world, and it is the birthright of the animal world and plant world also to remain on this earth. To recognize this right, and to get it recognized by the entire human society, the Renaissance movement will have to do something concrete.

points.body: Then there are physico-psychic ailments. Some people argue that animals have been created by Parama Puruśa for our food. I knew a certain person who used to say that if people do not eat goatsʼ meat, the world would become populated only by goats. And others said that if people do not eat chickens, there would not be even a single inch of space on this earth – it would be filled with chickens! Now my point is, even though human beings do not eat vultures, is there a crowd of vultures in the world? How foolish such people are! People do not eat earthworms – has there been an uncontrollable growth of earthworms on earth? Only out of excessive greed, people eat chickens and goats and are simply searching for logic to support their actions and cover up their weakness. This sort of cunning will not do. In the mobility of the psychic world, there are certain defective thoughts prevailing – that we humans are destined to rule this earth, and the creatures are destined to be ruled by us. You will have to fight against this type of psychology with the help of your strong weapon. What is that weapon? Neohumanism. All have the equal right to live here: this universe is for all. It is not the patrimony of human beings only. This is also the duty of renaissance people. ( 1 )

points.body: The formation of a World Government will require a world constitution. A charter of principles or bill of rights should be included in such a constitution and encompass at least the following four areas. First, complete security should be guaranteed to all the plants and animals on the planet. Secondly, each country must guarantee purchasing power to all its citizens. Thirdly, the constitution should guarantee four fundamental rights – spiritual practice or Dharma; cultural legacy; education; and indigenous linguistic expression. Fourthly, if the practice of any of these rights conflicts with cardinal human values then that practice should be immediately curtailed. That is, cardinal human values must take precedence over all other rights. All the constitutions of the world suffer from numerous defects. The above points may be adopted by the framers of different constitutions to overcome these defects. ( 3 )

points.body: Furthermore, never forgetting that human life is an ideological flow, human beings should always move towards the supreme ideology. They have been moving in this direction since time immemorial and, through this process of movement, have reached the present stage of humanity. Passing through many lives as worms, insects, birds, and animals, they have undergone countless pains, miseries, tortures and humiliations. Take for example the life of a goat. A goat spends its life eating grass, until the day comes when the butcher grabs it, kills it, skins it and sells its flesh piece by piece in the market. That goat at one time had to live such a miserable life. But today it has forgotten all this. Through a process of forward movement, today it may have attained a human life.

points.title: Human life is more secure than animal life
points.prompt: Recall and explain from memory: Human life is more secure than animal life
summary: Human life is more secure than animal life.
Animals fully trust human beings; they trust them even up to one minute before their death.
This is how wretched animal life can be.
points.body: Human life is more secure than animal life. Many animals live in the jungle where there is something to fear every minute; where the weak are the prey of the strong. To escape this atmosphere of fear and insecurity, many wild animals have sought refuge with human beings. They have been fed grass, leaves and other types of fodder until the right moment came to kill them for their flesh. Even today, this is generally what happens. Animals fully trust human beings; they trust them even up to one minute before their death. But when they see a person approaching them with a weapon in hand, they realize that those they had trusted as their friends are actually their enemies. Although human beings feed their animals, the love or attachment which they have for them is purely external. There is no genuine love in [humans]. This is how wretched animal life can be.

points.body: Every human being has had to pass through that sort of painful animal life in the past. But that does not mean we should be the cause of misery for those animals who have taken shelter with us today. On the contrary, we should have a merciful attitude towards them. A woman who has been badly treated or humiliated by her mother-in-law should be careful that she does not treat her daughter-in-law in the same way. Human beings should carry out their duties properly in the external world and should always ensure that no being suffers unnecessarily from any undue mistreatment. In the physical sphere, the rights of all should be protected. Each and every human being should be guaranteed the basic necessities of life: food, clothing, medicine, shelter and education. “I wonʼt exploit anyone, and I will not allow others to exploit me.” This is the spirit of proper objective adjustment. And while this proper objective adjustment is maintained, work must continue in a progressive way. You will have to move ahead on the path of life while keeping an adjustment with the external world.

points.body: You must always remember that your existence is not only a physical one. It is animals who are primarily concerned with the physical world, who struggle merely to survive. Those animals which live in jungles are constantly confronted by the fear of tigers, lions, bears, elephants, snakes, crocodiles and a host of other ferocious creatures; while those which have surrendered to human beings, such as goats, sheep and cows, are confronted in the last moment of their lives with the fear of being slaughtered by a human. points.body: In todayʼs world, human beings face difficulties in maintaining an objective adjustment with the physical world. As we have not yet been able to build an ideal human society, we will have to first concentrate on providing everyone with the basic requirements of life. summary: The subjective approach is to first withdraw the crude mind gradually from the external world and merge it in the subtle mind, and then to merge the subtle mind in unit consciousness.
In the present world, human beings face such tremendous difficulties in maintaining their objective adjustment that they cannot afford to give any time for their subjective approach.
That is why I would like to advise you to build a healthy human society as early as possible, so that each and every human being gets enough scope and time for spiritual progress.
points.body: The subjective approach is to first withdraw the crude mind gradually from the external world and merge it in the subtle mind, and then to merge the subtle mind in unit consciousness. When unit consciousness is merged in Cosmic Consciousness, a human being is said to have attained the supreme fulfilment in life. In the present world, human beings face such tremendous difficulties in maintaining their objective adjustment that they cannot afford to give any time for their subjective approach. This is the greatest tragedy of the day! That is why I would like to advise you to build a healthy human society as early as possible, so that each and every human being gets enough scope and time for spiritual progress. ( 1 )

points.body: CAKRA: Cycle or circle; psycho-spiritual centre, or plexus. The cakras in the human body are all located along the suśumná canal which passes through the length of the spinal column and extends up to the crown of the head. Some cakras, however, are associated with external concentration points. The concentration points: (1) for the múládhára cakra, the base of the spine, above the perineum; (2) for the svádhiśt́hána, the genital organ; (3) for the mańipura, the navel; (4) for the anáhata, the midpoint of the chest; (5) for the vishuddha, the throat; (6) for the ájiṋá, between the eyebrows; and (7) for the sahasrára, the crown of the head. There are two other cakras which are needed in certain spiritual practices, so the cakras are nine in number.

glossary.def: Cycle or circle; psycho-spiritual centre, or plexus. The cakras in the human body are all located along the suśumná canal which passes through the length of the spinal column and extends up to the crown of the head. Some cakras, however, are associated with external concentration points. The concentration points: (1) for the múládhára cakra, the base of the spine, above the perineum; (2) for the svádhiśt́hána, the genital organ; (3) for the mańipura, the navel; (4) for the anáhata, the midpoint of the chest; (5) for the vishuddha, the throat; (6) for the ájiṋá, between the eyebrows; and (7) for the sahasrára, the crown of the head. There are two other cakras which are needed in certain spiritual practices, so the cakras are nine in number.
